title: 📚 Era 5 Works: The Nineteenth Century
subtitle: Verify publication dates, summaries, characters, storylines & exam traps for 474 works

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Odes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1747 (Sort Year: 1747)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Gray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The database title for Gray's early odes, led by the Eton College ode published in 1747.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database title is only Odes, dated 1747. That year matches the Eton College ode. The Progress of Poesy and The Bard are separate works, printed together in 1757.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A man looking back at the boys of his old school)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This slug is not the 1757 book of two Pindaric odes.
The dated poem is the Eton College ode, published in 1747.
The speaker looks at the schoolboys at play.
He sees the griefs that wait for them in adult life.
He will not warn them, because warning cannot save them.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Fragments of Ancient Poetry

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1760 (Sort Year: 1760)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Macpherson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short pieces he offered as translations of ancient Highland poems about Fingal.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The University of Galway says two editions appeared in 1760. Britannica also dates the book to 1760. The database year is correct. The pieces are prose poems, not a novel. The database genre Fiction does not match the form.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ossian (The supposed ancient bard, son of Fingal); Fingal (The Highland hero whose wars the fragments recall)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book appeared in Edinburgh in 1760, in two editions that year.
Macpherson says he translated the pieces from Gaelic.
Most of them sound like episodes from a longer war story.
That story is an invasion of Ireland and Fingal's voyage to help.
The preface hopes a full heroic poem can still be recovered.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Fingal

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1761 (Sort Year: 1761)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Macpherson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An epic in six books on Fingal's war in Ireland, plus other poems said to be by Ossian.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The University of Galway says copies appeared in December 1761 and again in January 1762. The London title page reads 1762. Britannica often gives 1762. The database year 1761 matches the first issue. Use both dates if a question is precise.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fingal (King of the western Caledonians, the hero of the epic); Ossian (Fingal's son, the bard who narrates); Cuchullin (The Irish champion who holds the field before Fingal lands); Swaran (King of Lochlin, the invader of Ireland)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Swaran, a king from Lochlin, invades Ireland.
Cuchullin guards the young Irish king and fights before help arrives.
Fingal sails from Scotland and drives the invaders out.
Ossian, Fingal's son, is the poet who tells the war.
The same volume also prints many shorter poems, including one called Temora.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Fatal Sisters

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1768 (Sort Year: 1768)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Gray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twelve huge women weave a battle's fate and sing a song of coming slaughter.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poetry Foundation places the poem in Poems by Mr. Gray in 1768, with The Descent of Odin.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Fatal Sisters (Twelve huge women who weave the fate of the slain)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Twelve giant women stand at a loom of fate.
They sing while they weave the deaths of warriors.
The web runs with blood as the battle nears.
Gray drew the vision from an old Norse poem.
He wrote it in 1761, and the book printing came in 1768.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Temora

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1763 (Sort Year: 1763)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Macpherson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An epic in eight books on Fingal's war to restore the Irish royal house.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The University of Galway dates this eight book quarto to March 1763. Britannica also gives 1763. The database year is correct. Do not confuse it with the shorter Temora already printed in the Fingal volume.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fingal (The Scottish king who invades to restore the Irish line); Cairbar (The chief who kills Cormac and seizes the throne); Cathmor (Cairbar's brother, who marches to continue the war); Ossian (The narrator, son of Fingal)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Cairbar murders Cormac, the young king, at the palace of Temora.
Cairbar takes the Irish throne.
Fingal crosses to Ireland to put the royal family back.
Cairbar's brother Cathmor brings another army to the war.
Ossian again tells the fighting, in the voice of an old bard.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1773 (Sort Year: 1773)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anna Laetitia Barbauld

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first book of verse, published under the name Anna Laetitia Aikin.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1773 is correct. Corsica and other poems were written earlier. The author was still Anna Laetitia Aikin. The book went through several editions in that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Mouse (The speaker of The Mouse's Petition, a captive begging release); The speaker of Corsica (A voice that praises the island's love of liberty)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Joseph Johnson printed the book in London in 1773.
The dedication from Warrington is dated 1 December 1772.
The volume holds odes, hymns, songs, and verse letters.
Corsica praises a people fighting for liberty.
The Mouse's Petition begs mercy for a mouse kept for an experiment.

items.title: "Poems, Supposed to Have Been Written at Bristol, by Thomas Rowley" (1777) — Thomas Chatterton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems, Supposed to Have Been Written at Bristol, by Thomas Rowley

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1777 (Sort Year: 1777)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Chatterton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1777 book that first printed most of the Rowley poems, edited by Thomas Tyrwhitt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Thomas Tyrwhitt edited it for Payne and Son in London. Chatterton had been dead since 1770.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Rowley (The supposed 15th century author named on the title page.); Thomas Tyrwhitt (The scholar who edited and published the 1777 book.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Chatterton died in 1770, so he never saw this book.
Thomas Tyrwhitt edited it and published it in London in 1777.
The title page says the poems were supposed to be by Thomas Rowley.
It prints Aella, the Bristowe Tragedy, and the Balade of Charitie.
A 1778 edition added a note arguing that Chatterton wrote them all.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1782 (Sort Year: 1782)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Cowper

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His 1782 volume of long moral satires and shorter pieces.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1782 is right. The Poetry Foundation and the Wikisource preface both start his independent Poems in 1782. The database period tag that points to the nineteenth century does not fit this book. He published it in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Cowper, judging the manners and writing of his age)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After Newton left Olney, Cowper turned back to original poems.
In the early 1780s he wrote eight long moral satires.
They attack luxury, bad writing, and a careless age.
The book Poems by William Cowper appeared in 1782.
Shorter poems sit in the same volume beside the long satires.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Elegiac Sonnets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1784 (Sort Year: 1784)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Smith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A growing book of mournful sonnets that revived the form in English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poetry Foundation dates the writing to 1783. The database wrongly marks this 1784 book as published after her death. She was alive. A later edition after 1800 added more poems. Sources disagree on whether that edition is 1811 or 1812.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A mournful voice that tells private sorrow.); Werther (The sad hero of a Goethe novel, used in a few sonnets.); The Solitary Man (A lone man on a sea cliff in one famous sonnet.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Smith wrote many of these sonnets in 1783, in a debtors' prison with her family.
The first book came out in 1784 with sixteen sonnets and three other poems.
The first title was Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Essays.
Some sonnets translate Petrarch, and others speak as Goethe's sad hero Werther.
The full collection grew to about ninety-two sonnets.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1786 (Sort Year: 1786)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Helen Maria Williams

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A two volume poetry book of 1786, mixing revised early poems with new ones.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1786 is right for this collection. Peru dates from 1784. Older poems were revised, not first written, for the 1786 book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Williams, speaking in her own feeling voice); The daughter in An American Tale (A young woman who searches a battlefield for her father)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Poems was published in two volumes in 1786.
Williams revised older work, including Peru and An Ode on the Peace.
New poems praise sensibility, meaning strong tender feeling.
An American Tale follows a daughter who seeks her wounded father.
The poems speak against war, slavery, and Spanish rule in Peru.
A long subscriber list shows her fame in London society.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Edinburgh edition

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1787 (Sort Year: 1787)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Burns

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The enlarged 1787 Edinburgh printing of his Kilmarnock poems.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1787 is right. It is not a separate Romantic book. Tam o' Shanter is not in this 1787 printing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Burns, now writing for a national Scottish audience)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After Kilmarnock, Burns went to Edinburgh to arrange a new edition.
William Creech published it at Edinburgh in 1787.
It keeps most of the Kilmarnock poems and adds some new ones.
To a Haggis is one poem readers meet in this Edinburgh book.
The success made him a national name, not only a local one.

items.title: "Letters Written in France" (1790) — Helen Maria Williams

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Letters Written in France

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1790 (Sort Year: 1790)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Helen Maria Williams

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eyewitness letters from Revolutionary France, begun in 1790 and continued to 1796.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first volume came out in 1790. Eight volumes were published by 1796.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Helen Maria Williams (The letter writer, an English visitor who supports the Revolution); The friend in England (The person who receives the letters); Monsieur du F and Madame du F (A French couple whose story is told inside the 1790 letters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The first letters describe the summer of 1790 in France.
Williams writes to a friend in England about the Revolution.
She visits the festival built on the ruins of the Bastille.
She also tells the story of Monsieur du F and his wife.
She shares the crowd's hope and repeats Vive la Nation.
Further volumes followed, and the series reached eight by 1796.

items.title: "An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice" (1793) — William Godwin

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1793 (Sort Year: 1793)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Godwin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long argument that reason can replace oppressive government.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1793 is right, but the genre label drama is wrong. It was published on 14 February 1793. Revised editions followed in 1796 and 1798.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Godwin (The author, setting out a system of morals and politics)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Godwin says institutions such as monarchy and harsh law corrupt people.
He thinks humans can improve if reason is free to work.
As public opinion grows wiser, government should fade.
He rejects violent revolution and asks for enquiry and discussion.
The book cost over a pound, so Pitt said the poor would not buy it.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Emigrants

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1793 (Sort Year: 1793)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Smith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem in unrhymed lines about French refugees and war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1793 is correct. The database wrongly marks this poem as published after her death. Smith died in 1806. This is a poem. The database genre label Fiction is a catalog error.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (The poet's voice, full of sorrow about war.); The Emigrants (French people who fled violence at home.); Liberty (A calm figure in the poem who refuses to join the killing.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Smith published this poem in 1793, while she was still alive.
It is written in two books of blank verse (unrhymed lines with ten syllables).
She dedicated it to William Cowper, author of the poem The Task.
The poem shows French refugees after the Revolution turned into terror and war.
The speaker looks at English hills, but sorrow blocks the joy.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Doll's House

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1879 (Sort Year: 1879)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henrik Ibsen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wife discovers she has been a doll in her marriage and leaves home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Oslo and Britannica date the play 1879. It was first staged that year at the Royal Theatre in Copenhagen.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nora Helmer (The wife who leaves to become a free person); Torvald Helmer (A bank manager who treats Nora like a child); Krogstad (The man who threatens to expose Nora's forgery); Mrs. Linde (Nora's old friend, who tries to mend the secret); Dr. Rank (A sick family friend who loves Nora)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Doll's House is a three act play in prose published and premiered in1879.
The play is significant for its critical attitude towards 19th century marriage norms.
It aroused great controversy at the time, as it concludes with the protagonist Nora leaving her husband and children because she wants to discover herself.
Ibsen was inspired by the belief that "A woman cannot be herself in modern society"
Torvald uses the nickname "Peaches" for Nora.
Nora Helmer seems a happy and playful wife.
She once forged a signature to borrow money and save Torvald.
Krogstad threatens to reveal the forgery.
Torvald learns the secret and thinks first of his reputation.
Nora sees that she has lived as a doll, not as a person.
She leaves her husband and children, and the door slams.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Anna Karenina

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1878 (Sort Year: 1878)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Leo Tolstoy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Anna leaves her husband for Vronsky, while Levin finds a hard but real marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Installments ran from 1875 to 1877. Britannica gives those serial years. Project Gutenberg dates the first book edition to 1878. The family sentence is the wording quoted by Britannica.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anna Karenina (A married woman whose affair leads her to suicide); Aleksey Karenin (Anna's cold husband, anxious about public shame); Count Vronsky (The officer who becomes Anna's lover); Konstantin Levin (A landowner whose marriage to Kitty contrasts with Anna's fate); Kitty (The young woman who refuses Vronsky and marries Levin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a realist novel by Tolstoy, published in book form in 1878.
It is regarded as a pinnacle in realist fiction.
Various authors commented differently about it as:.
Fyodor Dostoyevsky declared it "Flawless as a work of art"
Vladimir Nabokov admired it as "The flawless magic of Tolstoy's style".
William Faulkner described it as "the best ever written".
Anna Karenina is the tragic story of a married aristocrat Princess Anna Karenina and her affair with the affluent Count Vronsky.
Vronsky, a bachelor is eager to marry Anna, if she will agree to leave her husband Karenin.
There is another parallel story in the novel in which Konstantin Levin wanted to marry Kitty, sister of Dolly.
The novel is divided into eight parts with epigraph "Vengeance is mine, I will repay".
The novel opens with the world famous quote: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way".
In the novel Levin and Kitty marries and start their life on his country estate.
Anna commits suicide as she thinks that her relationship with Vronsky is over by throwing herself under the carriage of a passing train.
It is the jumbled trivia of day-to-day life and believes in social progress and scientific advancement.
It has insistent quest for meaning.
The main reason of unhappiness in Oblonsky's house was the husband's affair with a French governess.
Anna, wife of Karenin, meets the officer Vronsky and begins an affair.
She bears Vronsky's child and leaves her husband and son.
Society shuts her out, and her jealousy of Vronsky grows.
In despair she throws herself under a train.
Beside this tragedy, Levin and Kitty marry and build a working life.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Billy Budd

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1924 (Sort Year: 1924)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herman Melville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished sea story, published in 1924, about innocence, envy, and military law.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Berkshire Historical Society dates the writing to 1888-1889. Melville left the story unfinished at his death in 1891. The Poetry Foundation and the Berkshire list date the first publication to 1924.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Billy Budd (A handsome, innocent sailor who cannot speak in his own defence); John Claggart (The master-at-arms who envies Billy and accuses him); Captain Edward Vere (The captain who condemns Billy under the law of the navy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Billy Budd is a young sailor forced onto a warship.
He is innocent and popular, but he stammers when upset.
Master-at-arms Claggart falsely accuses him of mutiny.
Billy strikes Claggart and kills him with one blow.
Captain Vere loves Billy but condemns him under navy law.
Billy is hanged, and his last words bless Captain Vere.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Civil Disobedience

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1849 (Sort Year: 1849)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry David Thoreau

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay arguing that conscience can require a person to disobey an unjust government.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He lectured in 1848. Poetry Foundation and the Digital Thoreau project date the print essay to 1849, under the title Resistance to Civil Government. The title Civil Disobedience was used in 1866, after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Henry David Thoreau (The speaker, a citizen who refuses an unjust tax)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Thoreau refuses to pay a poll tax.
He will not fund slavery or the war against Mexico.
The state jails him for one night.
He argues that conscience stands above an unjust law.
A just person may have to go to prison.
The 1849 title was Resistance to Civil Government.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Crime and Punishment

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Fyodor Dostoevsky

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor student murders a pawnbroker and is broken by guilt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Serialised in 1866 in the journal The Russian Messenger. The book edition followed in 1867. Britannica and Project Gutenberg both give 1866 as the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rodion Raskolnikov (The poor student who murders and then cannot bear his theory); Sonya Marmeladova (A young woman forced into prostitution, who stands for Christian goodness); Porfiry Petrovich (The investigator who hunts Raskolnikov by talk, not by force); Svidrigailov (A vicious man who overhears the confession and later kills himself)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Raskolnikov, a former student, lives in poverty in St. Petersburg.
He kills the pawnbroker Alyona and, by chance, her half sister Lizaveta.
He tells himself that extraordinary men may break the moral law.
The investigator Porfiry presses him, and Sonya urges confession.
He confesses, goes to Siberia, and begins to repent.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Essays

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1841 (Sort Year: 1841)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ralph Waldo Emerson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1841 essay book that holds Self-Reliance, History, and The Over-Soul.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Essays, First Series, was published in 1841 and includes Self-Reliance, Circles, History, and The Over-Soul. Essays: Second Series followed in 1844 and includes Experience.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph Waldo Emerson (The lecturer and essayist addressing a single reader)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
a. Self-Reliance b. Compensation c. Circles d. The Over Soul.
a. The Poet b. Experience c. Politics d. Gifts e. Manners f. Characters g. Nature 3. Nature, Addresses and lectures (1849)
The First Series appeared in 1841 and made Emerson famous abroad.
Self-Reliance tells the reader to trust an inner conviction.
History treats the past as a story each mind can relive.
The Over-Soul describes one spirit shared by all persons.
A Second Series in 1844 adds Experience and other later essays.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Eugene Onegin

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1825 (Sort Year: 1825)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alexander Pushkin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel in verse about a bored nobleman and the woman he first rejects.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Pushkin began the poem in May 1823. Chapters appeared from 1825 to 1832. The first complete book was 1833, with revisions in 1837. 1794 is not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Eugene Onegin (A bored, skeptical nobleman, a type called the superfluous man); Tatyana Larina (A sincere country girl who later becomes a married princess); Vladimir Lensky (A romantic poet, Onegin's friend, killed in their duel); Olga Larina (Tatyana's lively sister, loved by Lensky)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Eugene Onegin, a bored city dandy, inherits a country estate.
He befriends the poet Lensky, who loves Olga Larina.
Olga's sister Tatyana loves Onegin and writes him a letter.
Onegin refuses her, then flirts with Olga at a name-day ball.
Lensky challenges him, and Onegin kills Lensky in a duel.
Years later Tatyana, now a princess, refuses Onegin in turn.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Faust

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1808 (Sort Year: 1808)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A scholar wagers with the devil, ruins Gretchen, and is saved at last.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Early drafts, called the Urfaust, belong to about 1772-1775. A fragment appeared in 1790. Part I was published in 1808. Goethe finished Part II in 1831, and it was published in 1832, after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Faust (A scholar who wants all human experience); Mephistopheles (The devil who serves Faust and tries to win the wager); Gretchen (The young woman Faust loves in Part I, also called Margarete); Helen of Troy (The ancient beauty Faust seeks in Part II)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faust despairs of study and calls on magic.
Mephistopheles bets that he can satisfy Faust's endless desire.
Faust loves Gretchen, and the affair destroys her family and her life.
In Part II he seeks power, beauty, and Helen of Troy.
He dies still trying to do more, and heavenly love saves his soul.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Germinal

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Emile Zola

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A coal miners' strike in northern France ends in violence, then a hint of new growth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period label, not the novel's year. Zola wrote it from April 1884 to January 1885. It ran in Gil Blas from November 1884 to February 1885. Charpentier issued the book in March 1885. Britannica dates Germinal to 1885.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Etienne Lantier (An unemployed mechanic who helps lead the strike); Maheude (The miner's wife who holds a hungry family together); Catherine Maheu (A young hauler in the mine, loved by Etienne); Bonnemort (The old grandfather, worn out by a life in the pits); Souvarine (An anarchist engineman who wants the mine destroyed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Etienne Lantier arrives at the Montsou pits and takes work underground.
He lives with the Maheu family and learns their hunger and danger.
The miners strike, and the protest turns violent.
Soldiers fire on the crowd, and the pit called Le Voreux collapses.
Etienne leaves, but the last pages show new life stirring under the fields.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hedda Gabler

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henrik Ibsen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A bored general's daughter destroys a rival's hope and then kills herself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Oslo says he wrote and published it in 1890. The first performance was at the Residenztheater in Munich on 31 January 1891. Britannica says it was published in 1890 and produced the next year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hedda Gabler (A proud, bored wife who wants control over another's fate); Jorgen Tesman (Hedda's scholarly husband); Eilert Lovborg (A brilliant writer whom Hedda pushes toward ruin); Thea Elvsted (The woman who helps Lovborg write his book); Judge Brack (A cynical judge who tries to trap Hedda)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hedda Gabler comes home from a honeymoon already bored.
Her husband, Jorgen Tesman, is a dull scholar.
Judge Brack wants a hold over Hedda.
Thea Elvsted has left home to help the writer Eilert Lovborg.
Hedda burns Lovborg's manuscript and gives him a pistol.
Lovborg dies, Brack threatens Hedda, and she shoots herself.

items.title: "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" (1861) — Harriet Jacobs

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Harriet Jacobs

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jacobs's own story, published as Linda Brent, of slavery, hiding, and a mother's escape.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The UNC title page says Boston, published for the author, 1861. A legal record was entered in 1860 by L. Maria Child. Britannica also dates the book to 1861. She had escaped north in 1842. The exact year she began writing is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Linda Brent (The narrator, the pen name of Harriet Jacobs); Dr. Flint (The enslaver in the book, who pursues Linda); Linda's grandmother (The elder who shelters the family and keeps a home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator, Linda Brent, is taught to read while enslaved in North Carolina.
Her enslaver, called Dr. Flint, harasses her and tries to control her.
She has two children and then hides to protect them from him.
She spends nearly seven years in a tiny garret, watching her children in secret.
She escapes north, and she asks free women to see what slavery does to women.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Madame Bovary

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1857 (Sort Year: 1857)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Gustave Flaubert

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Emma Bovary's borrowed dreams of passion destroy her dull country marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The queue span 1794-1900 is a period label. His life years are 1821 and 1880. He wrote the novel from 1851 to 1856. The Revue de Paris printed it from 1 October to 15 December 1856. He was acquitted on 7 February 1857. Michel Levy published the book in April 1857.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Emma Bovary (A farmer's daughter whose romantic dreams wreck her life); Charles Bovary (Emma's kind, limited husband, a country doctor); Rodolphe Boulanger (A local landowner and Emma's first lover); Leon Dupuis (A clerk who becomes Emma's second lover); Homais (The boastful pharmacist who worships progress and public praise); Lheureux (A moneylender who traps Emma in debt)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
3- Sentimental Education 4- Dictionary of Received Ideas Madame Bovary (1857)
It is the debut of the novel of Flaubert.
The novel focuses on a doctor's wife Emma Bovary who has adulterous affairs and lives beyond her means in order to escape the banalities and emptiness of provincial life.
Public prosecutors attacked the novel for obscenity. On the ground of avert sexuality the novel was banned in 1857 (in the year of publication).
The work is regarded as a seminal work of literary realism.
British critic James Wood writes: "Flaubert established, for good or ill, what most readers think of as a modern realist narration and his influence is almost too familiar to be visible". Flaubert's unconventional views of marriage, love and sexuality were considered an affront to public morals and church, and the book was banned". Main Characters: 1- Emma Bovary: She is the protagonist of the novel. She has highly romanticized view of the world and craves beauty, wealth, passion as well as high society.
The disparity between the romantic ideals and the realities of her country life that drive most of the novel, leading her into two affairs and to accrue an insurmountable amount of debt that eventually leads her to suicide. The first affair of Emma was with Leon Dupuis. She commits suicide by injecting arsenic. Her second affair was with Rodolphe Boulanger. 2- Charles Bovary: He is Emma's husband, who is a very simple and common man. He is a doctor by profession but not very good at it. He never suspects her affairs and gives her complete control over his finances, thereby securing his own ruin. Unable to tolerate the loss of his dear wife, Charles sinks into depression and dies.
He fails to detect the extra marital affairs of his wife Emma with Rodolphe and Leon.
When Emma begins to run up debts, he grants her power of attorney over all his properties, an act that leads to his financial ruin.
He came to know the infidelities of his wife by her love letters only after her suicide; and dies of broken heart. 3- Rodolphe Boulanger: He is Emma's second lover, a wealthy landowner. He plots his seduction of Emma with strategic precision, begins an affair with her and then abandons her when he becomes bored of her romantic fancies and emotional demands. 4- Other Minor Characters: Leon, Monsieur Homais, Monsieur Lheureux, Abbe Baunisien, Hyppolyte, Berthe, Binet. etc.
Charles Bovary, a dull country doctor, marries Emma Rouault.
Emma wants the passion she has met in romantic novels.
She is bored by her small Norman town and by Charles.
She takes lovers, first Rodolphe and later Leon.
The shopkeeper Lheureux feeds her debts until the lies collapse.
Emma poisons herself.
Charles dies soon after, still loving her.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Nature

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1836 (Sort Year: 1836)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ralph Waldo Emerson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short book that sets out Emerson's idea of spirit in nature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published anonymously in Boston in 1836. Britannica and the Stanford Encyclopedia both give 1836.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph Waldo Emerson (The essayist speaking as a single observing self)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Emerson published this little book anonymously in Boston in 1836.
He says nature serves man with commodity, beauty, language, and discipline.
In the woods, the self feels joined to a universal spirit.
He argues that intuition can pass beyond the material world.
The book gathered the group later called the Transcendentalists.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1827 (Sort Year: 1827)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Derozio's first poetry book, printed in Calcutta in 1827, when he was 18.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is the period, not the book. Poems was published at Calcutta in 1827. The Harp of India is dated March 1827 inside the volume.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Derozio, a young man asking to sing for India); The harp of India (A silent harp that stands for India's lost poetry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Poems was printed for the author at the Baptist Mission Press in 1827.
The preface says he was eighteen and wrote in hours saved from work.
The Harp of India opens the book and mourns a silent national song.
The speaker asks to wake that harp and sing for his country.
Other poems treat slavery, Greece, love, and Indian scenes.
The book made him known to readers in Calcutta.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Brothers Karamazov

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Fyodor Dostoevsky

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His last novel, about a father, three sons, faith, and a murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First published as Bratya Karamazovy in serial parts in 1879 and 1880. Britannica and Project Gutenberg agree on 1879-1880. It is his last novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov (The sensual father who is murdered); Dmitry Karamazov (The eldest son, accused of the killing); Ivan Karamazov (The intellectual son who tells the Grand Inquisitor legend); Alyosha Karamazov (The youngest son, a novice under Father Zosima); Father Zosima (The monk who teaches love as the path to harmony)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The coarse father, Fyodor Karamazov, quarrels with his sons over money and love.
Dmitry is passionate, Ivan is the doubter, and Alyosha is a gentle novice.
Ivan tells the story called The Legend of the Grand Inquisitor.
The elder Zosima answers that harmony comes through the heart, not the mind.
The father is murdered.
Dmitry is accused.
The book searches for faith.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Cherry Orchard

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1904 (Sort Year: 1904)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anton Chekhov

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old estate is sold, and the cherry orchard is cut down.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Bibliotheque nationale de France dates the writing from 1901 to 26 September 1903. The Moscow Art Theatre opened the play on 17 January 1904, by the old Russian calendar. It was published in 1904. Britannica also gives the January 1904 first night.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lyubov Ranevskaya (The owner who loves the orchard and cannot manage money); Leonid Gaev (Her brother, full of fine talk and no practical plan); Yermolai Lopakhin (A merchant, son of a serf, who buys the estate); Anya (Ranevskaya's daughter, ready to greet a new life); Pyotr Trofimov (A student who says the orchard stands for all Russia); Firs (The old servant forgotten in the locked house)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Madame Ranevskaya returns from Paris to an estate deep in debt.
Lopakhin urges the family to cut the orchard into building plots.
They delay, talk, and cannot face the loss of the old life.
Lopakhin buys the estate at auction.
The family leaves, axes sound in the orchard, and Firs is locked inside.

items.title: "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839) — Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Fall of the House of Usher

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1839 (Sort Year: 1839)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A visitor watches Roderick Usher, his dying sister, and their house collapse together.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First printed in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine in September 1839.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (Roderick's boyhood friend and the teller of the tale); Roderick Usher (The last male of the family, sick with extreme sensitivity); Madeline Usher (Roderick's twin sister, buried and then returning)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator rides to the gloomy House of Usher.
Roderick Usher is ill with fear, and his twin Madeline is dying.
They place Madeline in a vault under the house.
She returns during a storm, and Roderick dies of terror.
The narrator flees as the house splits and sinks into the tarn.

items.title: "The Literature of Bengal" (1877) — Romesh Chunder Dutt

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Literature of Bengal

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1877 (Sort Year: 1877)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Romesh Chunder Dutt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical history of Bengali literature, first published under a pen name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Dutt was born in 1848, so that year is impossible. The first edition appeared at Calcutta in 1877 under the pen name Ar Cy Dae. The 1895 edition used his own name. Pennsylvania and Toronto both list that 1895 book.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is a prose history of writers, not a poem.
The 1877 Calcutta book used the pen name Ar Cy Dae.
It gives lives of writers and a judgment of Bengali literature.
It moves from early poets toward his own century.
In 1895 the book was printed again under his own name.
The database label poetry is wrong for this work.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Raven

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1845 (Sort Year: 1845)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A grieving man questions a raven about his lost love and hears only Nevermore.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It first appeared in the New York Evening Mirror on 29 January 1845, from advance sheets of the American Review.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A student grieving for Lenore); The raven (A bird whose only word is Nevermore); Lenore (The dead beloved, named but never seen)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
At midnight a speaker mourns the lost Lenore.
A raven taps and then perches above his door.
The bird sits on a bust of Pallas, the goddess of wisdom.
Every question about Lenore gets one answer, Nevermore.
The raven will not leave, and the speaker's hope dies.

items.title: "The Red Badge of Courage" (1895) — Stephen Crane

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Red Badge of Courage

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Stephen Crane

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young Union soldier runs from battle, then returns and carries the flag.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A cut version was serialized in newspapers in December 1894. D. Appleton published the book in October 1895. The database said only a period span. Use 1895 for the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Henry Fleming (The young private whose fear and return are the whole story); Jim Conklin (A tall soldier, Henry's friend, who dies of his wounds); Wilson (The loud young soldier who later becomes steady in battle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Henry Fleming, a farm boy, joins the Union army and dreams of glory.
In his first fight he is terrified and flees into the woods.
Shame burns him.
He wants a wound, a red badge of courage.
He meets the dying Jim Conklin and wanders back toward the lines.
In the next battle he carries the flag and fights without the old panic.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Seagull

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1897 (Sort Year: 1897)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anton Chekhov

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young writer loves an aspiring actress, and both are hurt by older artists.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica says the play was performed in 1896 and published in 1897 as Chayka. The St. Petersburg premiere had a poor reception. The Moscow Art Theatre opened its production on 17 December 1898, and that staging made the play famous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Konstantin Treplev (A young writer who wants a new kind of theatre); Nina Zarechnaya (A young woman who becomes an actress and survives by her art); Irina Arkadina (Konstantin's famous mother, jealous of youth and of Nina); Boris Trigorin (A successful writer, Arkadina's lover, who fascinates Nina)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Konstantin stages a new play by a lake for his actress mother.
Arkadina mocks it, and Nina is drawn to the famous writer Trigorin.
Konstantin kills a seagull and lays it at Nina's feet.
Two years later Nina returns, worn by work, loss, and Trigorin.
She leaves to act, and Konstantin shoots himself offstage.

items.title: "The Song of Hiawatha" (1855) — Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Song of Hiawatha

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1855 story poem about the Ojibwa hero Hiawatha, his deeds, and his departure.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period, not the book. Britannica, Poetry Foundation, and Project Gutenberg date publication to 1855. The Gutenberg note says he began it on 25 June 1854 and finished it on 29 March 1855.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hiawatha (An Ojibwa hero, son of the West Wind, who leads his people); Nokomis (His grandmother, who raises him); Minnehaha (His wife, from the land of the Dacotahs); Mudjekeewis (The West Wind, Hiawatha's father)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ticknor and Fields published the poem in 1855.
Longfellow took legends from Henry Rowe Schoolcraft's books.
He used the unrhymed beat of the Finnish Kalevala, a folk epic.
Hiawatha, raised by Nokomis, does great feats for his people.
He marries Minnehaha, who later dies in a time of famine.
He leaves his people and goes toward the Isles of the Blessed.

items.title: "The Sorrows of Young Werther" (1774) — Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Sorrows of Young Werther

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1774 (Sort Year: 1774)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young man loves Charlotte, cannot have her, and kills himself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in German in 1774 as Die Leiden des jungen Werthers. The database gives only a period span, not this year. The quoted line is from the R. D. Boylan translation on Project Gutenberg.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Werther (A sensitive young artist who loves without hope); Charlotte (Lotte) (The woman Werther loves, engaged and then married to Albert); Albert (Charlotte's steady fiance and later her husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Werther writes letters to a friend about his new country life.
He falls in love with Charlotte, who is bound to Albert.
He leaves, but he cannot cure his hopeless love.
He returns, grows more isolated, and borrows Albert's pistols.
He shoots himself, and the novel ends with his burial.

items.title: "The Travels of Dean Mahomet" (1794) — Sake Dean Mahomed

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Travels of Dean Mahomet

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1794 (Sort Year: 1794)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sake Dean Mahomed

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Letters about his Indian army years, published in Ireland in 1794.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1794 is correct. Connor printed two volumes at Cork. The University of California Press edition reprints that 1794 text. The database calls the author a poet and the book fiction. It is a travel memoir in letters.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dean Mahomet (The writer and the traveler who speaks in the letters.); Captain Baker (The officer he followed from India to Ireland.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is a set of letters to a friend.
Dean Mahomet says he was born in Patna in 1759.
In 1769 he joined the Company camp as a boy.
He served until 1784, then sailed to Britain with an officer.
In Ireland he married Jane Daly.
Connor printed the book at Cork in 1794.
It is often called the first book in English by an Indian.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Walden

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1854 (Sort Year: 1854)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry David Thoreau

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book about two years of simple living at Walden Pond, shaped as one year of seasons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He lived at the pond from 1845 to 1847 and began the book there. Britannica and the Poetry Foundation date publication to 1854. It was the second and last book he published in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Henry David Thoreau (The narrator of his own experiment in simple living)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Walden or Life in the Woods by transcendentalist Thoreau is a reflection upon simple living in natural surroundings.
The book compresses the time into a single calendar year and uses passage of four seasons to symbolize human development.
It is a part memoir and part spiritual quest , It opens with the announcement that Thoreau spent two years at Walden Pond living a simple life without a support of any kind. This land was purchased by Thoreau's mentor R. W. Emerson.
'Economy' is the first chapter of this work.
John Updike compared Walden with Bible.
Skinner wrote Walden - 2.
When Henry David Thoreau was being criticized for his publications then George Eliot came with her review in support of Thoreau. Important Quote- "The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation".
Thoreau builds a cabin at Walden Pond in 1845.
He lives there for about two years.
He grows food, watches the seasons, and keeps accounts.
He attacks hurry, debt, and empty comfort.
The book turns those two years into one symbolic year.
He leaves the pond when the experiment has taught him enough.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: War and Peace

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1869 (Sort Year: 1869)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Leo Tolstoy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Russian families live through the Napoleonic wars and the invasion of 1812.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Serialization in Russkiy Vestnik began in 1865, at first under the title 1805. Britannica says Tolstoy worked on the book for six years. The complete volumes appeared in 1869. Project Gutenberg also dates the book to 1869. It is a novel, not a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pierre Bezukhov (An awkward heir who searches for faith and a good life); Andrey Bolkonsky (A proud officer who turns from glory toward private duty); Natasha Rostov (A lively young woman whose love and mistakes drive the family plot); Napoleon (The French emperor, shown as less powerful than he believes); Kutuzov (The patient Russian general who waits out the invasion)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story opens in St. Petersburg in 1805, as war with Napoleon nears.
Andrey seeks glory, is wounded at Austerlitz, and later loves Natasha.
Pierre inherits wealth, makes a bad marriage, and searches for a true life.
In 1812 Napoleon invades Russia, and Moscow is abandoned and burned.
Pierre suffers as a prisoner, Andrey dies, and Pierre later marries Natasha.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Joan of Arc

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1796 (Sort Year: 1796)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Southey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long epic that treats Joan as a hero of the people against tyranny.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates publication to 1796. The Poetry Foundation records Joan of Arc (1796; revised, 1798). The exact year he began the poem is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Joan of Arc (The peasant girl who leads France and dies for her mission); The Dauphin (The French prince whom Joan supports against the English)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an epic poem by Robert Southy.
Coleridge also helped him writing this poem of 1798 edition but in later editions Coleridge's collections was deleted.
The poem is divided into two-halves.
First describing Joan's quest to meet Charles, the Dauphin of France. Finally, she got the Dauphin support and begins to lead the French military.
The secondary half describes the French defeat of the British army at 'Orleans'.
The poem ends with Charles crowned as King of France.
The young Joan hears a call to save France.
She leaves home and wins the trust of the French prince.
She leads armies and lifts the siege of Orleans.
The poem honors her courage and attacks cruel kings and priests.
Her capture and death close the epic.

items.title: "The Heir at Law" (1797) — George Colman the Younger

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Heir at Law

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1797 (Sort Year: 1797)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Colman the Younger

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comedy in five acts about a tradesman wrongly told he is a lord.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1797 is the first night, not a proved print year. The play opened at the Little Theatre in the Haymarket on 15 July 1797. John Fawcett played Doctor Pangloss. A separate year of first printing was not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daniel Dowlas (A tradesman briefly known as Lord Duberly); Doctor Pangloss (A pompous tutor hired to polish the new lord's family); Dick Dowlas (Daniel's son, in love with Cicely Homespun); Cicely Homespun (A country girl whom Dick loves); Caroline Dormer (The woman loved by the true heir)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Daniel Dowlas, a merchant, is raised to the title Lord Duberly.
He hires Doctor Pangloss, a greedy tutor who loves quotations.
Pangloss calls himself LL.D. and A.S.S. and tags each quote with a great name.
The true heir returns, and Dowlas gives up the estate.
The true heir marries Caroline Dormer, and Dick Dowlas marries Cicely Homespun.
Pangloss loses the rich yearly pay he had been promised.

items.title: "A Defence of Poetry" (1840) — Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Defence of Poetry

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1840 (Sort Year: 1840)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose essay that calls poets the makers of human values.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written in February and March 1821. Mary Shelley first published it in 1840. The database posthumous flag is false, but the essay appeared after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley (The essayist answering an attack on poetry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Thomas Love Peacock had mocked modern poetry in The Four Ages of Poetry.
Shelley answers that poetry wakes the moral imagination (the mind that feels for others).
He says reason analyses, while poetry creates the forms of a better life.
A great people, he argues, is led by its poets.
He ends by calling poets the unacknowledged legislators of the world.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Series of Plays

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1798 (Sort Year: 1798)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Joanna Baillie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1798 first volume of plays that trace one strong passion in a tragedy and a comedy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1798 is correct for the first edition, printed for Cadell and Davies. The volume was first anonymous. De Monfort was later acted at Drury Lane by John Kemble and Sarah Siddons. Do not date the whole book to that staging.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Count Basil (A soldier whose love for Victoria ruins his honour); Victoria (The woman Basil loves in Mantua); De Monfort (A proud man destroyed by hatred of Rezenvelt); Jane De Monfort (His sister, a calm and strong woman); Rezenvelt (The rival De Monfort cannot forgive)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The 1798 book is the first volume of her plays on the passions.
Each strong feeling is shown in one tragedy and one comedy.
Count Basil shows love pulling a soldier away from duty.
De Monfort shows hatred between two old rivals.
An opening essay asks readers to watch how a passion grows.

items.title: "Childe Harold's Pilgrimage" (1812-1818) — George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A traveling noble broods on war, ruins, and his own restless sorrow.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.value: Childe Harold (A weary young noble whose travels carry the poem); The Narrator (A voice close to Byron that reflects on history and the self)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A weary young noble leaves England to wander abroad.
Cantos I and II follow him through Portugal, Spain, Albania, and Greece.
He broods on war, ruined glory, and his own sadness.
Canto III moves through Waterloo and the Swiss mountains.
Canto IV travels through Italy and ends at the ocean.
Harold is the first great Byronic hero (a proud, gloomy outsider).

He falls in love with Queen Charoba, the ruler he came to fight.
Her nurse Dalica pretends to help, then poisons Gebir.
His brother Tamar, a shepherd, loves a sea nymph.
The poem closes on Gebir's death and on Tamar's new life.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
2. Lines Composed A Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey 3. Lyrical Ballads along with Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800) 4. Lucy Grey (Lucy Poems) or Solitude a. It is a collection of 5 poems. 5. Poems in Two Volumes (1802). 6. "The World Is Too Much with Us" is a sonnet by Wordsworth. In it, he criticises the world of the First Industrial Revolution for being absorbed in materialism and distancing itself from nature. Composed in 1802, the poem was first published in Poems, in Two Volumes(1807). Like most Italian sonnets, its 14 lines are written in iambic pentameter. 7. I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, also called Daffodils (1807, Poem in 2 vols). 8. Ode: Intimation of Immortality 9. The Solitary Reaper (1804, Poems in 2 Vols) a. "The world is too much with us"
(1798 & 1800)
It contains total 23 poems, 19 by Wordsworth & 4 by Coleridge.
Lyrical Ballad, with a few other poems is a collection of poems by Wordsworth and Coleridge published in 1798.
Most of the poems of Lyrical Ballads were written by Wordsworth while Coleridge contributed only 5 including "Rime of the Ancient Mariner" (Qty - 4 in the first edition and one in the second.)
The second edition appeared in 1800 along with Preface to Lyrical Ballads in two volumes.
Another edition was published in 1802.
Wordsworth added an Appendix titled "Poetic Diction" in which he expanded the ideas set forth in 'the Preface' in edition of 1802.
French revolution had a greater influence on Lyrical Ballads.
The poem "The Convict" (by Wordsworth) was there in 1798 edition but was omitted in 1800 edition and added Love (by Coleridge).
In the Preface, Wordsworth claims that "the rigid aesthetics of Neo-classical poetry are arbitrary and distort the freedom and naturalness of poetic expression".
The 1798 edition has a short "Advertisement" as an introduction to ascertain how far the language of conversation in the middle and lower class of society is adapted for the purpose of poetic pleasure.
In Lyrical Ballads Wordsworth said "Poetry is the breath and a finer spirit of all knowledge".
The Preface is also called Manifesto of Romantism. Works Contributed by Coleridge in Lyrical Ballads.
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.
It remained in all four editions of Lyrical Ballads i.e. 1798, 1800, 1802 and 1805.
The Foster Mother Tale.
It is a dramatic fragment from Coleridge's 1797 play 'Osorio' called Foster-Mother Tale.
The Nightingle.
It is included in 1798 edition.
The Dungeon.
Love.
It was added in 1800 edition, and "The Convict" by Wordsworth was omitted.
'Michael', 'Ruth' and 'The Brothers' are the poems that appeared in the 1800 edition of Lyrical Ballads.
In this work Wordsworth gave his famous definition of poetry "Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerfull feelings; it takes it's origin from emotion recollected in tranquility".
Wordsworth stated the purpose in publishing 'The Lyrical Ballads' in his preface as "To choose incidents from common life and to relate or describe them thoughout as far as possible in a selection of language really used by men."
i) "Nature Never did betray a. The heart that loved her". ii) "Rest and be thankful". iii) "Come grow old with me. The best is yet to be". iv) "Bliss it was in that Dawn to be alive a. but to be young was very heaven".
It is an essay composed by Wordsworth published in second edition in Jan 1801 (often called 1800 edition) of Lyrical Ballads.
The essay's opening lines: "The first volume of these poems has already been submitted to general persual. It was published as an experiment, which I hoped might be of some use to ascertain, how far, by fitting to metrical arrangement a selection of the real language of men in a state of a vivid sensation, that short of pleasure and that quantity of pleasure may be imparted which a poet may rationally endeavour to impart."
The preface was written to explain the theory of poetry guiding Wordsworth's composition of the poems.
Wordsworth defends the unusual style and subjects of the poems as experiments to see how far popular poetry could be used to convey profound feeling.
Here Wordsworth defines his aesthetic as "I have therefore altogether declined to enter regularly upon this defence."
In preface he discusses his ideas of what the poet is?, what the poetry is?, and most importantly what the language of poetry is?.
Wordsworth first implies that 'a poet is one who arranges language expressing ideas in metrical form. This language he arranges is in a state of vivid sensation'.
Wordsworth also tells about What a poet is not. He says that anti-poets think that "they become honoured poets this way but really only 'furnish food' for poor taste that has no solid bearings and is 'fickle'".
Regarding poetry, Wordsworth implies that poetry is in part a matter of what is customary. Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerfull feelings, it takes its origin from emotion recollected into tranquility.
According to Wordsworth - Poetic language is the language of common people speaking everyday expressions and expressing everyday sensations of rural people in an idealised rural life.
Wordsworth and Coleridge planned the volume during walks in Somerset.
The book contained twenty-three poems and appeared anonymously in 1798.
Coleridge contributed four poems, including The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere.
Wordsworth contributed nineteen poems, ending with Tintern Abbey.
Wordsworth added a famous prose Preface to the two-volume second edition in 1800, and expanded it in 1802.

Maria wakes in a private asylum where her husband George has confined her.
The attendant Jemima learns she is sane and brings her books.
Maria falls in love with another inmate, Henry Darnford, through notes in books.
Jemima and Maria each tell a life of abuse, poverty, and a bad marriage.
The manuscript breaks off, and Godwin printed several possible endings.

Godwin reread her books and letters, then wrote this life in about four months.

He tells of her affairs, her child with Imlay, and her suicide attempts.
Many readers were shocked, and a second edition followed in August 1798.

items.title: "Ode to the West Wind" (1820) — Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: Work Title

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An ode in which the poet asks the autumn wind to scatter his words.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written near Florence in 1819. First printed in 1820 in the Prometheus Unbound volume, with Ode to Liberty, The Cloud, and To a Skylark.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (The poet praying to the wind in a time of need); The West Wind (A wild spirit that destroys and also prepares new life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It was written in 1819 but published with the volume of Prometheus Unbound in 1820.
It is written in Terza Rima (consisting a stanza of three lines) aba bcb cdc.
He wrote a note about this poem "This poem was conceived and chiefly written in a wood that skirts Arno near Florence and on a day when that tempestuous wind whose temperature is at once mild and animating was collecting the vapours, which pour down the autumn al rains".
The poem is addressed to the west wind.
The poet appeals to the west wind to infuse him with a new spirit and a new power to spread his ideas.
The west wind is personified both as 'a preserver' and 'a destroyer'.
The speaker describes the effect of west wind on land, air and water.
The speaker wants to be like wind's lyre and implores the wind to blow his thoughts over the universe so that they might become seeds to cause a new birth.
Opening lines of 'Ode to the West Wind' "O wild west wind thou breath of Autumn's being Thou, from whose unseen presence the leaves dead."
The speaker invokes the 'wild west wind' of autumn, which scatters the dead leaves and spreads seeds so that they may be nurtured by the spring and asks that the wind "the destroyer and preserver".
The speaker calls the wind the "dirge" (of the dying year) and describes how it stirs up violent storms and again implores it to hear him.
Important line "If winter comes can spring be far behind."
The speaker calls the West Wind both destroyer and preserver.
Dead leaves, storm clouds, and the sea all hear its voice.
He wishes he were a leaf, a cloud, or a wave, free like the wind.
He asks the wind to drive his dead thoughts over the world.
He ends with hope that winter will lead to spring.

Ode on a Grecian Urn faces a silent work of art.

To Autumn, written in September, praises a ripe season without a story of escape.

Edward Drury was also named as the Stamford publisher.

Further editions came in 1820, and a fourth edition came in 1821.

fields.label: Work Title

fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Keats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: On St. Agnes' Eve, a lover enters a hostile castle and flees with Madeline.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written in January and February 1819. First published in the 1820 volume.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Madeline (A young woman who keeps the St. Agnes rite); Porphyro (Her lover, who enters the enemy castle); Angela (An old servant who helps Porphyro); The Beadsman (An old man saying prayers in the cold)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
His sensuousness is revealed in this poem through picturing of undressing of a woman "Anon his heart revives: her vespers done, Of all its wreathed pearls her hair she frees; Unclasps her warmed jewels one by one; Loosens her fragrant boddice; by degrees Her rich attire creeps rustling to her knees: Half-hidden, like a mermaid in sea-weed, Pensive awhile she dreams awake, and sees, In fancy, fair St. Agnes in her bed, But dares not look behind, or all the charm is fled.
Keats thinks that the highest truth can only be realized through the enjoyment of senses.
It is a poem of 42 stanzas, written in Spenserian stanza rhyming abab bcbc c.
The title comes from The Feast of St. Agnes.
The Eve falls on 20th January and The Feast Day is 21st January.
Like Romeo and Juliet, Madeline and Porphyro in this poem also belongs to hostile families.
The poem ends with a note of triumph of lovers.
It is a freezing night, the eve when maids hope to dream of a husband.
Porphyro slips into the castle of his enemies, the Beadsman praying outside.
Angela helps him hide near the sleeping Madeline.
He sets a feast and wakes her from the dream of St. Agnes.
The lovers escape into the storm, and the poem looks back from long ago.

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Blake

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long unfinished poem of Blake's private myth, in nine Nights (nine books).

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says it was composed in the 1790s and early 1800s and not published in his life. That outline is fair. He began it in 1797, abandoned it by 1807, and it was first printed in 1893.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Urizen (The Zoa of reason, often a tyrant maker of laws); Luvah (The Zoa of love and emotion); Tharmas (The Zoa of the body and the senses); Urthona (The Zoa of imagination, linked with Los); Vala (A female figure of nature, and the poem's first title)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an incomplete prophetic book by Blake, begun in 1797.
The titular main characters of the books are the four Zoas: Urthona Urizen Luvah Tharmas (Ahania is the wife of Urizen)
They were created by the fall of Albian in Blake's mythology.
It consists of 9 books, referred to as "nights".
Blake intended the book to be a summation of his mythic universe but, dissatisfied, he abandoned the effort in 1807, leaving it unfinished.
The final night describes Los witnessing a vision of Christ's Crucification at the hands of Urizen.
The Four Zoas form the four aspects of body, mind, emotion, and spirit.
Blake began the poem in 1797, first under the title Vala.
Albion (Blake's giant man) falls and splits into four Zoas (parts of one self).
Urizen, Luvah, Tharmas, and Urthona fight their female partners.
Blake retitled the manuscript The Four Zoas in 1807 and then left it.
The text was first published in 1893 by W. B. Yeats and Edwin John Ellis.

fields.value:
(1798)
The Rime of The Ancient Mariner is the longest major poem by Coleridge written in 1797-98 and published in 1798 in the first edition of Lyrical Ballads.
It is written in VII parts. It has total 625 lines.
The Mariner stops a wedding guest and begins his tale.
At sea he shoots an albatross, a great seabird, and the crew suffers.
The ship is becalmed.
His companions die, and he is left alive.
He blesses water snakes, the curse breaks, and he returns home.
He must wander and retell the story as a warning.

Sir Patrick, Sir Murtagh, Sir Kit, and Sir Condy each inherit the estate.

Thady's son Jason, a sharp lawyer, gathers the family's debts.
Sir Condy dies poor, and Jason holds what the Rackrents have lost.

fields.value: A daily record of walks, weather, and household life at Dove Cottage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database wording written 1800-03 and published 1897 matches the main book. Knight's 1897 Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth is the fuller printing. He had given a large share in 1889. A few fragments were in Christopher Wordsworth's Memoirs. Knight dates those Memoirs to 1850. Romantic Circles dates them to 1851.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dorothy Wordsworth (The diarist, recording daily life at Grasmere); William Wordsworth (Her brother, whose poems draw on her notes); Samuel Taylor Coleridge (Their friend, often named in the journal)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dorothy began this journal at Grasmere in 1800.
She records walks with William, visits, gardens, and the weather.
In April 1802 she describes daffodils beside Ullswater.
William later used that picture in I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud.
The journal was not printed as a book until 1897, after her death.

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Maria Edgeworth

fields.value: A young woman enters London society and learns whom she should trust and marry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1801. The database year is correct. Jane Austen admired the book. It is a novel of English society, not an Irish estate tale.

fields.value: Belinda Portman (The young heroine who watches London society and chooses carefully); Lady Delacour (A brilliant society hostess whose gay manner hides pain); Clarence Hervey (A fashionable man whose experiments in love Belinda must judge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Belinda Portman is sent to London to find a husband.
She stays with Lady Delacour, a witty woman hiding a private fear.
Clarence Hervey and other men test Belinda's judgment.
Fashion, gossip, and a forced happy ending shape the plot.
Belinda chooses a marriage based on sense, not on show.

fields.value: Thalaba (A pious young Muslim chosen to destroy a college of sorcerers); The sorcerers (Magicians who killed Thalaba's family and live by evil spells)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
4.
Sorcerers murder Thalaba's family and leave him to a vowed revenge.
He travels through deserts and magic places, guided by faith.
Charms and tempters try to turn him from his task.
He reaches the sorcerers' hidden cavern under the sea.
He destroys their power, and the quest ends with his own death.

fields.value: Agnes Fitzhenry (The daughter who elopes, repents, and nurses her father); Fitzhenry (Agnes's father, a merchant driven mad by her loss); Clifford (The officer who seduces Agnes and later claims their son); Edward (The child of Agnes and Clifford)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Agnes Fitzhenry is the loved daughter of a country merchant.
Clifford persuades her to run away and then delays marriage.
She returns with their son and finds her father mad.
She nurses him, and at last he knows her and forgives her.
Father and daughter die close together and are buried in one grave.
Clifford sees the funeral and takes the boy as his heir.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Job Thornberry (An honest brazier and ironmonger, the plain Englishman of the title); Mary Thornberry (Job's daughter, abandoned by Frank Rochdale); Frank Rochdale (A baronet's son who loves Mary but left her under his father's orders); Peregrine (A returned sailor who is the true heir of the Rochdale family); Sir Simon Rochdale (Peregrine's younger brother, who has been holding the title)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mary Thornberry has been seduced and left by Frank Rochdale.
She flees, and Peregrine, a shipwrecked stranger, saves her from harm.
Her father, Job Thornberry, is an honest brazier facing ruin.
Peregrine pays Job's need and recalls a gift Job once gave a runaway boy.
Peregrine then proves he is the elder brother and the true Rochdale heir.
Sir Simon must yield, and Mary and Frank are brought together.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He wrote it in March 1799. It was first printed in 1803 in William Hayley's Life and Posthumous Writings of William Cowper. The database phrase The Works, 1803 names the year correctly but not the book. Posthumous means printed after the author died. He died in 1800.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (Cowper, telling the sailor's death and then reading his own life in it); The castaway (A sailor washed from a ship and left to drown)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem retells a true drowning from Anson's sea voyage.
A sailor is swept overboard and swims until he is lost.
Cowper compares that abandoned man with his own fear of God.
He wrote it in 1799, near the end of his life.
It was printed in 1803, after his death in 1800.
