fields.label: Author
fields.value: Amelia Opie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young woman lives unmarried with a philosopher and is cast out by society.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says 1804, and the old DNB does too. She delivered the manuscript in late 1804. The Opie Archive dates the printed book to January 1805, and the title page says 1805.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Adeline Mowbray (The heroine who tries to live by radical ideas); Mrs Mowbray (Adeline's mother, who taught the ideas and then rejects her daughter)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Adeline is raised to question the usual rules of marriage.
She loves a philosopher who writes against marrying.
They live together without a wedding, and society rejects her.
Her mother turns away, and the philosopher dies.
The tale shows both the hope in those ideas and their social cost.
Readers saw hints of Mary Wollstonecraft and William Godwin.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown

This 1804 book gathers plays outside the passion series.
It was issued in London and Edinburgh.
The plays still aim at the stage, not only at the reader.
The book shows her range beyond one feeling per play.
Students should not treat the title as one single plot.

fields.value:
9.
An old minstrel sings a border tale at a lady's request.
The Lady of Branksome Hall feuds with an enemy clan.
Her daughter Margaret loves Lord Cranstoun, a man from that clan.
William of Deloraine rides to Melrose Abbey for a magic book.
A goblin page uses the book and delays peace.
The feud ends, and Margaret marries Lord Cranstoun.

Smith wrote this poem near the end of her life, in 1806.
The 1807 volume is called Beachy Head, with other poems.
The University of Nebraska calls that 1807 book incomplete.
A speaker on the cliff imagines England broken away from the continent.
The poem also watches birds, the tide, and the history of the place.

This was Byron's first book offered to the public.
It gathers early lyrics, school memories, and classical translations.
The title page calls the author a minor, meaning under 21.
A harsh review in the Edinburgh Review followed in 1808.
That attack led Byron to write English Bards and Scotch Reviewers.

Wordsworth published this major collection in two volumes in May 1807.
It includes famous nature lyrics like I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud and The Solitary Reaper.
It features his great Immortality Ode and Resolution and Independence.
It contains celebrated political and reflective Petrarchan sonnets.

8. The Adventures of Ulysses 9. Specimens of English Dramatic Poets Who Lived about the Time of Shakespeare 10. On the Tragedies of Shakespeare 11. Witches and Other Night Fears.

Sir John Stevenson, and later Moore himself, sets the words to music.
Songs such as The Last Rose of Summer and The Minstrel Boy become famous.
Harp, exile, and Tara stand for an Ireland under English rule.
The numbers come out over many years for a London audience.

The poem has three main plots; the contest among three men: i)
Lord Marmion is an English knight before the Battle of Flodden.
He has ruined Ralph De Wilton and wants Clara de Clare.
Constance, a nun who loved him, is punished for broken vows.
De Wilton returns in disguise and wins back his honor.
Marmion dies at Flodden in 1513.
A song in the poem tells how Lochinvar takes his bride away.

Byron answers the reviewers in a long satiric poem.
He uses heroic couplets (rhyming pairs of ten-syllable lines).
He attacks Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey, and Scott.
He also attacks literary critics, especially the Edinburgh Review.
The first edition in March 1809 did not print his name.

The poem opens beside the Susquehanna River, in a ruined Wyoming.
It recalls a happy valley of shepherds, dances, and quiet joy.
It promises to paint Gertrude as she lived before the ruin.
That peace is broken by the Battle of Wyoming in 1778.
Campbell gives a sad, romantic picture of the killing.
He had not seen Pennsylvania, and he used a travel book for details.
Many historians think the poem helped to name the state of Wyoming.

The set was published in London in 1810.
Barbauld chose the novels and wrote a preface for each writer.
Her opening essay traces how the novel grew in Britain.

She is the editor, not the novelist.
The project treats the novel as a serious kind of writing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kehama (A proud raja who tries to make himself a god); Ladurlad (A humble father who bears Kehama's curse and protects his child); Kailyal (Ladurlad's daughter, whose purity resists Kehama)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
9.
It is an epic poem composed by Southy.
The origin of the poem can be traced to Southy's school days when he suffered from insomnia along with his memories of dark and mysterious schoolmate that later formed the basis for one of the poem's villains.
The poem is divided into 12 books. Half part of the book describes how the evil priest Kehama is able to gain significant amounts of demonic power on a quest of becoming a god.
The poem describes Hindu Myth. It is heavily influenced by Zorastrian trilogy.
It focuses on India stems from the recent British colonial expansion into India and the increasing interest by British citizens in Indian culture.
Kehama, a mighty raja, kills Ladurlad's son and curses the father.
The curse will not let Ladurlad die, sleep, or feel ordinary joy.
Ladurlad and his daughter Kailyal flee through a Hindu myth world.
Kehama forces his way toward divine power and overreaches.
His ambition destroys him, and patient love outlasts the curse.

His followers hate this union of two hostile clans.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sense and Sensibility

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1811 (Sort Year: 1811)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jane Austen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two sisters balance good judgment and strong emotion while seeking love and financial stability.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Austen drafted it around 1795 as Elinor and Marianne. She revised it in 1797-1798 and again in 1809-1810 at Chawton. Thomas Egerton published it anonymously in October 1811 with the phrase By a Lady. Database sort_year 1811 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elinor Dashwood (The sensible elder sister who keeps her deep feelings under control); Marianne Dashwood (The impulsive younger sister who gives in to strong emotions); Edward Ferrars (A quiet gentleman who loves Elinor but is trapped by an old promise); Colonel Brandon (An honorable older officer who patiently loves Marianne); John Willoughby (A charming but selfish young man who abandons Marianne for money); Lucy Steele (A shrewd, dishonest woman who is secretly engaged to Edward)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It appeared in 1811 under the pseudonym "A Lady".
It is a work of romantic fiction better known as a comedy of manners.
It portrays the life and loves of the Dashwood sisters, Elinor and Marianne.
Both of them find their private fate but resulted in an unhappy love story but their parallel plot gives the demonstration of dual thesis.
Sense in the book means good judgment and sensibility means sensitivity or emotionality.
It includes total 50 chapters. Plot:.
When Mr. Henry Dashwood dies, he left all his money to his first wife's son John Dashwood.
His second wife and three daughters are left with no permanent home and a very little income.
Mrs. Dashwood and her three daughters Elinor, Marianne, and Margaret are invited to stay with their distant relation, The Middletons, at Barton Park.
Elinor was sad to leave her home at Norland because she was closely attached to Edward Ferrars, the brother in law of her half-brother John.
At Barton Park, Elinor and Marianne discover the retired officer Colonel Brandon and a bachelor John Willoughby.
Willoughby has rescued Marianne, after she twists her ankle.
Willoughby and Marianne flaunt their attachment to one another.
Willoughby suddenly announces that he is departing for London, leaving Marianne lovesick and miserable.
Anne and Lucy are two recently discovered relation of Lady Middleton's mother, Mrs. Jennings who arrives as a guest to Middletons.
Lucy reveals that she had been in love with Edward Ferrars for last one year with whom Elinor was also in love. Thus she is shocked.
In Vol II, Elinor and Marianne visits London with Mrs. Jennings.
Colonel Brandon informs Elinor that in London, everyone is talking about the marriage of Marianne and Willoughby, while she has not told her attachment to her family.
Rather Marianne was anxious to be reunited with Willoughby but later she rejects him when she sees him at a party in the town saying that he ever had feeling for her.
Colonel Brandon tells Elinor about Willoughby's history of callousness and debauchery.
Mrs. Jennings confirms that Willoughby is engaged to a wealthy heiress Miss Grey.
In Vol III, Anne, Lucy's older sister inadvertently reveals the secret engagement of Lucy and Edward Ferrars.
Edward's mother is outraged at this and disinherits him.
Meanwhile, the Dashwood sisters visit family friends at Cleveland, while returning from London.
At Cleveland Marianne falls deathly ill and Willoughby comes to visit her and explains for his misconduct and ask for forgiveness.
Elinor pities Willoughby and Marianne realizes that she could never been happy with Willoughby.
Colonel Brandon and Mrs. Dashwood arrive at Cleveland and finds that Marianne is recovering.
When all the Dashwoods return to Barton they learned that Lucy is engaged to Mr. Ferrars.
But Edward Ferrars himself reveals the secret that Lucy was in love with Robert not him, thus he is free to marry Elinor, and proposes her.
Marianne and Colonel Brandon are engaged as well.
Both couples live together at Delaford happily.
Mr. Dashwood dies, and his estate passes to his son John from his first marriage.
John and his greedy wife Fanny leave almost nothing to his widowed stepmother and half-sisters.
Mrs. Dashwood and her three daughters move to Barton Cottage in Devonshire.
Elinor represents good judgment and quietly falls in love with Edward Ferrars.
Edward is secretly engaged to the scheming Lucy Steele.
Marianne represents romantic emotion and falls for the dashing John Willoughby.
Willoughby abandons Marianne to marry a wealthy woman for money.
Marianne falls dangerously ill from heartbreak but slowly recovers.
Edward is disowned by his mother when his secret engagement is revealed.
Lucy deserts Edward to marry his wealthy younger brother Robert instead.
Elinor marries Edward, and Marianne marries the faithful Colonel Brandon.

items.title: "Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, cantos I–II" (1812) — George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, cantos I–II

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1812 (Sort Year: 1812)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The travel poem that made Byron famous overnight in 1812.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Begun on 31 October 1809. Canto II was finished at Smyrna in March 1810. John Murray published cantos I and II on 10 March 1812. Database year 1812 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Childe Harold (The disillusioned young traveler of the first two cantos); The Narrator (The reflecting voice that readers linked with Byron himself)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Byron began this poem in Greece on 31 October 1809.
Harold leaves England and travels through Spain, Albania, and Greece.
He is sick of pleasure and looks for a new life abroad.
John Murray published these two cantos on 10 March 1812.
Byron then said he awoke and found himself famous.

items.title: "Eighteen Hundred and Eleven" (1812) — Anna Laetitia Barbauld

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Eighteen Hundred and Eleven

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1812 (Sort Year: 1812)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anna Laetitia Barbauld

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A political poem that warns Britain it may decline in a long war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The title names the year 1811. Joseph Johnson published the poem in 1812. The database year 1812 is correct. The database genre Fiction is wrong, because this is a poem. The Quarterly Review attacked it in June 1812.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A prophetic voice addressing Britain); The Genius (A spirit of civilization that leaves one country for another)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Britain is still at war, and families lose sons abroad.
The speaker says a nation that shares the guilt must share the woe.
Commerce and luxury can rot a rich country from within.
A future visitor finds London in ruins, like older empires.
The spirit of arts and liberty moves west toward the Americas.
Harsh reviews followed, and she published little verse afterward.

fields.value: The Absentee

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1812 (Sort Year: 1812)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Maria Edgeworth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An Irish heir sees the harm done when landlords live in London and neglect the estate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It appeared in Tales of Fashionable Life, published in parts from 1809 to 1812. The database year 1812 fits that collection. It attacks absentee English landowning in Ireland.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lord Colambre (The son who inspects the Irish estate and judges his parents' absence); Lady Clonbrony (His mother, who spends in London and hides her Irish roots); Lord Clonbrony (The absentee landlord whose estate is mismanaged in his absence)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lord and Lady Clonbrony live fashionably in London, away from Ireland.
Their spending and her wish to seem English strain the family.
Their son, Lord Colambre, travels to see the Irish estate himself.
He finds agents who cheat tenants while the owners stay absent.
He rejects a false marriage and works to bring the family home.

fields.label: Work Title

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1813 (Sort Year: 1813)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Southey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short, clear life of Admiral Nelson, written as a model for young sailors.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both Britannica and the Poetry Foundation date Life of Nelson to 1813, the year Southey became Poet Laureate. The Poetry Foundation notes that the book expands his 1809 review of an earlier life of Nelson. The database year 1813 is correct. The dying words are quoted in the Project Gutenberg text.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Horatio Nelson (The British admiral whose life is the subject of the book); Emma, Lady Hamilton (The woman Southey blames for Nelson's errors at Naples); Captain Hardy (The officer who hears Nelson's last requests at Trafalgar)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
5.
Southey follows Nelson from his frail boyhood into the navy.
He tells the great victories, including the Nile and Copenhagen.
He praises Nelson's courage but blames the affair with Lady Hamilton.
The book then reaches Trafalgar in 1805 and Nelson's fatal wound.
It closes on his death and the duty he claimed to have done.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pride and Prejudice

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1813 (Sort Year: 1813)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jane Austen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy overcome their initial misjudgments to find mutual respect and love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Austen drafted it between October 1796 and August 1797 under the title First Impressions. Thomas Cadell rejected it unread in 1797. She revised it in 1811-1812 at Chawton. Thomas Egerton published it on 28 January 1813.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elizabeth Bennet (The witty, intelligent second daughter of Mr. Bennet); Fitzwilliam Darcy (A wealthy, haughty landowner who learns humility and marries Elizabeth); Jane Bennet (The gentle, beautiful eldest daughter of the Bennet family); Charles Bingley (A good-natured, wealthy gentleman who loves Jane Bennet); Mr. Bennet (An indolent, sarcastic father with an unhappy marriage); Mrs. Bennet (A foolish mother desperate to marry off her five daughters); George Wickham (A charming, deceitful militia officer who elopes with Lydia); Mr. Collins (A vain, sycophantic clergyman who will inherit the Bennet estate); Lady Catherine de Bourgh (Darcy arrogant aunt who tries to forbid his marriage to Elizabeth)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Original title is -First Impression.
Genre- Novel of Manners, Satire.
It is a romantic novel by Jane Austen, published anonymously in three volumes in 1813.
The novel opens with the line, " It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife".
It is written in the free indirect speech.
The Title "Pride and Prejudice" has been taken from a passage in Fanny Burney's popular 1782 novel Cecilia.
Darcy says in the play-" A lady's imagination is very rapid ; it jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony."
Elizabeth Bennet is the main character who is second of the five daughters of a gentleman.
Mr. Bennet is a Bookish man.
Mrs. Bennet is a women Lacking is social grace and concerned with finding husband for his five daughters.
The five daughters are Jane Bennet Elizabeth Bennet Mary Kitty (Catherine)
The wealthy Charles Bingley leases Netherfield Park near the Bennet family home.
Bingley likes Jane Bennet, while his proud friend Fitzwilliam Darcy snubs Elizabeth Bennet.
Elizabeth forms an immediate dislike of Darcy because of his cold pride.
George Wickham charms Elizabeth and tells her false stories about Darcy.
The pompous clergyman Mr. Collins proposes to Elizabeth, but she firmly refuses him.
Bingley leaves Netherfield abruptly, which breaks Jane heart.
Darcy proposes to Elizabeth in Kent, but she furiously rejects him for his arrogance.
Darcy gives Elizabeth a letter that clears his name and exposes Wickham deceit.
Elizabeth visits Pemberley and sees Darcy true kindness and generosity.
Wickham elopes with Lydia Bennet, threatening the Bennet family with social ruin.
Darcy secretly pays Wickham debts and arranges the wedding to save the family.
Bingley returns to marry Jane, and Darcy and Elizabeth marry happily.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Queen Mab

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1813 (Sort Year: 1813)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long early poem in which a fairy shows a girl a reformed world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Shelley privately printed Queen Mab in London in 1813. Database year 1813 is correct. The database posthumous flag is wrong. He issued it during his life. It was his first major poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Queen Mab (The fairy who guides the vision); Ianthe (The sleeping girl whose soul travels with Mab)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1813)
It is the earliest poetic work of Shelley, produced in 1813.
The poem is immature and contains much of Shelley's cruder atheism. It represents the Shelley's mind for which he was expelled from Oxford.
The poem is an attack on dogmatic religion, government, industrial tyranny and war, in which poet presents a world of his dreams free from tyranny of kings and barons.
The poet hopes that soon there will be the dawn of a new millennium where everything will be for the good of mankind, in which the force of tyranny, oppression and cruelty will disappear.
He hopes that in the new world lion and lamb shall live together "The lion now forgets the thirst for blood: There might you see him sporting in the sun."
It consists of 9 cantos.
After substantial re-working, a revised edition of a portion of the text was published in 1816 under the title 'The Daemon of the World'. Alaster or The Spirit of Solitude (1816)
It was published in 1816.
It is a kind of spiritual autobiography, in which the chief character, a shadowy projection of Shelley's own moods travels through a wilderness in quest of the ideal beauty.
The poem represents the wandering of a traveler (Shelley himself) in search of ideal beauty.
The traveler wanders through Athens, Babylon and Jerusalem till he comes to the valley of Kashmir, where he sees a vision.
In the vision a beautiful girl emerges before him and the traveler is captivated by her beauty.
The vision soon disappears and the traveler moves ahead passing through all barriers but success doesn't greet him.
But he doesn't lose courage and continues ahead in search of great secrets of life. A faint picture of it he got in Kashmir.
After passing through many attractive and dreadful sites the traveller is exhausted and unable to go ahead.
Death ends his life and the lifelong quest of the traveler thus ends in tragedy.
The fairy Queen Mab comes to the sleeping girl Ianthe.
She carries Ianthe's soul through past, present, and future.
The vision attacks war, commerce, the church, kings, and forced marriage.
It also attacks the eating of meat and other customs Shelley hated.
It closes with a hope that humanity can be freed from these evils.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Giaour

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1813 (Sort Year: 1813)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dark Eastern tale of forbidden love, murder, and remorse.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in June 1813. Database year 1813 is correct. It is the first of Byron's famous Eastern tales.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Giaour (A Christian outsider who loves Leila and later kills Hassan); Leila (The woman killed for loving the Giaour); Hassan (The Turkish lord who punishes Leila and dies by the Giaour's hand)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem is a set of broken scenes from an Eastern story.
Leila loves a Christian outsider called the Giaour.
Hassan kills Leila for that love.
The Giaour kills Hassan and then lives with guilt.
John Murray published it in June 1813.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Queen’s Wake

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1813 (Sort Year: 1813)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Hogg

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem in which bards compete before Mary Queen of Scots.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the University of Stirling date the book to 1813. The exact writing year is unknown. The database year 1813 is correct for publication. The database genre Fiction is wrong, because the book is a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Queen of Scots (The queen who holds the contest of bards); Kilmeny (A girl in one inset poem, taken into a fairy world); The bards (Singers from across Scotland who compete for the harp)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mary Queen of Scots calls the bards of Scotland to a contest.
Each bard sings a tale, and the prize is a harp.
The songs include Kilmeny, about a girl taken among the fairies.
The Witch of Fife is another tale inside the same frame.
Kilmeny and The Witch of Fife are the songs readers still remember.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Mansfield Park

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1814 (Sort Year: 1814)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jane Austen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor, timid girl preserves her moral integrity while growing up among her wealthy cousins.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Austen began writing Mansfield Park in February 1811 and finished it in 1813 at Chawton. Thomas Egerton published it in three volumes in May 1814. Database sort_year 1814 and display_date 1814 are correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fanny Price (The shy, morally upright heroine raised by her wealthy relations); Edmund Bertram (Sir Thomas younger son, an aspiring clergyman who loves Fanny); Sir Thomas Bertram (Fanny wealthy, stern uncle who owns Mansfield Park and Antigua estates); Mrs. Norris (Fanny selfish, penny-pinching aunt who treats her harshly); Mary Crawford (A charming, worldly London woman who attracts Edmund); Henry Crawford (Mary charming, immoral brother who courts Fanny); Maria Bertram (Fanny vain cousin who enters a loveless marriage and ruins herself with Henry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the third novel of Austen written at Chawton Cottage between Feb 1811 and 1813 and was published in May 1814.
It is a Pygmalion morality epic. Plot:.
A young girl named Fanny Price comes to live with her uncle and aunt, Sir Thomas and Lady Bertram.
Fanny's family is quite poor. Her father is a sailor who is disabled and drinks heavily.
Fanny is abused by her other aunt, Mrs. Norris.
The Bertram daughters Maria and Julia are shallow and cruel but intended on marrying well and being fashionable.
Bertram's elder son Tom is an unspoiled labourer and drunk.
Fanny finds comfort only in the friendship with younger son Edmund who is planning to be a clergyman.
Fanny grows up in the family of Bertram.
Sir Thomas leaves Mansfield Park for Antigua where he owns plantations.
In his absence two new figure arrive at Mansfield, Henry and Mary Crawford, the brothers and sister of the local minister.
Henry and Mary are attractive and cheerful.
Henry flirts Maria extensively, but Maria is engaged to a boring but wealthy man Rushworth.
He also flirts with Julia to suit his purpose.
At first Mary is interested in Tom, but she soon realizes that he is boring and not interested in her.
Now Mary finds herself attracted to Edmund.
'Yates' a visiting friend of 'Tom', proposes that the group should put on a play.
Edmund and Fanny disagree to this idea but plays go on anyway.
Fanny is also pressured when one of the women could not make a rehearsal (play-within novel).
As the play continues, Sir Thomas enters suddenly having returned from Antigua.
Sir Thomas was unhappy about the play and put a stop to it.
Since Henry has not declared his love, Maria is married to Rushworth.
Maria and Julia leave the Mansfield Park for London.
Henry decides to woo Fanny, because he was in sincere love with her.
Henry helps William to get promotion in Navy and using it as a leverage he proposes Fanny (William is the brother of Fanny).
But Fanny refuses it. Her uncle is disappointed to see that she refused such a wealthy man.
As a result, Fanny is sent back to her parent's filthy house.
Henry comes to see Fanny at her parents and renews his suit.
Henry leaves to take care of his business. Mary continues to encourage Fanny through letters to take Henry's proposal.
A series of events take place suddenly in succession: Tom Bertram falls seriously ill. Henry runs off with married Maria. Julia is upset over her sister's rash elopes with Yates, Tom's friend. Fanny is recalled to Mansfield bringing her younger sister Susan with her.
Mary wanted Tom to be died so that Edmund could be heir.
Edmund is heartbroken but consoled by Fanny.
Maria and Henry eventually split and he goes to live with Mrs. Norris.
Julia and Yates are reconciled to the family.
Edmund finally comes to his senses and marries Fanny and Susan takes her place with Bertrams.
Edmund, Fanny, and rest of those at Mansfield live happily while Henry, Maria, and Mary are cast out.
Fanny Price is sent at age ten to live with her rich uncle, Sir Thomas Bertram.
Fanny is treated unkindly by Aunt Norris and her cousins Maria and Julia.
Only her kind cousin Edmund treats Fanny with affection and respect.
Sir Thomas sails to Antigua to attend to his plantation business.
Henry and Mary Crawford arrive from London and charm the young Bertrams.
The young people decide to stage the improper play Lovers Vows at the house.
Fanny refuses to act in the play because she believes it is wrong.
Sir Thomas returns home unexpectedly and cancels the play at once.
Henry Crawford proposes to Fanny, but she refuses him because she distrusts his character.
Henry elopes with the married Maria, bringing scandal to the Bertram household.
Edmund realizes that Mary Crawford lacks moral principles and turns to Fanny.
Edmund and Fanny marry and live happily at the parsonage.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Corsair

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1814 (Sort Year: 1814)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A pirate chief is captured, freed by Gulnare, and returns to a dead beloved.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written between 18 and 31 December 1813. Published in February 1814. Database year 1814 is correct. About 10,000 copies sold on the first day.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Conrad (A pirate chief, proud, secret, and devoted to Medora); Medora (Conrad's beloved, who dies before his return); Gulnare (The woman who kills Seyd and frees Conrad); Seyd (The ruler who captures Conrad)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Conrad is a pirate leader who loves Medora.
Seyd captures him during a raid.
Gulnare kills Seyd and sets Conrad free.
Conrad comes home and finds Medora dead.
The poem was written in late December 1813.
On publication day in February 1814, 10,000 copies sold.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Excursion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1814 (Sort Year: 1814)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Wordsworth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long philosophical poem in nine books presenting moral and spiritual conversations across the countryside.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1814 is correct. Published by Longman in London. It was the only long portion of The Recluse printed during Wordsworth's lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Poet (The narrator who records the travels and philosophical dialogues); The Wanderer (A wise elderly pedlar who teaches faith in nature and human goodness); The Solitary (A depressed man who lost his family and his hope in the French Revolution); The Pastor (A country clergyman who narrates the life stories of deceased parish members); Margaret (A suffering country wife in Book One whose home decays while awaiting her husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Wordsworth published The Excursion in 1814 in nine books of blank verse.
It was planned as the second part of a grand three part poem called The Recluse.
Four characters travel through the Lake District landscape and discuss loss, faith, and hope.
Book one incorporates an earlier tragedy called The Ruined Cottage or The Story of Margaret.
Critic Francis Jeffrey famously mocked it in the Edinburgh Review with the phrase This will never do.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Wanderer

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1814 (Sort Year: 1814)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Fanny Burney

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A nameless woman tries to earn a living in England during the Terror.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1814 is right. Longman published it on 28 March 1814. The database calls it poetry, but it is a novel. She had worked on it for many years.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Juliet Granville (The nameless heroine, later known as the Earl of Granville's daughter); Harleigh (The cautious suitor who learns her secret and returns to her); Elinor Joddrel (A rich woman who loves Harleigh and argues for women's freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the last novel of Burney. It is a historical novel. 5. Journals and Letters.
It is the diary that she started at the age of 15 until the end of her life. 6. The Witlings.
Juliet Granville reaches England while hiding her name and her past.
She tries music and sewing, but the rich often refuse to pay her.
Elinor Joddrel loves Harleigh and speaks for the freedom of women.
Juliet had been forced into a French marriage to save her guardian.
That husband dies, her birth is proved, and Harleigh proposes.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Waverley

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1814 (Sort Year: 1814)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sir Walter Scott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young English officer is pulled into the Jacobite rising of 1745.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1814 is correct. It was published anonymously on 7 July 1814. Scott began it about 1805 and finished it in 1814. He publicly owned the Waverley novels in 1827.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Waverley (A young English officer who wavers between two sides); Fergus Mac-Ivor (A Highland chief who fights for the Jacobites); Flora Mac-Ivor (Fergus's sister, devoted to the Stuart cause); Rose Bradwardine (The Lowland woman Edward marries)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
6.
The Waverly novels are a long series of novels.
As Scott did not publicly acknowledge authorship until 1827 then took its name Waverly.
The first novel of the series was released in 1814.
The later books bore the words "by the author of Waverly" on their title pages.
Edward Waverley is a young English officer with romantic dreams.
In Scotland he is drawn to the Highland chief Fergus Mac-Ivor.
Fergus's sister Flora cares more for the Jacobite cause than for Edward.
Edward joins the 1745 rising for Prince Charles Edward Stuart.
The rising fails, and Edward is parted from the Highland leaders.
He is pardoned and marries Rose Bradwardine.
The book shows old Highland life giving way to modern Britain.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Emma

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1815 (Sort Year: 1815)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jane Austen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wealthy, self-assured young woman causes trouble through misguided matchmaking before finding her own match.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Austen began writing Emma on 21 January 1814 and finished it on 29 March 1815. John Murray published it on 23 December 1815, though the title page says 1816. Austen dedicated the book to the Prince Regent.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Emma Woodhouse (A clever, wealthy, and headstrong heroine who loves matchmaking); Mr. George Knightley (A sensible local landowner who acts as Emma moral guide and marries her); Mr. Woodhouse (Emma eccentric, health-obsessed father who dislikes change); Harriet Smith (A sweet, gullible parlor boarder manipulated by Emma); Frank Churchill (Mr. Weston charming, secretive son who is secretly engaged to Jane); Jane Fairfax (A talented, reserved orphan faced with becoming a governess); Miss Bates (A harmless, chatterbox spinster whom Emma cruelly insults at Box Hill); Mr. Elton (An ambitious, proud clergyman who rejects Harriet and marries Augusta Hawkins)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Emma Woodhouse is a 20 year old resident of the Village Highbury.
She convinced herself that she will never marry but imagines herself to be naturally gifted in conjuring love matches.
Emma takes the responsibility to find a match for her friend Harriet Smith.
Mrs. Weston is Emma's Governess.
Emma thinks that Harriet deserves to be a gentleman's wife so she sets her friend's sight at Mr. Elton.
Meanwhile Emma persuades Harriet to reject the proposal of Robert Martin, a well to do farmer for whom Harriet has clear feelings.
Harriet becomes infatuated with Mr. Elton under Emma's encouragement.
Emma is surprised to know that Elton's affection was towards her not Harriet.
Mr. Knightly, Emma's brother-in-law, proposes that Mr. Martin is a worthy good man, whom Harriet can marry.
Emma and Mr. Knightly quarrels and Knightly proves to be wiser.
As Elton is refused by Emma, he leaves for the town of Bath and marries a girl there immediately.
Mr. Frank Churchill is the new visitor now, in Highbury.
Emma finds Frank, delightful and notices that his charms are dissected mainly towards her.
Emma plans to discourage Frank's charm.
Emma greets Jane Fairfax, who is beautiful and accomplished. But Emma dislikes her because of her reserve.
Mr. Knightly defends Jane, as he had romantic feelings for Jane.
Everyone assumes that Frank and Emma are forming attachment while Emma thought him to be suitor of Harriet.
At a village ball Knightly dances with Harriet who is just humiliated by Mr. Elton and his new wife.
Harriet tells Emma that she is in love with a man above her social status and Emma believes that she is talking about Frank.
Mr. Knightly began to think that Emma and Frank are in a secret understanding.
News comes that Frank's aunt is died.
Frank and Jane are secretly married.
Emma comes to know about Mr. Knightley's affair with Harriet.
Emma feels upset by this revelation.
Emma expects Knightly to tell her that he loves Harriet, but Knightly declares his love for Emma.
Harriet is comforted by a second proposal from Robert Martin, which she accepts.
The novel ends with marriage of Harriet and Mr. Martin and that of Mr. Knightly and Emma.
Emma Woodhouse lives comfortably at Hartfield with her nervous father.
After matchmaking for her governess, Emma decides to arrange more local marriages.
Her close friend Mr. Knightley warns her against meddling in romance.
Emma takes the naive Harriet Smith as a project and discourages her from marrying Robert Martin.
Emma tries to match Harriet with the vicar Mr. Elton.
Mr. Elton rejects Harriet and shocks Emma by declaring love to Emma herself.
Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax arrive in Highbury, concealing their secret engagement.
Emma flirts with Frank and wrongly imagines Jane has a secret lover.
At Box Hill, Emma publicly insults the poor, garrulous Miss Bates.
Mr. Knightley sternly scolds Emma, which causes her deep regret and shame.
Harriet reveals that she now loves Mr. Knightley, which alarms Emma.
Emma realizes she loves Mr. Knightley, and they marry with joy.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Alastor

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A blank verse tale of a young poet who chases a dream and dies alone.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written in 1815 and published with shorter poems in 1816. Database year 1816 is the book year. The database posthumous flag is wrong. Shelley was alive in 1816.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (The voice that warns against a lonely search for a dream); The Poet (A youth who follows an ideal vision until he dies); The Veiled Maid (The dream woman the Poet cannot find in waking life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A narrator speaks to earth, ocean, and air as a brotherhood.
A young Poet leaves home to seek a perfect vision of love.
He dreams of a veiled maid, then wakes and cannot find her.
He wanders into wild country and wastes away.
The poem warns idealists not to abandon sweet human love.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Bertram

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Robert Maturin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Gothic tragedy about a ruined nobleman whose return brings murder and death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1816 is correct for the Drury Lane production and the published play. The database genre label Fiction is misleading. This is a tragedy, not a novel. Edmund Kean played the lead. Oxford Reference notes the recommendation of Sir Walter Scott and Byron.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bertram (A ruined noble outlaw, played in 1816 by Edmund Kean); St. Aldobrand (The lord whose castle gives the play its subtitle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bertram, once a nobleman, returns as a wrecked and desperate man.
Scott and Byron helped the play reach the London stage.
Edmund Kean played Bertram at Drury Lane in 1816.
The story turns on the castle of St. Aldobrand and a fatal return.
The run was a success, but later plays by Maturin failed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Christabel

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished Gothic poem about a pure girl who shelters a strange woman in the wood.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Part one was written in 1797 and part two in 1800. It was left unfinished and dropped from Lyrical Ballads. John Murray published it in 1816 with Kubla Khan. Database year 1816 is the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Christabel (The innocent daughter of Sir Leoline); Geraldine (A supernatural stranger who seems to be a lamia, or snake woman); Sir Leoline (Christabel's father, a baron still mourning his wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a long narrative poem by Coleridge in 2 parts, the first written in 1797 and the second in 1800.
He had planned 3 additional parts but not completed.
Coleridge prepared first two parts to be included in "Lyrical Ballads" but on the suggestion of Wordsworth it was left.
It was published in a pamphlet in 1816.
Christabel prays at night in the woods for her distant lover.
She finds Geraldine, a beautiful stranger who claims to be in distress.
Christabel takes her home and hides her from Sir Leoline.
Geraldine casts a spell, and Christabel cannot tell what she saw.
The poem breaks off.
Sir Leoline turns toward Geraldine and away from his daughter.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Headlong Hall

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Love Peacock

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Guests at a Welsh country house argue about progress, taste, and almost everything else.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the novel 1816. The Poetry Foundation says it appeared in 1815. The database year 1816 matches the title page used in exams.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Squire Harry Headlong (The Welsh host who wants clever guests in his house); Mr Foster (A guest who believes society can keep getting better); Mr Escot (A guest who believes the world is getting worse); Mr Jenkison (A guest who defends the present state of things); Dr Gaster (A clergyman whose main talent is enjoying food)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Squire Headlong invites thinkers to his house in Wales.
Mr Foster trusts progress, and Mr Escot fears decay.
Mr Jenkison defends things as they are.
Dr Gaster cares most about eating well.
They debate diet, landscape, and philosophy at the table.
Nobody really changes his mind, and the comedy stays light.

fields.value: Kubla Khan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream fragment about Kubla Khan's pleasure dome, a sacred river, and a poet's lost vision.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kubla Khan decrees a stately pleasure dome in Xanadu.
The sacred river Alph runs through caverns to a sunless sea.
A fountain bursts, and ancestral voices prophesy war.
The speaker recalls a vision of an Abyssinian maid and her song.
He wishes he could rebuild the dome in air, but the vision broke off.

items.title: "The Restoration of the Works of Art to Italy" (1816) — Felicia Hemans

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Restoration of the Works of Art to Italy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Felicia Hemans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem welcoming the return of looted art from France to Italy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1816 is correct. Oxford and London issued it in 1816. A second, expanded London edition also appeared in 1816. The University of Nebraska bibliography records both 1816 printings.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Poet (The speaker who hails Italy and its returning art); Italy (The fallen land addressed as the home of the arts)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Napoleon's armies had taken famous paintings and statues from Italy to Paris.
After his fall, many of those works were sent back.
The poem hails Italy as the home of art and ancient fame.
It names Florence, Venice, and Rome, and works such as the Laocoon.
The speaker hopes war will not strip Italy of its art again.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Story of Rimini

fields.value: 1816 (Sort Year: 1816)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Leigh Hunt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A narrative poem on the forbidden love of Paulo and Francesca.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1816 is the publication year. He wrote the poem while jailed from 1813 to 1815. It is a book poem, not a magazine serial. The database serial flag on this title is a generic error.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Paulo (Giovanni's brother, who falls in love with Francesca); Francesca (The woman brought from Ravenna to marry Giovanni); Prince Giovanni (Paulo's brother and Francesca's husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hunt drafted the poem in prison and published it in 1816.
It retells Dante's story of Francesca and Paulo.
Paulo takes Francesca from Ravenna to marry his brother, Prince Giovanni.
Paulo and Francesca fall in love while they read together.
Their secret is discovered, and the love ends in death.
The verse uses open couplets and a warm, easy style.
Byron read drafts, and Hunt dedicated the poem to him.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Biographia Literaria

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1817 (Sort Year: 1817)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mixed book of life story and criticism that defines imagination and poetic faith.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He dictated much of it in 1815. It was published in 1817. Database year 1817 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (The author, speaking as critic and as the subject of the life story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
vii) Aids to Reflection in the Formation of A Manley Character. viii) Confession of an Inquiring Spirit. ix) Hints Towards the Formation of more Comprehensive Theory of Life (1848)
(1817)
Biographia Literaria is also called Biographical Sketches of My Literary Life and Opinions.
It is an autobiography in discourse by S. T. Colerigde, published in 2 volumes written in 1817.
It has 23 chapters.
Chapter XIV is the origin of the famous critical concept "Willing Suspension of Disbelief".
Coleridge discarded the mechanical system for the belief that mind is not an active agency in the apprehension of reality.
He believed in the self-sufficing power of absolute genius and talent as between "an egg and an eggshell".
The book has numerous essays on Philosophy. In particular, it discusses and engages the Philosophy of Immanuel Kant, Johann Gottlieb Fichte and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling.
Later Chapters deals with the nature of poetry and with the question of diction raised by Wordsworth.
Important Quote - "Now it is clear to me, that in the most interesting of the poems, in which the author is more or less dramatic as 'The Brothers', 'Michael', 'Ruth', 'The Mad Mother and Others', the person introduced are by no means taken from low or rustic life in the new common acceptance of those words."
In these lines, Coleridge is contradicting the statement of Lyrical Ballads with these poems.
1. "Good sense is the body of poetic genius"
Coleridge tells how he became a poet and how he left some early beliefs.
He attacks the idea that poetry is only a mechanical arrangement of words.
He separates fancy (a combining memory) from imagination (a creative power).
He says readers grant a willing suspension of disbelief to supernatural poems.
Later chapters praise and also judge Wordsworth's poetry and theories.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Characters of Shakespeare’s Plays

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1817 (Sort Year: 1817)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Hazlitt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays on the people in Shakespeare's plays, written for ordinary readers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1817 is correct. The preface is dated 15 April 1817. The old title page spells the name Shakespear.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Hazlitt (The critic whose voice runs through the essays); Hamlet (One of the Shakespeare characters he studies, not a person in a new plot)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hazlitt discusses major plays, including Hamlet, Macbeth, Lear, and Othello.
He treats each main person as a living character, not as a school exercise.
He praises Shakespeare's range of human feelings.
He often prefers reading the plays to seeing them badly acted.
The book made his name as a critic of drama.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lalla Rookh

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1817 (Sort Year: 1817)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Moore

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An eastern princess hears four verse tales and falls in love with the poet who tells them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1817 by Longman. The database year is correct. Britannica notes the high price paid for the poem and its wide fame.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lalla Rookh (The princess who travels to her wedding and listens to the tales); Feramorz (The poet of the caravan, who is really the king she must marry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Princess Lalla Rookh travels from Delhi to marry the king of Bukhara.
A young poet, Feramorz, joins the caravan and tells four long tales.
The tales use Persian and Indian settings, love, faith, and revolt.
The princess loves the poet and dreads the royal husband.
At the wedding she finds that Feramorz is the king in disguise.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Northanger Abbey

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1817 (Sort Year: 1817)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jane Austen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A naive young woman learns to separate gothic fantasy from real life during visits to Bath and an abbey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Austen drafted it in 1798-1799 under the working title Susan. In 1803, she sold the manuscript to bookseller Benjamin Crosby for ten pounds, but he never printed it. Her brother Henry bought it back in 1816 for the same amount. Austen revised the heroine name to Catherine. John Murray published it posthumously in late December 1817 with Persuasion, although the title page is dated 1818. Database sort_year 1817 and display_date 1817, posthumous reflect this publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Catherine Morland (An innocent, novel-reading young girl who misreads real life through gothic romance); Henry Tilney (A sensible, humorous clergyman who loves Catherine and guides her judgment); General Tilney (A mercenary, controlling father who runs Northanger Abbey like a fortress); Eleanor Tilney (Henry gentle, lonely sister who becomes Catherine friend); Isabella Thorpe (A false, deceitful friend who seeks a wealthy husband); John Thorpe (Isabella vulgar, boastful brother who brags about carriages and horses)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The only novel in which Austen's name was there is: "Persuasion" (1817).
'Northanger Abbey' and 'Persuasion' are the novels which were published posthumously, in 1817.
Austen began to write as early as 1787 for her own and her family amusement. Later she compiled four copies of 29 of these early works into three bound notebooks which is now referred as "Juvenilia".
In 1793 she began and then abandoned a short play, later entitled "Sir Charles Grandison or The Happy Man"; A Comedy in 6 Acts. But she completed it in 1800.
This was a parody to Samuel Richardson's The History of Sir Charles Grandison.
Between 1793-1795 she wrote Lady Susan, a short epistolary novel.
The Persuasion was initially titled "The Elliots".
She probably died of Tuberculosis.
Her sister Cassandra was the closest friend of her.
Love and Friendship is the dark satirical comedy by Jane.
She said about "Emma", a heroine whom no one but myself will much like.
The incomplete works of Austen are Lady Susan, The Watsons and Sanditon.
It was completed for publication in 1797-1798 but was published posthumously in 1818. It is set in Bath.
Initially it was called 'Susan' but was revised as Katherine. Means the name of lead character is changed from Susan to Catherine.
Main characters: Catherine Morland Henry Tilney Eleanor Tilney General Tilney Isabella Thorpe John Thorpe James Morland Mrs. Thorpe Plot.
Northanger Abbey is the coming-of-age story of a young woman named Catherine Morland. It is divided into two sections, Book I and Book II.
Catherine Morland is an ordinary, sheltered country girl who loves reading gothic novels.
Family friends invite Catherine to visit Bath for the winter social season.
In Bath, Catherine meets the witty clergyman Henry Tilney at a dance.
Catherine also befriends the shallow Isabella Thorpe and her boastful brother John.
Catherine reads gothic thrillers like The Mysteries of Udolpho and lets her fancy run wild.
General Tilney invites Catherine to stay at his historic home, Northanger Abbey.
At the abbey, Catherine imagines mysterious secrets and horrific crimes.
She foolishly suspects General Tilney of having murdered his late wife.
Henry Tilney discovers her suspicions and gently scolds her for her wild fantasy.
Catherine feels deep shame and resolves to see real life as it is.
General Tilney angrily expels Catherine upon learning she is not an heiress.
Henry follows Catherine to her home, proposes to her, and they marry.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Persuasion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1817 (Sort Year: 1817)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jane Austen

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An overlooked woman reunites with her former fiancé after years of regret and silent devotion.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Austen wrote Persuasion between August 1815 and August 1816 at Chawton under the working title The Elliots. She revised the final chapters in summer 1816. John Murray published it posthumously on 20 December 1817 with Northanger Abbey. The title page is dated 1818. Database sort_year 1817 and display_date 1817, posthumous are correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anne Elliot (The quiet, intelligent, and deeply constant heroine who gets a second chance at love); Captain Frederick Wentworth (A gallant naval officer whose devotion to Anne endures despite past hurt); Sir Walter Elliot (Anne vain, spendthrift father who judges people entirely by rank and appearance); Lady Russell (A well-meaning godmother who originally persuaded Anne to give up Wentworth); Louisa Musgrove (A stubborn young woman who falls at the Cobb in Lyme Regis); William Elliot (Sir Walter smooth, mercenary nephew who plots to secure the family title); Captain Harville (A kind naval officer whose conversation prompts Wentworth letter)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published together, because both stories are set partly in Bath, a fashionable city.
Chief characters: Sir Walter Elliot Elizabeth Elliot Anne Elliot Mary Musgrove Charles Musgrove Lady Russel Captain Fredrick Wentworth Admiral Croft Sophia Croft Mr. William Elliot Mrs. Smith.
Anne Elliot was persuaded eight years earlier by Lady Russell to break her engagement to Frederick Wentworth.
Wentworth had no fortune at the time, leaving Anne with lasting sadness.
Anne vain father, Sir Walter Elliot, spends recklessly and must rent out Kellynch Hall.
Kellynch Hall is leased to Admiral Croft, whose brother-in-law is Captain Wentworth.
Wentworth returns from naval service rich, famous, and eligible.
Wentworth treats Anne with polite coolness and pays attention to Louisa Musgrove.
During a trip to Lyme Regis, Louisa falls from the Cobb and suffers a severe injury.
Wentworth admires Anne calm, capable behavior during the accident.
Louisa recovers and becomes engaged to Captain Benwick, freeing Wentworth.
In Bath, Wentworth overhears Anne defend the constancy of women devotion.
Overcome with feeling, Wentworth writes Anne a letter declaring his unending love.
Anne and Wentworth marry with deep joy and mutual understanding.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1817 (Sort Year: 1817)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Keats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Keats's first book, a 1817 collection that includes the Chapman Homer sonnet.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poems, by John Keats was published on 10 March 1817. Database year 1817 is correct. The unfinished flag on this book is wrong.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book gathers early poems of nature, friendship, and literary ambition.
A dedication praises Leigh Hunt, which later hostile reviews used against him.
Sleep and Poetry sets out his hopes for a poetic life.
The Chapman sonnet records the shock of reading Homer in a strong English version.
The book sold poorly, but it announced a new poet.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Endymion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1818 (Sort Year: 1818)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Keats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poetic romance in four books about the shepherd Endymion and his search for the moon goddess.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Endymion: A Poetic Romance was published in early May 1818. Database year 1818 is correct. Database genre Drama is wrong. The unfinished flag is also wrong. Keats finished this poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Endymion (A young shepherd who seeks the goddess he dreamed); Cynthia (The moon goddess, also called Diana); The Indian maid (A sad maiden who is Cynthia in disguise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem opens by saying a thing of beauty is a joy for ever.
Endymion, a shepherd, has seen a goddess in a dream and cannot rest.
He wanders under the earth, through the sea, and in the air.
He meets an Indian maid, who is the goddess in another form.
Cynthia, the moon goddess, reveals herself, and the quest ends in love.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Frankenstein

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1818 (Sort Year: 1818)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mary Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young scientist creates a living being, then faces the ruin that follows.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first edition was anonymous in January 1818. The 1831 third edition adds her introduction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Robert Walton (An Arctic explorer whose letters frame the novel); Victor Frankenstein (The student who creates a living being and then rejects it); The Creature (Victor's creation, first lonely, then bent on revenge); Elizabeth Lavenza (Victor's bride, killed on the wedding night); Henry Clerval (Victor's close friend, later a victim of the creature)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1818)
Frankenstein or The Modern Prometheus was written in three volumes.
It is about a young science student - Victor Frankenstein.
Shelley started writing this novel when she was 17 and completed at the age of 20.
The first edition was published in London in 1818.
Shelley's name appeared on the second edition published in France in 1823.
It's multiple narrative science fiction. Note: Brian Aldirs has argued that it should be considered first true science fiction story.
P. B. Shelley, Mary, Byron and Polidori decided to have a competition to see that who could write the best horror story and after thinking for many days Mary wrote Frankenstein.
The novel contains Captain Walton's introducing frame narrative and Victor Frankenstein narrative followed by Captain Walton's concluding frame narrative.
Victor begins by telling of his childhood that he was born in Naples.
Victor was obsessed with studying outdated theories that focus on simulating natural wonders.
He fell in love with an orphan, Lavenza, an orphan adopted by his parents.
His mother dies before he leaves for the university.
At university he developed a secret technique to import life to non-living matters which eventually leads to his creation of Monster.
Because of the difficulty in replicating the minor parts of the body, he made the creature about 8 feet tall.
The dream of Frankenstein remains incomplete because he could not make beautiful creations. He was unsatisfied by creature's yellow eye and skins, so he flees.
The creature became sad by Victor's rejection and disappears.
Victor falls ill but recovers and returns home where he learned about the death of his brother William.
He finds the monster at the crime scene. He believed that monster was responsible for the crime. The monster plants a picture on Justine, William's nanny, to frame her for this crime.
Victor is ravaged by grief and guilt, he retreats into the mountains.
The monster locates him to hear his tale.
Creature says that his encounters with people led to his fear of them, driving him in wilderness.
Creature, while living near a cottage, grew fond of the family living there. He learned to speak by listening to them.
He found his physical reflection was hideous when he saw his reflection in a pool.
The creature burnt the cottage in rage because no one in the cottage was agreeing to make friendship with him and thus he also killed his brother William.
The monster demands a female companion like himself.
He promised Victor that he will disappear into South American wilderness if he accepts his request.
He started working on the female creature on the Orkney Islands but he is plagued by premonitions of disaster, particularly the idea that creating a mate for the creature would breed a race that could plague mankind.
He destroys the female creature after he finds the creature (Monster) looking through the window.
The monster kills Henry Clerval (Friend & schoolfellow of Victor) but Victor is imprisoned for Clerval's murder and suffers a mental breakdown in the prison.
After released he returns home with his father.
In Geneva, Victor plans to marry Elizabeth. The night before their wedding, Victor asks Elizabeth to stay in her room while he looks for the monster.
While Victor searches 'Monster' in the house and ground, the creature murders Elizabeth.
Victor is grieved stricken to see monster through the window killing Elizabeth.
Victor's father dies of grief through the death of William, Justine, Clerval and Elizabeth.
Victor pursues the monster to the North Pole but he does not kill his creation. Creature vanishes after few days.
Robert Walton writes letters from an Arctic voyage.
He meets Victor Frankenstein, who tells his own story.
Victor builds a living being from dead body parts.
He flees in horror and abandons the creature.
The creature learns language, then turns to revenge after rejection.
Victor refuses to make a female companion for the creature.
The creature kills people Victor loves, and Victor dies at sea.
The creature mourns his maker and disappears into the ice.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hyperion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Keats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished blank verse epic on the fall of the Titans and the rise of Apollo.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Begun in autumn 1818 and abandoned in 1819. The publishers printed the fragment in the 1820 volume against Keats's wish. Database composition note is right, but it omits the 1820 publication. The Fall of Hyperion, a rewrite, was published in 1856.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Saturn (The fallen king of the Titans); Hyperion (The sun Titan who has not yet fallen); Thea (Hyperion's sister, who comforts Saturn); Apollo (The young god who is rising to replace Hyperion); Mnemosyne (Memory, who meets Apollo as he becomes a god)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
12. Bright Star, Would I Were Stead Fast as Thou Art Endymion: A Poetic Romance (1818)
This is the first long poem of Keats.
It is based on Greek myth of Endymion, a shepherd loved by the moon goddess, Selene.
The poem is in Heroic couplets.
Keats called this poem "a test, a trial of his power of imagination and of his inventions".
The poem was dedicated to Thomas Chatterton.
This poem was attacked by 'The Quarterly Review' and 'Blackwood Magazine'.
Opening Lines: "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever: Its loveliness increases; it will never Pass into nothingness; but still will keep A bower quiet for us, and a sleep Full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing".
It is dedicated to Thomas Chatterton, and it has 4000 lines.
Keats is known for his Hellenic spirit.
It is an incomplete epic poem by Keats.
It relates the story of the despair of the Titans and after their fall to the Olympians.
He left this poem incomplete because it was criticized of being Miltonic.
It exists in 2 versions but both are incomplete.
The main theme is the war between Titans and the later Olympian. The Hyperion, the old sun-god is dethroned by Apollo. On First Looking into Chapman's Homer.
It is a sonnet by Keats written in 1816.
He was overwhelmed while going through the translation of Chapman's Homer's Iliad.
This poem is a Petrarchan sonnet divided into an octave and a sestet, with rhyme scheme - abba, abba cd cd cd.
Saturn, a fallen Titan, sits in a dark vale and mourns his lost power.
Thea leads him to the other defeated Titans.
Hyperion, the sun Titan, still holds his brightness but feels doom coming.
The council of Titans cannot understand why beauty and new gods replace them.
Apollo awakes into godhood.
Keats broke the poem off there.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Marriage

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1818 (Sort Year: 1818)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Susan Ferrier

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about a foolish elopement and two very different daughters.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1818 is correct. An 1809 letter already describes the plan. William Blackwood of Edinburgh published the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lady Juliana (A selfish English beauty who elopes and then regrets it); Henry Douglas (The Highland officer she marries); Mary Douglas (The neglected twin, raised with sense and kindness); Adelaide (The twin raised in London fashion); Alicia Douglas (Mary's aunt and moral guide)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lady Juliana elopes with Henry Douglas and goes to his Highland home.
She hates the rough house, the aunts, and the poor life.
She has twin girls, Mary and Adelaide, and she neglects Mary.
Aunt Alicia raises Mary, while Juliana takes Adelaide to London.
The grown Mary stands up to fashion and to selfish relatives.
She marries a worthy Scotsman, and the ending praises that match.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Nightmare Abbey

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1818 (Sort Year: 1818)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Love Peacock

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel that laughs at Romantic gloom and at Shelley, Coleridge, and Byron.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in October 1818. Database year 1818 is correct. Shelley read it in Italy and praised it in 1819.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Scythrop Glowry (A melancholy reformer drawn from Percy Bysshe Shelley); Mr Flosky (A misty talker drawn from Samuel Taylor Coleridge); Mr Cypress (A gloomy poet drawn from Lord Byron); Marionetta O'Carroll (One of the two women Scythrop loves); Celinda Toobad (The other woman in Scythrop's tangled love plot)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Scythrop Glowry mopes in a tower and plans to reform the world.
His pamphlet sells only seven copies.
He is torn between Marionetta and Celinda.
Mr Flosky talks in cloudy, mystical phrases.
Mr Cypress broods like a gloomy exile.
The jokes stay light, and Shelley himself enjoyed the book.

items.title: "The Heart of Midlothian" (1818) — Sir Walter Scott

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Heart of Midlothian

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1818 (Sort Year: 1818)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sir Walter Scott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jeanie Deans walks to London to save her condemned sister.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1818 is correct. It appeared as Tales of My Landlord, Second Series, still without Scott's name.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jeanie Deans (An honest young woman who walks to London for her sister); Effie Deans (Jeanie's sister, accused of child murder); Davie Deans (Their strict religious father); Duke of Argyle (The nobleman who helps Jeanie meet the queen)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
7.
It was published in 4 volumes under the title "Tales of My Landlord" in 1818.
Jeanie Deans is the heroine of the novel.
The story opens in Edinburgh after the Porteous riots of 1736.
Effie Deans is accused of killing her newborn child.
Jeanie will not lie in court, so Effie is condemned.
Jeanie walks from Scotland to London to seek a pardon.
The Duke of Argyle helps her reach Queen Caroline.
Effie is spared, but shame and loss still follow the family.

items.title: "The Revolt of Islam" (1818) — Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Revolt of Islam

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1818 (Sort Year: 1818)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A twelve canto romance of a peaceful revolution that tyrants crush.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written at Marlow in 1817 as Laon and Cythna. The printer suppressed it. It was reissued in 1818 as The Revolt of Islam. A few copies of that issue are dated 1817. Database year 1818 is the usual book year. The posthumous flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Laon (The young revolutionary hero); Cythna (Laon's beloved, a leader who speaks for women's freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The chief characters are Loan and Cythna.
They have dedicated their lives to the cause of liberty and freedom.
They are presented as true freedom fighters.
The main theme of the poem is to glorify liberty and work for the liberation of mankind.
Cythna's united work with Loan rouses the spirit of revolt among the heroic souls who rise against their tyrants and try to throw off the oppression exercised upon the people prophesying Islam.
The revolt is temporarily successful.
Soon the tyrants come back with increased forces and bring desolation, famine and plague with them.
The Loan and Cythna are burnt alive.
Shelley first called the poem Laon and Cythna.
Laon and Cythna lead a nonviolent rising in a golden city.
Kings and priests crush the revolt with blood.
The lovers are killed, but their hope of liberty does not die.
The poem says the ideal of freedom is larger than any one defeat.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Don Juan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1819 (Sort Year: 1819)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gordon, Lord Byron

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic epic about an innocent youth and the false manners around him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He began it in 1818. Cantos I and II appeared in July 1819. He completed 16 cantos and started a 17th. Cantos XV and XVI appeared in March 1824. He died in April 1824. The database span 1819-24 matches the publication run.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (A joking voice, close to Byron, who comments on every adventure); Don Juan (A young Spaniard who is more often pursued than cruel); Donna Inez (Juan's strict, mathematical mother, a comic hit at Lady Byron); Haidee (The Greek woman who loves Juan after the shipwreck)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1819 - 1824)
It is a satiric poem of Byron called Magnum Opus.
It is written in 17 cantos, so it is called an epic.
He published first two cantos anonymously in 1819.
In Canto 3, he expresses his determination for poets as Wordsworth and Coleridge.
In a letter to Francis Hodgson, Byron referred to Wordsworth as "Turdsworth".
It is about the legend Don Juan who is easily seduced by women.
He could not complete its 17th canto because of his death in 1824.
It starts with the birth of Don Juan who has an affair with a friend of his mother.
On finding, Juan is sent to Cadiz where his ship wrecks and he survived but then meets a pirate's daughter whose men sell Juan as a slave.
The narrator says he wants a hero and chooses Don Juan.
Young Juan is sent abroad after a scandal in Spain.
On a Greek island, Haidee loves the shipwrecked Juan.
He is sold into slavery in Constantinople.
He later fights for Russia and is sent to England.
The narrator keeps breaking the story to mock society and poets.
Byron left the poem unfinished at his death in 1824.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ivanhoe

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1819 (Sort Year: 1819)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sir Walter Scott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Saxon knight returns from the Crusades to a divided England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1819 is correct. Scott dictated it while ill, and it was published at the end of 1819. It was still anonymous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Wilfred of Ivanhoe (A Saxon knight loyal to King Richard); Rowena (A Saxon heiress whom Ivanhoe loves); Rebecca (A Jewish healer, daughter of Isaac of York); Brian de Bois-Guilbert (A Templar knight who desires Rebecca); King Richard (The king who returns from the Crusade in disguise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in England in 1194, after the Crusades.
Wilfred of Ivanhoe returns in disguise to his father, Cedric.
Cedric wants Rowena to marry a Saxon lord, not Ivanhoe.
At a tournament, Ivanhoe defeats the Norman knight Bois-Guilbert.
Bois-Guilbert's allies seize Rowena, Isaac, and Rebecca.
King Richard and Robin of Locksley's men free the prisoners.
Rebecca is tried as a witch, and Ivanhoe fights for her.
Ivanhoe marries Rowena, and Rebecca leaves England.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Indicator

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1819 (Sort Year: 1819)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Leigh Hunt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A weekly paper of short personal essays, mostly written by Hunt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database span 1819 to 1821 is correct. Britannica and the Poetry Foundation both date the weekly Indicator to those years. It is the paper itself, not a poem printed first in a magazine. Hunt's later Autobiography recalls writing it at York Buildings and ending it at Mortimer Terrace.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leigh Hunt (The editor and the main essay writer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hunt edited this weekly paper from 1819 to 1821.
Most of the writing is his own familiar essay.
The pieces talk of books, manners, nature, and daily life.
Charles Lamb liked the paper so much that he wrote a sonnet for it.
Hunt later said he wrote part of it at York Buildings.
He finished the paper at Mortimer Terrace in Kentish Town.

items.title: "The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent" (1819) — Washington Irving

fields.label: Work Title
