fields.value: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1819 (Sort Year: 1819)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Washington Irving

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Stories and essays, including Rip Van Winkle and The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Seven American parts ran from 1819 to 1820. London volumes appeared in 1820. Rip Van Winkle was in the first part. Sleepy Hollow came in a later part.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Geoffrey Crayon (The polite narrator, and Irving's pen name); Rip Van Winkle (A kind, lazy husband who sleeps for twenty years); Dame Van Winkle (Rip's sharp-tongued wife); Ichabod Crane (A lank schoolmaster who hopes to marry Katrina); Brom Bones (Katrina's rival, often suspected of the midnight trick); The Headless Horseman (A ghostly rider said to be a Hessian trooper)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Irving publishes the book under the name Geoffrey Crayon.
American readers received it in seven parts from 1819 to 1820.
A London edition in two volumes followed in 1820.
Rip Van Winkle sleeps twenty years and wakes after the Revolution.
Ichabod Crane is chased by the Headless Horseman in Sleepy Hollow.

items.title: "Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems" (1820) — John Keats

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Keats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Keats's last book, gathering Lamia, Isabella, St. Agnes, the great odes, and Hyperion.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in late June 1820. The advertisement is dated 26 June 1820. It holds Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, the odes, and the Hyperion fragment. Database year 1820 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lamia (A serpent who becomes a woman and loves Lycius); Lycius (The young man whom Lamia loves); Apollonius (A philosopher whose stare destroys Lamia); Isabella (A woman who hides her murdered lover's head in a pot of basil)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lamia tells how a serpent woman loves a young man, until wisdom destroys her.
Isabella retells a Boccaccio story of love, murder, and a pot of basil.
The Eve of St. Agnes tells Porphyro and Madeline's escape.
The other poems include the 1819 odes, except Ode on Indolence.
The publishers added the unfinished Hyperion at the end.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Melmoth the Wanderer

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Robert Maturin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Gothic novel about a man who sold his soul and searches for someone to take his bargain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1820 is correct. The preface is dated Dublin, 31 August 1820. Constable of Edinburgh and Hurst, Robinson of London published four volumes. The title page says it is by the author of Bertram. It is a novel, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Melmoth (A Dublin student who inherits the terrible family story); Melmoth the Wanderer (The ancestor who still lives and tempts the desperate); Stanton (An English traveller whose manuscript tells an early tale)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Young John Melmoth leaves college to sit with a dying uncle.
He finds a portrait of an ancestor who should have died long before.
A manuscript tells of Stanton and of the man who still walks.
The Wanderer has extra years of life and tries to pass on his curse.
Tale sits inside tale, and the terror is religious as well as physical.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Prometheus Unbound

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lyrical drama in which Prometheus forgives Jupiter and the world is renewed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Act I was drafted in 1818. Shelley finished the drama at Florence in autumn 1819. It was published in 1820 with the Ode to the West Wind and other lyrics. Database year 1820 is correct. The posthumous flag is wrong. It is a reading drama, not a stage tragedy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prometheus (The Titan who stands for moral will and refuses revenge); Asia (His beloved, a spiritual ideal beyond ordinary humanity); Jupiter (The tyrant god who is overthrown); Demogorgon (The mysterious power that casts Jupiter down)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1820)
It is a 4 acts lyrical drama by Shelley, published in 1820.
It is concerned with the torments of the Greek mythological figure Prometheus who defies the gods and gives fire to humanity, for which he is subjected to eternal punishment and suffering at the hands of Zeus.
It is inspired by the classical "Promethia" a trilogy of plays by Aeschylus.
It is a closet drama.
Shelley's play concerns Prometheus release from captivity but unlike Aeschylus' version there is no reconciliation between Prometheus and Jupiter (Zeus).
The play begins (Act I & II) in the Indian Caucasus where titan Prometheus is bound to a rock face and he is surrounded by the Oceanides Panthea and Lone.
Act III scene takes place in heaven. Act IV opens a voice fills the forest near Prometheus cave as Lone and Panthea sleep.
Shelley compares his Romantic hero Prometheus to Milton's Satan from Paradise Lost.
Prometheus is tortured for giving mankind moral freedom.
He recalls his curse on Jupiter and chooses to forgive.
Asia, his beloved, questions the deep power Demogorgon.
Demogorgon overthrows Jupiter.
Prometheus does not take the throne.
The last act sings a renewed earth and a renewed human mind.

items.title: "The Four Ages of Poetry" (1820) — Thomas Love Peacock

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Four Ages of Poetry

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Love Peacock

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A witty essay that calls modern poetry a decline and mocks the Lake Poets.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It appeared in November 1820 in Ollier's Literary Miscellany. Shelley wrote his reply in 1821. That reply was published in 1840.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Love Peacock (The essayist attacking the claims of modern poets)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
As per Thomas Love Peacock there are four ages of poetry: i.
Peacock divides poetry into four ages, like metals.
He says early poetry was useful to a young society.
He argues that later poetry grows artificial and weak.
He mocks the Lake Poets as ignorant of real life.
Shelley answered with A Defence of Poetry.

items.title: "The Precepts of Jesus" (1820) — Raja Rammohun Roy

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Precepts of Jesus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Raja Rammohun Roy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A selection of the moral sayings of Jesus, offered as a guide to peace.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1820 is correct. The full title is Precepts of Jesus, the Guide to Peace and Happiness. Roy wrote it in English. It is not a translation of an Indian book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jesus (The teacher whose moral sayings are collected here.); Rammohun Roy (The man who selected the sayings and argued for them.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1820 Roy published this book in English.
He took the moral teachings of Jesus from the four Gospels.
He offered them as a guide to peace and happiness.
He did not present a full church creed.
He denied that Christianity was the only true path.
The book sits with his reform writings, apart from the Upanishad tracts.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Vampire

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1820 (Sort Year: 1820)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Planché

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A two act romantic melodrama about a vampire who seeks a bride in the Scottish isles.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1820 is correct. HathiTrust dates the first performance to 9 August 1820 at the Lyceum. Notre Dame holds the 1820 London edition printed for John Lowndes. That copy says it was acted at the English Opera House.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lord Ruthven (The earl whose body hides a vampire); Lady Margaret (The young woman he wants to marry); Ronald (Baron of the Isles and Margaret's father); Unda (A spirit who speaks in the opening vision)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An opening vision warns that a vampire walks in the Scottish isles.
A vampire here is a dead being who preys on the living.
Lord Ruthven must win a bride before the full moon sets.
He pursues Lady Margaret, daughter of Ronald, Baron of the Isles.
The play was acted at the English Opera House on 9 August 1820.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Adonais

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1821 (Sort Year: 1821)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A pastoral elegy mourning John Keats and claiming his spirit lives on.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written in May and June 1821, after Keats died in February 1821, and published in 1821. Database year 1821 is correct. The database posthumous flag is wrong. Shelley was still alive. The Triumph of Life, not Adonais, is the posthumous fragment.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (Shelley as the mourning poet); Adonais (John Keats, figured as a young god who has died); Urania (The heavenly muse who grieves for her son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker weeps for Adonais, the poetic name of Keats.
Urania, a mighty mother of poets, mourns her son.
Fellow poets come as shepherds to the dead man's bier.
The poem turns from grief to a claim that Keats is not dead.
His spirit has outsoared the shadow of our night.

items.title: "Confessions of an English Opium-Eater" (1821) — Thomas De Quincey

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1821 (Sort Year: 1821)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas De Quincey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An autobiography of how De Quincey came to take opium, and of the dreams that followed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: London Magazine printed it in September and October 1821. A book, with an appendix, followed in 1822. He rewrote and expanded it in 1856 for his collected works.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas De Quincey (The narrator, telling his own life as an opium eater); Ann (A young woman who befriended him during his hungry months in London)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The writer tells of a lonely boyhood and of running away to London.
He remembers a poor girl named Ann who helped him in the streets.
At Oxford he first takes opium to ease a painful face.
He describes the early pleasures, then the nightmares of long use.
He says he writes to warn readers, yet the dreams still sound beautiful.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Table-Talk

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1821 (Sort Year: 1821)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Hazlitt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Personal essays on art, travel, reading, and everyday feeling.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database span 1821-22 is correct. Volume 1 appeared on 6 April 1821. Volume 2 appeared on 15 June 1822.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Hazlitt (The essayist speaking in his own person)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a collection of essays by Hazlitt.
Originally published in 2 volumes, first of which appeared in 1821.
The essay deals with topics such as art, literature and philosophy.
The essay "The Indian Jugglers" is an essay of this anthology.
Hazlitt gathers essays that had often begun in magazines.
Topics include painting, going on a journey, and the style of familiar prose.
The speaker is Hazlitt himself, talking as if at a table.
He mixes private memory with general ideas about art and manners.
A second volume followed a year after the first.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Spy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1821 (Sort Year: 1821)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Fenimore Cooper

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tale of divided loyalty in the Neutral Ground during the American Revolution.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Project Gutenberg date the novel to 1821. It followed the weak imitation Precaution in 1820. The database year 1821 is correct. It is an English original. Later translations do not make it a translated work.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harvey Birch (A peddler whom both sides suspect of being a spy); Mr. Harper (A quiet stranger who seeks shelter with the family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The setting is Westchester County, between the British and American lines.
A mysterious stranger, Mr. Harper, takes shelter with a Loyalist family.
The peddler Harvey Birch is suspected of spying for pay.
Disguises, captures, and family ties test who is truly loyal.
The book made Cooper famous in America and abroad.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Bracebridge Hall

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1822 (Sort Year: 1822)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Washington Irving

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Further sketches of an English country house and its odd residents.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Irving delivered the manuscript in March 1822. London and American editions both appeared in 1822. The database year 1822 is correct. The database genre Poetry is wrong, because the book is prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Geoffrey Crayon (The narrator, still using Irving's pen name); Frank Bracebridge (The young friend who brings the narrator into the household)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Geoffrey Crayon returns to the Bracebridge family.
The setting is an English manor, based loosely on Aston Hall.
The book describes manners, servants, and country customs.
Separate tales, including The Stout Gentleman, sit inside the frame.
It is a sequel to the Sketch Book, and it appeared in 1822.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hellas

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1822 (Sort Year: 1822)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse drama on the Greek fight for freedom from Turkish rule.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written at Pisa in autumn 1821 and published in 1822, before Shelley died that July. Database year 1822 is the publication year. The posthumous flag is wrong. The University of Toronto text dates the writing to autumn 1821.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mahmud (The Turkish ruler who hears reports of the war); The Chorus (Greek captives who sing of a renewed Hellas)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The scene is the palace of Mahmud, the Turkish sultan.
Messengers and visions bring news of the Greek rising.
Greek captives form a chorus and hope for liberty.
The last news in the play is a Turkish victory, which shocks them.
The final chorus still dreams that a brighter Hellas will rise.

items.title: "The Triumph of Life" (1824) — Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Triumph of Life

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1824 (Sort Year: 1824)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Percy Bysshe Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished vision of a chariot of Life that conquers almost everyone.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Begun at San Terenzo in 1822 and left unfinished at his death on 8 July 1822. Mary Shelley printed it in Posthumous Poems in 1824. Database wording written 1822; published 1824 is correct. The posthumous flag is right for this poem only.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (The dreaming poet who watches the procession); The Chariot of Life (The conquering car that drags humanity behind it); Rousseau (A ruined guide who explains the captives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet lies near the sea and falls into a vision.
A cold glare and a triumphal chariot rush through a crowd.
People of every rank are chained to the car of Life.
A guide, the figure of Rousseau, explains the captives.
Shelley left the poem unfinished when he drowned.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Essays of Elia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1823 (Sort Year: 1823)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Lamb

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Personal essays, first signed Elia, about memory, the city, friends, and odd tastes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Single essays ran in the London Magazine from 1820. The collected book Essays of Elia is 1823. Database year 1823 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elia (Lamb's essay persona, playful, nostalgic, and fond of London)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lamb began the essays in the London Magazine in 1820.
He writes as Elia, a gentle and slightly odd persona.
Dream Children recalls a family life that never really was.
A Dissertation upon Roast Pig turns a joke into a fond essay.
The essays were collected as a book in 1823.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Pioneers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1823 (Sort Year: 1823)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Fenimore Cooper

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first Leatherstocking novel, about an old scout facing a new frontier town.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Project Gutenberg date the book to 1823. Natty appears here as an old man. Later tales go back to his youth. The database year 1823 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Natty Bumppo (An old wilderness scout, here called Leatherstocking); Judge Marmaduke Temple (The founder of Templeton, based on Cooper's father)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Templeton is a new settlement, drawn from Cooperstown.
Judge Marmaduke Temple stands for law, farms, and the march of settlement.
Old Natty Bumppo, called Leatherstocking, defends the wild woods.
A young hunter and an aged Mohican are caught in the same quarrel.
The book is the first full portrait of American frontier life in a novel.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Valperga

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1823 (Sort Year: 1823)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mary Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In medieval Italy, a rising lord and a free-minded countess are torn between love and power.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1823 is correct. The subtitle is The Life and Adventures of Castruccio, Prince of Lucca.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Castruccio Castracani (A historical soldier who becomes prince of Lucca); Euthanasia (The Countess of Valperga, who chooses liberty over Castruccio's power)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is set in fourteenth-century Italy.
Castruccio Castracani rises as a soldier and lord of Lucca.
He loves Euthanasia, the countess who rules Valperga.
She supports liberty, while he seeks personal power.
The story tests love against political liberty.

items.title: "“On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth”" (1823) — Thomas De Quincey

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: “On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth”

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1823 (Sort Year: 1823)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas De Quincey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay on why the knock after Duncan's murder feels so solemn in Macbeth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First printed in the London Magazine in October 1823. It was part of Notes from the Pocket-Book of a Late Opium-Eater. The database year 1823 is correct. It is criticism, not a drama by De Quincey.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The essayist (De Quincey, speaking as a reader who trusts feeling over dry reason); Macbeth (The murderer in Shakespeare's play, named as the subject of the essay); Lady Macbeth (His partner in the murder, who has tried to put human pity aside)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Since childhood the writer has felt a strange awe at the knock in Macbeth.
Reason says a knock should not change the murder, but feeling says it does.
He compares this with a real murder, where a knock also came afterward.
Macbeth and Lady Macbeth have stepped outside ordinary human life.
The knock calls the ordinary world back, and that return makes the crime more terrible.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Imaginary Conversations

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1824 (Sort Year: 1824)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walter Savage Landor

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Prose dialogues in which historical people discuss politics, art, and life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Volumes 1 and 2 appeared in 1824, volume 3 in 1828, and volumes 4 and 5 in 1829. More talks came as late as 1853. The database span 1824-1829 is right for the main series.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aesop (The fable writer, in a dialogue with Rhodope); Rhodope (The woman who hears Aesop on fame and death)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Landor imagines talks between people who often never met.
Speakers include Greeks, Romans, and later European writers.
Many talks attack tyrants and praise liberty.
The style is rich, formal, and close to classical prose.
The series began in 1824 and the fifth volume came in 1829.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Inheritance

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1824 (Sort Year: 1824)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Susan Ferrier

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about a false heiress who must learn honesty.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1824 is correct. Blackwood published it. Many readers of her time called it her best novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gertrude St Clair (A young woman who believes she is heir to Rossville); Colonel Delmour (The charming spendthrift she nearly marries); Edward Lyndsay (The steady nephew who loves her and uncovers the truth); Lewiston (The coarse man who claims to be her father); Sarah St Clair (The woman who has pretended to be Gertrude's mother)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gertrude St Clair thinks she will inherit the Rossville estate.
She is charmed by reckless Colonel Delmour and spends far too much.
Edward Lyndsay gives sound advice, which she long ignores.
A man named Lewiston claims to be her father, so she gives up the estate.
Lyndsay finds that her true mother was not the woman who raised her.
She marries Lyndsay, and later she is mistress of Rossville again.

items.title: "The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner" (1824) — James Hogg

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1824 (Sort Year: 1824)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Hogg

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dark novel about a man who thinks God has already saved him, so he may kill.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica, the University of Stirling, and Project Gutenberg date the novel to 1824. The database year is correct. It was published in the Romantic period.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Editor (The frame narrator who gathers reports and a found memoir); Robert Wringhim (A strict Calvinist who writes the confession); George Colwan (Robert's brother, heir of Dalcastle, and his enemy); Gil-Martin (A mysterious double who shares Robert's face and his plans)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An editor tells the story of the Colwan house from outside evidence.
Robert Wringhim believes he is one of the elect, already saved by God.
A strange companion, Gil-Martin, urges him toward murder.
Robert's own memoir then retells the same events in his voice.
The two accounts do not match, so the reader cannot settle the truth.

items.title: "The Spirit of the Age" (1825) — William Hazlitt

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Spirit of the Age

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1825 (Sort Year: 1825)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Hazlitt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sharp prose portraits of the leading writers and public men of his time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1825 is correct. Henry Colburn published it in London on 11 January 1825. That first London edition did not put Hazlitt's name on the title page. A Paris edition the same year did.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Hazlitt (The critic who draws the portraits); Samuel Taylor Coleridge (A real poet Hazlitt both admires and blames); William Wordsworth (A real poet whose early hope Hazlitt contrasts with later fame); Sir Walter Scott (A real novelist included among the portraits)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
v)
Hazlitt sketches living figures such as Bentham, Wordsworth, and Coleridge.
He also portrays Scott, Byron, Southey, and other public men.
Each sketch mixes praise with a hard judgment.
He asks what happened to the radical hopes of the 1790s.
The book reads as a group portrait of one generation.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Last Man

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1826 (Sort Year: 1826)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mary Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In a future England, a plague leaves Lionel Verney to record the end of humankind.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1826 is correct. The story is set in the late twenty-first century.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lionel Verney (The narrator who lives to tell how the plague ends human society); Verney's circle (Companions whose lives recall Percy Shelley and Lord Byron)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lionel Verney tells the story of a future England.
The novel imagines Britain as a republic (a state without a king).
A plague spreads across the world and kills almost everyone.
Friends around Verney recall Shelley and Byron.
Verney survives to record the end of humankind.

items.title: "The Last of the Mohicans" (1826) — James Fenimore Cooper

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Last of the Mohicans

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1826 (Sort Year: 1826)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Fenimore Cooper

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A chase through the woods in 1757, during the French and Indian War.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Project Gutenberg date the book to 1826. The story is set in 1757, in the French and Indian War. The database year 1826 is correct. Do not use 1757 as the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hawkeye (Natty Bumppo in middle age, a scout for the British); Chingachgook (A Mohican chief and Hawkeye's companion); Uncas (Chingachgook's son, called the last of the Mohicans); Magua (A Huron warrior who betrays the traveling party)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The full title calls it a narrative of 1757.
Two sisters travel toward Fort William Henry with a Huron guide.
The guide, Magua, betrays them in the forest.
Hawkeye, Chingachgook, and Uncas try to rescue the captives.
Uncas is the young Mohican whom the title calls the last of his people.

items.title: "Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries" (1828) — Leigh Hunt

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1828 (Sort Year: 1828)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Leigh Hunt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose memoir of Byron and other writers Hunt had known.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1828 is correct. Britannica says the Autobiography of 1850 partly rewrites this book. It is prose, not poetry. The database serial flag does not fit a single 1828 volume. Hunt returned to England in 1825 on an advance for the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leigh Hunt (The writer remembering his life with Byron and others); Lord Byron (The poet whose pride and habits Hunt describes); Percy Bysshe Shelley (The friend whose life Hunt sketches in the same book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After Shelley drowned, Hunt was stuck in Italy and needed Byron's help.
Byron disliked Hunt's family, and their journal The Liberal soon failed.
Henry Colburn paid Hunt in advance so he could write this book and come home.
The book appeared in 1828 and spoke harshly of Byron.
Many readers thought Hunt had attacked a dead friend for money.
It also includes a memoir of Shelley of about seventy pages.
The Autobiography of 1850 tells the same years in a gentler voice.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Records of Woman

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1828 (Sort Year: 1828)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Felicia Hemans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sequence of poems about women who face love, loss, courage, or death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1828 is correct for the book. The Homes of England had appeared in Blackwood's Magazine in 1827. The Penn text used here is a second edition, also dated 1828. The University of Nebraska lists the 1828 Edinburgh and New York editions.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Arabella Stuart (A historical woman shown in prison after a forbidden marriage); Properzia Rossi (A sculptor carving a last work for a lost love); Joan of Arc (The soldier saint, shown after her public triumph); The speaker of The Homes of England (A voice praising the great and cottage homes of England)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Each poem centers on a woman from history, legend, or home life.
Figures include Arabella Stuart, Properzia Rossi, and Joan of Arc.
The women often speak at a crisis of love, faith, or parting.
Miscellaneous poems in the same book include The Homes of England.
Hemans dedicated the volume to the dramatist Joanna Baillie.

items.title: "The Fakeer of Jungheera and Other Poems" (1828) — Henry Louis Vivian Derozio

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Fakeer of Jungheera and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1828 (Sort Year: 1828)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1828 story poem and collection that shows widow burning as misery, not glory.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1828 is right. The Calcutta title page names Samuel Smith and Company. The book is not posthumous. Derozio died in 1831.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nuleeni (The young widow who is led to the funeral fire); The fakeer (The wandering holy man whose double life suggested the tale)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Samuel Smith and Company published the book at Calcutta in 1828.
The long poem is set at Jungheera, a rock in the Ganges.
Derozio says a tale of a fakeer (a wandering holy man) suggested the plot.
The heroine Nuleeni is brought to her husband's funeral fire.
She walks around the pile and slowly mounts the pyre.
His note says Europe is wrong to call this death heroic love.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems, Chiefly Lyrical

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1830 (Sort Year: 1830)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Tennyson's first solo book, a mixed volume of lyrics that includes Mariana.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poetry Foundation dates the book June 1830. It was published by Effingham Wilson and signed Alfred Tennyson. It is not anonymous and not posthumous. The database flags that say otherwise are wrong. The database year 1830 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mariana (A lonely woman waiting in a moated grange for a lover who does not come)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book appeared in June 1830, while Tennyson was still a young Cambridge poet.
Many poems are uneven, but a few already show his gift for mood.
Mariana waits in a lonely grange and wishes she were dead.
The Kraken sleeps under the sea until fire wakes it.
Arthur Hallam praised the book, while some reviewers later attacked its manner.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Songs of the Affections

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1830 (Sort Year: 1830)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Felicia Hemans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A volume of lyrics about love, exile, grief, and the pull of home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1830 is correct. Wikisource prints the Edinburgh and London title page dated 1830. The University of Nebraska lists that 1830 edition and a Philadelphia edition in 1831.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The returned spirit (The beloved voice in the opening poem A Spirit's Return); The speakers of the songs (Lovers, exiles, wives, and mourners in separate lyrics)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens with A Spirit's Return, a poem of love beyond death.
Other poems tell of wives, exiles, soldiers, and parted families.
Affection is shown as loyal, painful, and often crossed by war or distance.
Hemans dedicated the volume to Sir Robert Liston.
It continues the interest in feeling that shaped Records of Woman.

items.title: "The Life of Lord Byron" (1830) — Thomas Moore

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Life of Lord Byron

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1830 (Sort Year: 1830)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Moore

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Moore's life of his friend Byron, built from letters, journals, and personal memory.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: John Murray published it in 1830. The database year is correct, but the genre label Poetry is wrong. This is prose. Moore and Murray burned Byron's memoirs in 1824. This book is not that burned manuscript.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lord Byron (The poet whose letters and life are the subject); Thomas Moore (Byron's friend, who edits the papers and tells the life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Byron left Moore his memoirs, and Moore later agreed they should be burned.
Moore then collected Byron's letters and journals for a public book.
He adds a running life of the poet between the documents.
The portrait shows the friend, the celebrity, and the exile.
The book became the standard early life of Byron.

items.title: "The Shair and Other Poems" (1830) — Kashiprasad Ghose

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Shair and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1830 (Sort Year: 1830)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Kashiprasad Ghose

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His only English poetry book, published in Calcutta, with the title poem about a poet.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1830 is kept. The Jackson bibliography and the Cambridge bibliography both give Calcutta, Scott, 1830. A review appeared in the Asiatic Journal in June 1831, so the book was already out. Representative Poetry Online dates the same title 1839. Jackson says the book came when he was just 21, which fits 1830, since he was born in 1809.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Shair (The poet speaker of the title poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Shair means a poet.
The book was published in Calcutta by Scott.
He dedicated the title poem to his teacher Horace Hayman Wilson.
He was about 21 and proud to publish as a Hindu poet in English.
The poems try English metres on Indian scenes and feelings.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Destiny

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1831 (Sort Year: 1831)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Susan Ferrier

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sober novel about a disinherited daughter who is rewarded at last.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1831 is correct. Cadell of Edinburgh paid her 1,700 pounds. The novel was anonymous. Her name appeared in the Bentley collected edition of 1841, which is the revision trap.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edith (The chief's daughter, patient and badly treated by her father); The Laird of Glenroy (Edith's proud father, who leaves his land away from her); Ronald Malcolm (The true heir of Inch Orran, long thought dead); Reginald (The nephew who inherits Glenroy and rejects Edith); Florinda (The wealthy young woman Reginald marries)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edith is the only daughter of the proud Laird of Glenroy.
He hopes to join his land with a neighbor's estate, but the plan fails.
The neighbor leaves the land to Ronald Malcolm, who is thought drowned.
Glenroy leaves his own land to his nephew Reginald.
Reginald will not marry Edith.
He marries the rich Florinda instead.
Edith nurses her dying father and faces a poor life.
Ronald returns under another name, and Edith marries him at Inch Orran.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Persecuted

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1831 (Sort Year: 1831)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Krishna Mohan Banerjee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young Hindu is cast out after he eats beef and drinks wine with his friends.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was published in Calcutta in 1831. It was never acted on a stage. The same year Banerjee was cast out by his family after friends ate beef and drank beer in his house. The database year 1831 is the publication year. There is no performance year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bany Lal (The young hero, drawn from Banerjee himself); Mohadeb (Bany Lal's orthodox father, forced to cast his son out); Bhyrub (A friend who wants Hindus freed from prejudice); Turkolankar (A Brahmin who lives on the gifts of frightened disciples); Bydhabagis (Another Brahmin who boasts of easy blessings and full pockets)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bany Lal and his friends eat forbidden beef and drink wine in his father's house.
A servant spies on them and tells the father, Mohadeb.
Brahmins press Mohadeb to excommunicate his son.
Excommunication here means being cast out of family and faith.
Bany Lal refuses to deny what he did.
He joins other young men who want Hindu society reformed.
The play was dedicated to Hindu youths and was not performed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1832 (Sort Year: 1832)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1832 volume, dated 1833, that first printed The Lady of Shalott and The Lotos-Eaters.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published at the end of 1832, with a title page dated 1833. Britannica and the Poetry Foundation both record that split. The database year 1832 is the real publication year. The book is not posthumous. Ulysses is not in this volume.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Lady of Shalott (A weaver cursed to see the world only in a mirror); The Lotos-Eaters (Sailors who abandon duty for a dreamlike calm)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book was published at the end of 1832.
The title page is dated 1833, which is the usual exam trap.
The Lady of Shalott weaves in a tower and dies when she looks at Camelot.
The Lotos-Eaters choose a drowsy life and refuse the voyage home.
Harsh reviews hurt Tennyson, and he published no new book for years.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Last Essays of Elia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1833 (Sort Year: 1833)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Lamb

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The second Elia book, gathering later essays on retirement, relatives, and old pleasures.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates The Last Essays of Elia to 1833. It is a new collection, not only a reprint of 1823. Database year 1833 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elia (The same persona, now older and newly retired)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After the 1823 book, Lamb kept writing Elia essays.
The Superannuated Man describes leaving his clerk's desk.
Poor Relations jokes, with a sting, about awkward family claims.
Old China looks back on poorer days with affection.
The pieces were gathered as The Last Essays of Elia in 1833.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pauline

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1833 (Sort Year: 1833)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An early confessional poem in which a young speaker tells Pauline about his mind and his hero Shelley.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published anonymously in 1833 as Pauline: A Fragment of a Confession. Database year 1833 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A young man confessing his inner life to Pauline); Pauline (The woman who listens); Sun-treader (Browning's name in the poem for Percy Bysshe Shelley)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem appeared with no author's name on the title page.
A young man addresses Pauline and unpacks his shifting beliefs.
He praises Shelley as the Sun-treader, a bringer of light.
The poem is a monodrama (one speaker, almost no outside action).
John Stuart Mill attacked its exposure of the poet's own feelings.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sartor Resartus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1833 (Sort Year: 1833)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Carlyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wild book on the philosophy of clothes, told through a German professor and an English editor.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He could not find a book publisher in 1831. Fraser's Magazine printed it from November 1833 to August 1834. Emerson arranged the Boston book in 1836. The London book came in 1838. The database phrase serial 1833-34, book 1836, matches the serial and the American book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Diogenes Teufelsdrockh (A made up German professor of things in general); The Editor (The English narrator who sorts the professor's paper bags)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An editor pretends to explain a German book by Diogenes Teufelsdrockh.
Clothes become a sign for the customs and creeds that cover the soul.
The professor passes through the Everlasting No, a mood of denial.
He reaches the Everlasting Yea, a choice to work and affirm life.
The editor never quite finishes the German puzzle, and the joke stays open.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Paracelsus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1835 (Sort Year: 1835)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dramatic poem about the scholar Paracelsus, who seeks perfect knowledge and learns its cost.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1835. Database year 1835 is correct. It was better received than Pauline.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Paracelsus (A Renaissance scholar hungry for ultimate knowledge); Festus (His friend, who argues for a humbler life); Aprile (A poet who stands for love, which Paracelsus has neglected)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Paracelsus tells his friend Festus that he will prove his soul by seeking knowledge.
He rejects a quiet life of love for a lonely quest.
Fame and failure both come, and his learning does not satisfy him.
Near death he sees that love and knowledge must go together.
The poem has long speeches and almost no stage action.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Pickwick Papers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1837 (Sort Year: 1837)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about Mr Pickwick and his club on a touring holiday in England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from April 1836 to November 1837. The book came out in November 1837. Database range 1836-37 matches the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong. This novel was completed.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Samuel Pickwick (A kind, naive gentleman who leads the Pickwick Club); Sam Weller (Pickwick's witty servant, famous for comic sayings); Tony Weller (Sam's coachman father); Mrs Bardell (Pickwick's landlady, who sues him for a broken promise of marriage); Alfred Jingle (A smooth talker who cheats the club)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Samuel Pickwick and three friends set out to report their travels.
The papers began as notes for pictures, then became a story.
Sam Weller becomes Pickwick's sharp and loyal servant.
Mrs Bardell sues Pickwick, and he chooses prison rather than pay.
Friends free him, and the club's adventures end in kindness.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Goblin Market

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christina Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two sisters meet goblin merchants, and one sister's love saves the other from a cursed fruit.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem first appeared in Goblin Market and Other Poems in 1862. The exact writing year is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Laura (The sister who eats the goblin fruit and falls ill); Lizzie (The sister who resists the goblins and saves Laura); The goblin men (Merchants whose fruit tempts and then harms Laura)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a children poem.
It is a fantastic allegorical tale.
It is set in a fairytale world and exploring themes of temptation, sacrifice and salvation.
'Goblin Market' tells the story of a fraught encounter between sisters Laura and Lizzie and evil goblin merchants.
When Laura exchanges a lock of her golden hair for the chance to taste the goblins' enchanted 'fruit forbidden', she deteriorates until she is 'knocking at Death's door'. Her sister Lizzie offers to pay the goblins 'a silver penny' for more of their wares, which she hopes will act as an antidote to Laura's malady.
The goblins violently attack Lizzie, smearing their fruits 'against her mouth' in a vain attempt 'to make her eat'. After the goblins are 'worn out by her resistance', Lizzie returns home, and Laura kisses the juices from her sister's face and is restored.
The fruits in the story are worldly pleasure and Laura falls for them and nearly ruined.
Lizzy resists the temptation and by her sacrifice redeems her sister's sin.
Laura and Lizzie hear goblin men crying their fruit.
Lizzie warns Laura not to look at the goblin men.
Laura pays with a lock of hair and eats the fruit.
She sickens when the goblins will not sell to her again.
Lizzie faces the goblins, and Laura is cured by her sister's courage.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Idylls of the King

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A series of blank verse tales about King Arthur, his knights, and the fall of his court.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A notebook Morte d'Arthur began in 1833 and was printed in 1842. The first Idylls volume is 1859. The set was nearly finished in 1885.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Arthur (The ideal king whose court rises and then falls); Guinevere (Arthur's queen, whose love for Lancelot helps break the court); Lancelot (Arthur's greatest knight and the queen's lover); Merlin (The wizard who is trapped by Vivien)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It contains a series of 12 connected poems. It is retelling of Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur.
First fragment "The Passing of Arthur" was published in 1842 and the other 11 stories were all added woven around King Arthur and his Round Table.
It is a story of bright hope followed by growing disillusionment with its chief characters Arthur, Guinevere, Lancelot, and Elaine.
Two shorter Arthurian poems "Sir Galahad" and "Lancelot and Guinevere" were in the same volume with Morte d'Arthur.
The 1859 edition contained only four of the twelve idylls: i) Enid ii) Merlin and Vivian iii) Lancelot and Elaine and iv) Guinevere.
But in the later edition eight more idylls were added (1869): v) The Coming of Arthur vi) Gareth and Lynette vii) Geraint viii) Balin and Balan ix) The Holy Grail x) Pelleas and Ettare xi) The Last Tournament xii) The Passing of Arthur (or Morte d'Arthur) This represents the last battle and end of Arthur's earthly lives.
In this poem Queen of Arthur, Guinevere was having affair with Lancelot.
The poem was dedicated to Prince Albert. Famous Quotes from Idylls of The King: 1. "The old order changeth, yielding plate to new And god fulfills himself in many ways Lost one good custom should corrupt the world"
The cycle grows from an early draft of Morte d'Arthur begun in 1833.
The 1859 book holds four tales, including Guinevere.
Later books add the coming of Arthur, the Holy Grail, and other knights.
Lancelot, Guinevere, and betrayal crack the fellowship of the Round Table.
The last idyll, Balin and Balan, appeared in 1885.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: In Memoriam

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long elegy for Arthur Hallam, moving from grief toward a hard won faith.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Hallam died in 1833. Tennyson wrote the lyrics over many years. The book came out in May 1850.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A mourner standing for Tennyson after Hallam's death); Arthur Hallam (The dead friend who is addressed but cannot answer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is written on the death of his friend Arthur Henry Hallam who died in 1833 at the early age of 22. It was a tribute to him.
The poem was written over a period of 17 years and includes 132 elegies, and was finally published in 1850.
Its original title was "The Way of the Soul".
It became the favorite poem of Queen Victoria.
It is written in iambic tetrameter quatrains rhyming abba, called "In Memoriam Stanza".
The poem concludes with an epilogue i.e. epithalamion on the occasion of his sister Emilia Tennyson's wedding in 1842.
Famous Quotes: 1. "It is better to have loved and lost Then never to have loved at all" 2. "Nature Red in tooth and claw"
After reading this poem after the death of Prince Albert, Queen Victoria was impressed and expressed her views about it as- 'what a comfort it had been'.
Arthur Hallam, Tennyson's closest friend, dies in 1833.
The speaker records grief in many short lyrics over the years.
He questions God, nature, and whether a person lives after death.
Famous sections ring out the old year and speak of nature's cruelty.
The book ends in a marriage poem and a cautiously hopeful faith.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Jane Eyre

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Bronte

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An orphan governess wins love without giving up her conscience.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It is not the book year. Britannica says she began the novel in August 1846. Smith, Elder published it on 16 October 1847 under the name Currer Bell. Project Gutenberg dates the book 1847.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jane Eyre (An orphan who becomes a governess and tells her own story); Edward Rochester (The master of Thornfield, whom Jane loves); Bertha Mason (Rochester's living wife, kept hidden at Thornfield); Helen Burns (Jane's gentle friend at Lowood school); St. John Rivers (A severe clergyman who later asks Jane to marry him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Orphan Jane suffers at Gateshead and at Lowood school.
She becomes governess at Thornfield and loves Mr. Rochester.
She learns that he already has a wife, Bertha Mason.
Jane leaves, then returns after the fire at Thornfield.
Rochester is blinded, Bertha is dead, and Jane marries him.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: My Last Duchess

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1842 (Sort Year: 1842)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A duke shows a visitor the portrait of his last wife and calmly reveals that he had her killed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First printed in Dramatic Lyrics in 1842. It was then titled Italy, paired with a poem called France. The title My Last Duchess was used in the 1849 Poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Duke of Ferrara (The speaker, who controls the portrait and the story); The envoy (A silent listener sent to negotiate the duke's next marriage); The last Duchess (The dead wife in the painting); Fra Pandolf (The painter of the portrait, named by the duke)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Duke of Ferrara draws a curtain from a painted portrait.
He says the duchess smiled too easily at everyone.
He resented that she ranked his gift of a nine hundred year old name with lesser joys.
He says he gave commands, and then all smiles stopped.
He turns to arrange a new marriage, and points out a bronze statue of Neptune.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Oliver Twist

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1838 (Sort Year: 1838)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor workhouse boy is pulled into a London gang of thieves, then finds a true home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial ran in Bentley's Miscellany from February 1837 to April 1839. Richard Bentley issued the three volume book in 1838. Database range 1837-39 is the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oliver Twist (An orphan boy who asks for more food); Fagin (The leader of a gang of child thieves); Bill Sikes (A violent burglar who kills Nancy); Nancy (A member of the gang who tries to protect Oliver); Mr Brownlow (A kind gentleman who takes Oliver in)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Theme- failure of charity, purity in a corrupt city and countryside.
Complete title: "The Adventures of Oliver Twist".
The other title is: "The Parish Boy's Progress".
It is a story about an orphan and illegitimate boy- Oliver Twist, who faces a miserable experience in a work house under the care of Mrs. Mann Oliver.
She only gives meager food to Oliver.
Mr. Bumble as a frequent visitor to this workhouse. He was an unsympathetic, cruel, and stone hearted man who did not care at all for the well beings of orphans.
Oliver is ill-treated by his apprentice Mr. Sowerberry along with Noah Claypole (servant of Mr. Sowerberry).
Both the apprentice made fun of Oliver's mother and even abused her.
Oliver prepared to go to London.
During his journey he met Jack Dawkins (also called Arthur Dodger) who was a member of a gang of pickpocketer.
Dodger took Oliver to London and introduced him to an old Jew Fagin who was the head of pickpocketing gang.
Thus Oliver is once again trapped with the illegal elements who were doing their business with a lot of innocent children who now use to drink alcohol, smoke cigarettes, etc.
In these gangs there were two girls also, named Nancy and Betsy.
Oliver was now under the supervision of this gang.
One day he was caught by the police for nothing because the crime for he was caught was done by Dodger and Betsy.
Because he was caught without mistake so Mr. Brownlow whose pocket was picked, felt a deep sympathy for Oliver and brought him to this own house, where he was looked after with great affection and kindness.
Oliver soon recovered from his illness and told his whole life story to Brownlow.
One day when Oliver was in way for some work he was seen by Nancy who tried to wrap him by using some powder to make him unconscious.
When Oliver protested her, she said to the public that, Oliver is her brother and thus public allowed her to take Oliver away.
Oliver again fell in the hands of criminals because Nancy took him to Fagin once again.
Fagin gave Oliver to Bill Sikes and again Oliver was forced to do robbery.
After a lot of attempts Mr. Brownlow came to know that Oliver is son of (illegitimate) Edwin Leeford.
Edwin Leeford was the intimate friend of Mr. Brownlow.
"Monks" was the legitimate son of Edwin Leeford and thus half-brother of Oliver.
After a lot of chaos Monks agreed to surrender and share his property with Oliver.
In the end Nancy was murdered and Bill Sikes while escaping through a rope got his neck entangled and struggled a lot.
Fagin was traced and sentenced to death.
Brownlow adopted Oliver as his own son.
Monk after sharing his properties with Oliver indulges into criminal activities and died in a fit.
Thus good men were rewarded and bad met their tragic end.
Oliver asks for more food at the workhouse and is punished.
He runs away to London and meets the Artful Dodger.
Fagin trains him to steal, and Bill Sikes uses him in a burglary.
Mr Brownlow shelters him, while Nancy tries to save him from the gang.
Sikes kills Nancy.
Oliver's real family is found, and Fagin is condemned.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Blessed Damozel

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dead woman leans from heaven and longs for her lover.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He drafted the poem in 1847. It first appeared in The Germ, number 2, in 1850. The Rossetti Archive chronology and the Germ contents page agree. He revised it later, including in Poems (1870). It is not the poem's year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Blessed Damozel (A dead young woman who leans from heaven); The earthly lover (The speaker who looks up and thinks he hears her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The damozel leans out from the gold bar of heaven.
She still wears her hair loose and looks down toward earth.
She pictures the lover's soul rising to meet her.
The lover on earth hears her voice and doubts the vision.
Love and heaven stay painfully far apart.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The French Revolution

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1837 (Sort Year: 1837)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Carlyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dramatic history of the French Revolution, written as a judgment on selfish rulers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The manuscript of the first volume was burned in 1835 and rewritten. Britannica dates the three volume book 1837. The database year 1837 is correct. A Victorian Web chronology wrongly says two volumes. The book is in three volumes.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Louis the Sixteenth (The king whose weak rule cannot hold the old order); Robespierre (Called the sea-green Incorruptible, a leader of the Terror); Napoleon (The soldier who ends the revolutionary turmoil with force)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Carlyle gathers sources with help from John Stuart Mill.
A draft of the first volume is burned while in Mill's keeping.
Carlyle rewrites the lost work and finishes the history.
He shows the fall of the old monarchy and the rise of new violence.
He treats the Revolution as a judgment, not as a dry list of laws.

items.title: "The House of Life" (1870) — Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The House of Life

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1870 (Sort Year: 1870)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sonnet sequence on love, art, change, and death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Some sonnets date from as early as 1847. The name The House of Life first heads a group in Poems (1870), called sonnets and songs toward that work. The finished sequence is in Ballads and Sonnets (1881), in the parts Youth and Change and Change and Fate. The introductory sonnet, A Sonnet is a moment's monument, belongs to the 1881 form.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (The lover who looks back on passion, art, and loss); Love (A personified power who appears through the sequence)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a famous sonnet sequence by D.G. Rossetti.
In this sonnet, Rossetti expresses his love for his wife.
Separate sonnets on love were gathered under one growing title.
The 1870 book offered an early, shorter form of the sequence.
One sonnet calls the form a moment's monument.
The 1881 book splits the work into Youth and Change, then Change and Fate.
The poems move from passion toward loss, art, and death.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Scholar-Gipsy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An Oxford scholar leaves books to wander with the gypsies.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem was written in 1853 and first printed in Poems (1853), published by Longman. It is not the poem's year. The correct year is 1853.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Scholar-Gipsy (An Oxford student who left the university for the gypsies); The Speaker (The poet who compares the scholar with modern unrest); The Shepherd (The country figure asked to watch for the scholar)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is based on an incident described by Joseph Glanvill (17th century writer) in the 20th chapter of his book "The Vanity of Dogmatising" (1660-1661).
The incident concerns a young Oxford student of great abilities, who left the university to live with gypsies and learn art.
Sometimes later, this scholar happens to meet his former friends who were surprised at his way of life.
He told his friends that gypsies were not imposters as they were supposed to be, but they possessed a traditional kind of learning. Imposter: one who attempts to deceive. Gypsy: a person making living from dishonest practices of theft.
Famous Lines 1. "Go, for they call you, Shepherd, from the hill; Go, Shepherd, and unite the wattled cotes:" 2. "For what wears out the life of mortal men? 'Tis that from change to change their being rolls 'Tis that repeated shocks, again, again, Exhaust the energy of strongest souls, And numb the elastic powers."
A shepherd is asked to look for the Scholar-Gipsy on the hills.
The scholar once left Oxford to learn a secret gypsy art.
He still haunts the Cumner hills, waiting for a spark from heaven.
The poet contrasts that hope with the sick hurry of modern life.
He tells the scholar to flee the fever of the present age.

items.title: "The Tenant of Wildfell Hall" (1848) — Anne Bronte

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1848 (Sort Year: 1848)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anne Bronte

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Helen flees a drunken husband, and her diary tells Gilbert why she hides.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year opens the early Victorian period. It is not the book year. Thomas Newby published it in June 1848 under the name Acton Bell. Her preface to the second edition is dated 22 July 1848.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Helen Huntingdon (The tenant, called Helen Graham while she hides); Gilbert Markham (The farmer whose letters hold the outer story); Arthur Huntingdon (Helen's husband, destroyed by alcohol and unfaithfulness)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gilbert Markham meets Helen, a reserved widow at Wildfell Hall.
The village gossips, and Gilbert misreads her silence.
Helen lets him read her private diary.
The diary records Arthur Huntingdon's drink, cruelty, and affairs.
Helen leaves with her son so the boy will not copy his father.
Huntingdon dies of his excesses, and Helen later marries Gilbert.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Wandering Heir

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1872 (Sort Year: 1872)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Reade

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short romance tied to the public fight over the Tichborne inheritance.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A scholarly list dates the Graphic Christmas serial to 25 December 1872 and marks the day as approximate. A works list also gives 1873. The London volume with Trade Malice is 1875. For sequence, use the 1872 serial.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The wandering heir (The central claimant, suggested by the Tichborne inheritance dispute)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Reade wrote the tale as a matter of fact romance, a story drawn from records.
He linked it to the Tichborne case, a famous dispute about identity and an estate.
The story ran in The Graphic Christmas number of 1872.
Critics accused him of plagiarism, which means copying another writer.
He answered in Trade Malice, printed with the tale in a London volume of 1875.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ulysses

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1842 (Sort Year: 1842)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The aged hero Ulysses refuses a quiet old age and calls his sailors to one more voyage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He finished it on 20 October 1833, after Hallam's death. It was printed in the 1842 Poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ulysses (The speaker, an old king who still longs to explore); Telemachus (His son, who will govern Ithaca with patience); The mariners (The old sailors whom Ulysses asks to sail again)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ulysses is home in Ithaca, but he is bored with ruling.
He remembers his travels and says he cannot rest from travel.
He leaves the kingdom to his careful son Telemachus.
He calls his old sailors to seek a newer world.
He ends by urging them to strive, to seek, and not to yield.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Villette

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Bronte

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lonely teacher builds a life at a school in a foreign city.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Project Gutenberg date Villette to 1853. Britannica's fuller account says it was published in January 1853. The exact month she began writing is not fixed here. The city of Villette stands for Brussels.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucy Snowe (The narrator, a quiet teacher who rebuilds her life); Madame Beck (The sharp mistress of the school in Villette); Dr. John Graham Bretton (The English doctor Lucy first loves); Paul Emanuel (The professor who becomes Lucy's deeper love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lucy Snowe leaves England after losses and seeks work abroad.
She teaches at Madame Beck's school in the city of Villette.
She is drawn first to Dr. John, then to Paul Emanuel.
She suffers a mental collapse, then recovers her strength.
She gains her own school, but Paul's fate is left uncertain.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: While the Billy Boils

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1896 (Sort Year: 1896)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Lawson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lawson's 1896 book of short stories about bush work, poverty, and endurance.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: This is a story book. First book publication is 1896. Some stories had appeared earlier in papers. The Drover's Wife was in print by 1892.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The drover's wife (A woman left for months on a poor farm with her children); Mitchell (A bush traveler who tells many of the sketches); The unknown drover (The dead man buried by a small union group)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Angus and Robertson published this story collection in 1896.
Many pieces had first appeared in the Bulletin and other papers.
The scenes move from small farms to work sheds and city lanes.
The Drover's Wife shows a woman left alone who must face a snake.
The Union Buries Its Dead and The Bush Undertaker are other key stories.
The title points to yarns told while a camp can boils for tea.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Wuthering Heights

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Emily Bronte

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A moorland story of Heathcliff's love for Catherine and his long revenge.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year opens the Victorian period. It is not the book year. Thomas Newby published it in December 1847. Emily began it about 1845.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lockwood (The tenant whose visit opens the story and who dreams of Cathy); Nelly Dean (The housekeeper who tells most of the family history); Heathcliff (An orphan who loves Catherine and later ruins both families); Catherine Earnshaw (Heathcliff's fierce beloved, who marries Edgar Linton); Edgar Linton (The gentle owner of Thrushcross Grange and Catherine's husband); Hareton Earnshaw (Hindley's son, who finds a gentler ending with young Cathy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lockwood visits Wuthering Heights and meets the harsh Heathcliff.
He dreams that Catherine's ghost begs to be let in.
The housekeeper Nelly Dean tells him the family history.
Mr Earnshaw brings home the orphan Heathcliff.
Catherine loves Heathcliff, but she marries Edgar Linton.
Heathcliff leaves, then returns rich and seeks revenge.
Catherine dies after the birth of her daughter Cathy.
Years later, young Cathy and Hareton begin to find peace.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Nicholas Nickleby

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1839 (Sort Year: 1839)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young man fights a cruel Yorkshire school and his uncle's plots against the family.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from April 1838 to October 1839. The book followed in 1839. Database range 1838-39 matches the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nicholas Nickleby (A young man who defends his family and Smike); Kate Nickleby (Nicholas's sister, whom Ralph tries to use); Ralph Nickleby (Their cold, rich uncle and enemy); Wackford Squeers (The cruel master of Dotheboys Hall); Smike (A starved boy whom Nicholas rescues from the school)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nicholas must earn money after his father's death.
He teaches at Dotheboys Hall, the brutal school of Wackford Squeers.
He beats Squeers and leaves with the abused boy Smike.
He protects his sister Kate from his greedy uncle Ralph.
Ralph's schemes fail, Smike dies, and Nicholas builds an honest life.

items.title: "The Seraphim and Other Poems" (1838) — Elizabeth Barrett Browning

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Seraphim and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1838 (Sort Year: 1838)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first book under her own name, led by a poem of two angels.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1838. The EBB Archive and the Poetry Foundation agree. It is the first volume with her name, apart from the private Battle of Marathon of 1820. Database year 1838 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Two Angels (Heavenly speakers who comment on the Crucifixion)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This 1838 volume was the first to print her name on the title page.
The title poem is a long talk between two angels in heaven.
They retell parts of the Bible and watch the Crucifixion.
Reviewers found that poem too high and misty.
They liked shorter pieces more, including the sad poem Isobel's Child.

items.title: "Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque" (1839) — Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1839 (Sort Year: 1839)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poe's first tale collection, mixing horror, comedy, and strange journeys in two volumes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The volumes appeared in December 1839. The title page is dated 1840, which is the database year. The first issue is 1839.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Carey and Lea issued the two volumes in Philadelphia.
The Fall of the House of Usher is one of the tales.
Ligeia and other early stories sit beside comic pieces.
Grotesque here means distorted or comic horror.
Arabesque means ornate, dreamlike design.

items.title: "The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood" (1840) — James Planché

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1840 (Sort Year: 1840)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Planché

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A fairy extravaganza that retells the tale of a princess who sleeps under a spell.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1840 is kept. A library catalogue of his 1879 Extravaganzas dates this piece to 1840. It calls the piece an extravaganza in three parts. The University of Toronto copy of volume 2 includes the play. Do not confuse it with the 1868 picture book An Old Fairy Tale.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
