fields.value: The Princess (The royal child who sleeps under the spell); The Prince (The young man who breaks the sleep)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An extravaganza is a light comic play with music and spectacle.
A princess is cursed to sleep for a long time.
A prince wakes her, and the court returns to life.
Comic scenes and showy changes of set fill out the old tale.
The collected extravaganzas date this piece to 1840.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: On Heroes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1841 (Sort Year: 1841)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Carlyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Six lectures on heroes, from gods and prophets to poets and kings.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The six lectures were given in London in May 1840. James Fraser published the book in 1841. The database year 1841 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Carlyle (The lecturer, sorting heroes into six kinds); The Hero (His name for the strong person who gives an age its direction)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Carlyle argues that world history is the story of great men.
He begins with the hero as divinity, using old pagan gods.
He treats the hero as prophet, then as poet, with Dante and Shakespeare.
He treats the hero as priest, then as man of letters.
He ends with the hero as king, naming Cromwell and Napoleon.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Dramatic Lyrics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1842 (Sort Year: 1842)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1842 collection that first printed My Last Duchess, Porphyria's Lover, and The Pied Piper.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1842 as number three of Bells and Pomegranates. Database year 1842 is correct. My Last Duchess is inside this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Duke of Ferrara (Speaker of My Last Duchess, here first called Italy); Porphyria's lover (The speaker who murders Porphyria); The Pied Piper (The figure who leads the rats, then the children, out of Hamelin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is number three in the pamphlet series Bells and Pomegranates.
My Last Duchess appears here under the early title Italy.
Porphyria's Lover lets a killer explain why he strangled Porphyria.
The Pied Piper of Hamelin tells how a town cheated the piper.
Each poem is spoken by a character in a tense moment.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Christmas Carol

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1843 (Sort Year: 1843)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A miser is shown his past, present, and future, and wakes as a generous man.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published on 19 December 1843. Database year 1843 is correct. Database genre Poetry is wrong. This is a short novel. The unfinished flag is also wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ebenezer Scrooge (A miser who learns to keep Christmas); Jacob Marley (Scrooge's dead partner, who returns as a ghost); Bob Cratchit (Scrooge's underpaid clerk); Tiny Tim (Bob's disabled young son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is one of the most famous short stories of Dickens written in 1843.
Chief characters are i)
Ebenezer Scrooge hates Christmas and refuses to help the poor.
The ghost of his partner Jacob Marley warns him to change.
Three spirits show his lonely past, the Cratchit home, and a dreaded future.
He sees that Tiny Tim may die if nothing changes.
He wakes on Christmas morning, sends a gift, and becomes a second father to Tim.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Modern Painters

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1843 (Sort Year: 1843)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Ruskin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Five volumes that defend Turner and teach how art should tell the truth of nature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database span 1843-60 is right for the whole work. Britannica dates volume one to 1843 and the fifth and final volume to 1860. The pathetic fallacy is named in volume three, in 1856.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Ruskin (The critic who argues for truth in painting); J. M. W. Turner (The painter whose late work Ruskin defends)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The first volume defends the landscape painter Turner.
Ruskin says great art tells particular truths of nature.
He studies skies, water, plants, and mountains in detail.
Later volumes ask what beauty and imagination mean.
Volume three names the pathetic fallacy.
The fifth volume appeared in 1860 and closed the work.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Past and Present

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1843 (Sort Year: 1843)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Carlyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A contrast between a strong medieval abbot and the troubled England of the 1840s.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1843, two years after On Heroes. The database year 1843 is correct. Victorian Web also lists 1843. It is a book, not a lecture series.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Abbot Samson (The medieval abbot of St Edmunds, Carlyle's model of a true ruler); The modern worker (The English labourer caught in unemployment and the cash nexus)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Carlyle looks at idle rich people and hungry workers in his own England.
He turns to the twelfth century abbey of St Edmunds.
Abbot Samson governs with work, order, and plain courage.
The modern section attacks cash payment as the only bond between people.
He calls for captains of industry who will lead work with a conscience.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Coningsby

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1844 (Sort Year: 1844)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Benjamin Disraeli

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A political novel about a young aristocrat who looks for a nobler Conservatism than Peel's.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1844 is correct. Henry Colburn published it in three volumes. The dedication is dated May Day 1844. The full title is Coningsby, or The New Generation.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harry Coningsby (A young nobleman who wants a better public life); Sidonia (A wealthy Jewish intellectual who guides Coningsby); Lord Monmouth (Coningsby's cynical, powerful grandfather); Edith Millbank (The manufacturer's daughter whom Coningsby loves)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Harry Coningsby is heir in spirit to the cynical Lord Monmouth.
He meets Sidonia, a rich Jewish thinker who challenges him.
Sidonia tells him the age of ruins is past and points to Manchester.
Coningsby loves Edith, daughter of the manufacturer Millbank.
The novel asks for a new Conservative generation based on duty.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1844 (Sort Year: 1844)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The two volume book of 1844 that made her a famous poet.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in two volumes in 1844. Britannica gives the title Poems, by Elizabeth Barrett Barrett, because she was not yet married. The American title was A Drama of Exile, and Other Poems (1845). Database year 1844 is the London book. This is not the 1850 Poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Children (The weeping child workers in The Cry of the Children); The Young Poet (The poor suitor in Lady Geraldine's Courtship)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Poems appeared in two volumes in 1844 and was widely praised.
The Cry of the Children attacks the mill and mine labour of children.
That poem had already been printed in Blackwood's Magazine in 1843.
Lady Geraldine's Courtship names Robert Browning with praise.
His letter of January 1845, loving her verses, began their courtship.

items.title: "Rambles in Germany and Italy" (1844) — Mary Shelley

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Rambles in Germany and Italy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1844 (Sort Year: 1844)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mary Shelley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A two-volume travel book about her journeys in Germany and Italy with her son.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The journeys were in 1840, 1842, and 1843. Edward Moxon published the two volumes in 1844. The database year 1844 is correct. The book is travel prose, though the database lists it as fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Shelley (The traveler and narrator of the two volumes); Percy Florence Shelley (Her son, who traveled with her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mary Shelley traveled in Germany and Italy with her son.
The trips took place in 1840, 1842, and 1843.
She describes roads, cities, art, and the people she meets.
She returns to Italy, where she had lived with Percy Shelley.
She also argues for Italian independence (freedom from foreign rule).

items.title: "Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass" (1845) — Frederick Douglass

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1845 (Sort Year: 1845)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Frederick Douglass

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first autobiography, from slavery in Maryland to escape in the North.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1845 is correct. The Anti-Slavery Office in Boston published it in 1845. His birth day stays unknown, which the book itself states.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frederick Douglass (The author, born Frederick Bailey, telling his own life); Sophia Auld (The Baltimore mistress who first helps him learn letters); Edward Covey (The slave-breaker Douglass resists); William Lloyd Garrison (The abolitionist who writes the preface)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1818 - 1895)
Frederic Douglass was an African American social, abolitionist, orator, writer and statesman.
After escaping from 'Slavery' he became a leader of 'abolitionist movement' gaining note for his dazzling oratory and incisive anti-slavery writings.
Douglass wrote several autobiographies. He describes his experiences of a slave in his 1845 autobiography Narrative of the life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, the second My Bondage and My Freedom (1855).
After the Civil War, Douglass remained an active campaigner against slavery and wrote his last autobiography Life and Times of Frederick Douglass first published in 1881, and revised in 1892.
He famously said - "I would unite with anybody to do right and with nobody to do wrong."
He later often said - "Knowledge is the pathway from Slavery to Freedom".
He remarked that in English he treated not "as a colour but as a man."
He first started publishing his abolitionist newspaper "The North Star", which motto was: "Right is of no sex - Truth is of no colour - God is the father of us all and we are all brethen."
His last major speech "The lesson of Hour",.
He is born enslaved in Talbot County, Maryland, and does not know his age.
Sophia Auld begins to teach him letters, then her husband stops the lessons.
He teaches himself to read and sees literacy as a road out of slavery.
The brutal overseer Edward Covey tries to break him.
Douglass fights Covey and calls that fight the turn toward manhood.
He escapes north.
William Lloyd Garrison writes the preface.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sybil

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1845 (Sort Year: 1845)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Benjamin Disraeli

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A condition of England novel that says the rich and the poor are two nations.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1845 is correct. The author's note is dated May Day 1845 at Grosvenor Gate. Orlando dates publication by 12 May 1845. Henry Colburn issued three volumes. The full title is Sybil, or The Two Nations.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Egremont (A young aristocrat who learns how the poor live); Sybil Gerard (A devout young woman who speaks for the poor); Walter Gerard (Sybil's father, a working class leader with an old claim)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Charles Egremont, a younger son of a noble house, enters politics.
He meets Walter Gerard and his daughter Sybil among ruined abbey walls.
They tell him the queen reigns over two nations, rich and poor.
The novel shows factory misery and Chartist unrest (workers demanding the vote).
Love and a revealed birth try to bridge the two nations.

items.title: "The Raven and Other Poems" (1845) — Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Raven and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1845 (Sort Year: 1845)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1845 poetry book that reprints The Raven with other poems of love, dreams, and death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wiley and Putnam published it on 19 November 1845. Database year 1845 is correct. Some poems in it were written years earlier.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Raven had already made Poe famous in January 1845.
Wiley and Putnam published this book in New York.
The Raven leads the collection.
Other poems treat dream landscapes, beauty, and loss.
The book let readers buy the famous poem with its companions.

items.title: "Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell" (1846) — Emily Brontë

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1846 (Sort Year: 1846)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Emily Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A small book of poems by the three Bronte sisters under the names Bell.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1846 is correct. Aylott and Jones of London printed it. The sisters paid the cost. It is a real book, shared by three authors.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ellis Bell (Emily Bronte's pen name on her poems in this book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Charlotte found poems by Emily and learned that all three sisters wrote verse.
They paid to print one volume in 1846.
Charlotte used Currer Bell, Emily used Ellis Bell, and Anne used Acton Bell.
Emily contributed 21 poems and hid some links to her Gondal stories.
Almost nobody bought the book in its first year.
Later readers judged Emily's poems the strongest in the volume.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Typee

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1846 (Sort Year: 1846)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herman Melville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sailor escapes into a Marquesan valley and fears he is a captive there.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the Brigham Young University catalogue date both the London and New York editions to 1846. The London title was different, but it is the same book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tommo (The sailor narrator, based on Melville's own escape); Toby (Tommo's companion, who leaves the valley); Fayaway (A Typee woman who befriends Tommo); Kory-Kory (The man who attends Tommo in the valley)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
2- Omoo: A Narrative of Adventures in the South Seas (1847): It is a sequel to Typee.
The sailor Tommo jumps ship in the Marquesas Islands.
He and Toby enter the valley of the Typee people.
The valley seems beautiful, but Tommo fears he is a captive.
Kory-Kory cares for him, and he meets Fayaway.
He worries that the Typee may be cannibals.
He finally escapes back to a ship.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Agnes Grey

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anne Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A governess tells how proud families treat her, and how she finds a good curate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1847 is correct for publication. Thomas Newby issued it in December 1847 as the third volume with Wuthering Heights. The pen name was Acton Bell. Britannica says she probably began it while a governess at Thorpe Green.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Agnes Grey (The narrator, a young governess who tells her own story); Edward Weston (A pious curate whom Agnes respects and later marries); Rosalie Murray (A vain pupil who becomes Lady Ashby by a loveless marriage); Mr Grey (Agnes's father, a poor clergyman)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Agnes, a clergyman's daughter, becomes a governess to earn her way.
Her first pupils are rude, and she cannot control them.
She later teaches Rosalie Murray, who marries a rich man for show.
Agnes loves Edward Weston, a poor and honest curate.
She leaves service, helps her mother, and marries Weston.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hellenics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walter Savage Landor

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English poems on Greek stories, many of them first drafted in Latin.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1847 is correct for The Hellenics. Many poems were written earlier, some first in Latin. A second version appeared in 1859.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rhaicos (A young man who loves a wood nymph); The Hamadryad (A nymph whose life is bound to an oak); Acon (A youth in the poem that follows The Hamadryad); Rhodope (The young woman linked with Acon)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Landor gathers poems about Greek gods, nymphs, and heroes.
Several pieces are talks in verse, like little dramas.
The Hamadryad tells of Rhaicos and a tree nymph.
Acon and Rhodope continues that story of love and loss.
The manner is calm, balanced, and classical.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Jane Eyre

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An orphan governess chooses love only when she can keep her conscience.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1847 is correct. Britannica says she began the book in August 1846. Britannica dates publication to 16 October 1847. Wikipedia dates the same Smith, Elder edition to 19 October 1847. Both fix the year as 1847. It appeared under the name Currer Bell.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jane Eyre (The orphan narrator, later a governess and Rochester's wife); Edward Rochester (Master of Thornfield, who hides a living wife); Bertha Mason (Rochester's first wife, locked in the upper rooms); St John Rivers (Jane's clergyman cousin, who wants a dutiful marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
As a child at Gateshead, Jane is punished in the red room.
At Lowood school she endures hunger, cold, and Mr. Brocklehurst's harsh rule.
She becomes governess at Thornfield and loves Edward Rochester.
Their wedding stops because he already has a wife, Bertha Mason.
Jane leaves, inherits money, and later marries the injured Rochester.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Tancred

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Benjamin Disraeli

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young lord leaves London politics for the East, seeking a faith worth a new crusade.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1847 is correct. Orlando dates publication March 1847. Henry Colburn published three volumes. The full title is Tancred, or The New Crusade.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tancred, Lord Montacute (A young nobleman who seeks faith in the Holy Land); Sidonia (The Jewish sage who also advised Coningsby)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tancred, Lord Montacute, is weary of empty English politics.
He wants a spiritual quest, not another London career.
A fashionable voice tells him that the East is a career.
He travels toward Jerusalem to seek religious truth.
Sidonia and figures from the earlier novels return in this last volume.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Vanity Fair

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1848 (Sort Year: 1848)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Makepeace Thackeray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A satire of English society during the Napoleonic wars, centred on Becky Sharp and Amelia Sedley.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from January 1847 to July 1848. The Bradbury and Evans book is dated 1848. The database span 1847-48 is the serial, not a different novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Becky Sharp (A poor, witty adventuress who climbs by charm and calculation); Amelia Sedley (A gentle, loyal young woman who trusts the wrong man); George Osborne (Amelia's vain husband, killed at Waterloo); Rawdon Crawley (Becky's husband, a soldier who finally sees through her); William Dobbin (The patient officer who loves Amelia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Becky Sharp leaves school poor, clever, and determined to rise.
Gentle Amelia Sedley loves George Osborne, who is proud of his rank.
Becky marries Rawdon Crawley and pushes her way into fashionable rooms.
George dies at the Battle of Waterloo, and Amelia is left with little money.
Loyal Captain Dobbin waits for years while Amelia mourns George.
Becky's schemes collapse, and the narrator shuts the puppet show.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Wuthering Heights

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1847 (Sort Year: 1847)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Emily Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wild tale of Heathcliff and Catherine on the Yorkshire moors.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1847 is correct. Thomas Newby published it in December 1847 under the name Ellis Bell. It filled two volumes of a set that also included Anne's Agnes Grey. Charlotte's edited edition is 1850.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lockwood (The outsider who hears the story and writes it down); Nelly Dean (The servant who tells most of the family history); Heathcliff (An orphan who grows into a cruel avenger); Catherine Earnshaw (The woman who shares Heathcliff's fierce nature and marries Edgar); Edgar Linton (The gentle owner of Thrushcross Grange)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Genre: Gothic novel. It is written under the pseudonym Ellis Bell.
It is written in three volumes. (34 chapters).
Heathcliff is Byronic hero.
Mr. Lockwood rents Thrushcross Grange and visits his landlord, Heathcliff.
Nelly Dean tells him the history of Wuthering Heights.
Mr. Earnshaw brings home the boy Heathcliff, and Hindley hates him.
Catherine Earnshaw loves Heathcliff but marries Edgar Linton.
Heathcliff returns rich and takes revenge on both families.
A second generation, young Cathy and Hareton, slowly breaks the curse.
Catherine's ghostly presence haunts the house and Heathcliff's death.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Eureka

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1848 (Sort Year: 1848)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edgar Allan Poe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose poem that explains the universe as born from one unity and destined to return to it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: George P. Putnam published Eureka in New York in June 1848. Database year 1848 is correct. The genre label Fiction misses that Poe called it a prose poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edgar Allan Poe (The essayist speaking in his own voice about the universe)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Poe dedicates the book to the scientist Alexander von Humboldt.
He asks readers to judge the work as a poem.
He says all things come from one original unity.
That unity holds the seed of a final collapse.
He mixes astronomy, metaphysics, and imagination.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Mary Barton

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1848 (Sort Year: 1848)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Gaskell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Manchester worker's daughter is caught in a murder born of class hatred.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1848 is correct. Chapman and Hall published Mary Barton in two volumes in 1848. Victorian Web says her husband urged the novel after their son died in 1845. Britannica links its success to the revolutionary year 1848. The subtitle is A Tale of Manchester Life.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Barton (A mill worker's daughter who must clear the man she loves); John Barton (Mary's father, a worker driven into class hatred); Jem Wilson (The working man Mary loves, who is accused of murder); Harry Carson (The mill owner's son who courts Mary and is killed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
John Barton, a mill worker, grows bitter in a trade depression.
His daughter Mary loves Jem Wilson but is courted by Harry Carson.
John Barton is sent to kill Harry Carson, the young master.
Jem is accused, and Mary races to find proof that saves him.
The tale asks masters and workers to see each other's suffering.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Pendennis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1849 (Sort Year: 1849)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Makepeace Thackeray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The youth of Arthur Pendennis, a tempted young man who passes through love, university, and London writing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Parts ran from November 1848 to December 1850. At the Circulating Library dates the Bradbury and Evans book 1849. The database span 1848-50 follows the parts. Illness interrupted the parts in 1849.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Arthur Pendennis (The young hero, proud, gifted, and often foolish); Major Pendennis (Arthur's uncle, a man of fashion and worldly advice); Laura (The cousin who sees Arthur clearly and loves him steadily)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Subtitle: His Fortune and Misfortunes, His Friends and His Greatest Enemy 4. The History of Henry Esmond (1852) - novel 5. The Newcomes (1855) - novel 6. The Four Georges (1860-1861)
Complete title is- "The History of Pendennis: His Fortune and Misfortunes, His Friends and His Greatest Enemy"
Protagonist: Arthur Pendennis.
At the age of 18 Pen fell in love with the actress Emily.
Young Arthur Pendennis falls in love and thinks himself a hero.
His worldly uncle, Major Pendennis, tries to manage his career.
Arthur studies at a university the narrator calls Oxbridge.
He works among London journalists and meets flattery and debt.
The story shows how pride and kindness fight inside one young man.

items.title: "The Tenant of Wildfell Hall" (1848) — Anne Brontë

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1848 (Sort Year: 1848)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anne Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A woman flees a drunken husband and hides at Wildfell Hall.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in three volumes in June 1848, again as Acton Bell. A second edition, with her preface dated 22 July 1848, followed in August 1848. The database year 1848 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gilbert Markham (A gentleman farmer whose letters frame the story); Helen Huntingdon (The tenant, who tells her marriage in a diary); Arthur Huntingdon (Helen's first husband, ruined by drink and affairs); Annabella Wilmot (A shallow woman who becomes Huntingdon's mistress)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gilbert Markham falls in love with Helen, the quiet new tenant.
Neighbours gossip, and Helen will not explain her past.
She gives Gilbert her diary so he can read the truth.
The diary shows her marriage to Arthur Huntingdon, a drunk and unfaithful man.
She leaves him to keep their son from copying his life.
After Huntingdon dies, Helen later marries Gilbert.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Yeast

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1848 (Sort Year: 1848)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Kingsley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A social novel about gentry, rural poor, and sanitary reform.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1848 is the serial, and that is the first publication. Victorian Web says Yeast ran anonymously in Fraser's Magazine in 1848. Britannica and the Circulating Library date the book form to 1851. The subtitle is A Problem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lancelot Smith (A rich young man who wakes up to rural poverty); Tregarva (A gamekeeper who guides Lancelot through the laborers' misery); Argemone Lavington (A landowner's daughter drawn toward reform)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lancelot Smith, a rich young man, sees the misery of country laborers.
The gamekeeper Tregarva shows him dirt, disease, and low wages.
Argemone Lavington, a landowner's daughter, shares the wish for reform.
The tale attacks bad cottages and calls for Christian duty.
It first ran without Kingsley's name in Fraser's Magazine.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: David Copperfield

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: David tells his own life, from a harsh childhood to work, love, and a career as a writer.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from May 1849 to November 1850. The book came out in 1850. Database range 1849-50 matches the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David Copperfield (The narrator, who grows from child to novelist); Aunt Betsey Trotwood (David's stern but loyal aunt); Uriah Heep (A false, humble clerk who steals and blackmails); James Steerforth (David's glamorous friend, who ruins Emily); Agnes Wickfield (David's wise second wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Original title: "The Personal History, Adventures, Experience, and Observations of David Copperfield, the Younger of Blunderstone Rookery"
It is an autobiographical novel by Dickens.
In the preface of 1867 edition, Dickens wrote- "Like many fond parents I have in my heart of hearts a favorite child and his name is David Copperfield."
David was born after the death of his father so his early years were spent in the company of his mother and the housekeeper Peggotty.
His mother remarried when David was only 7 years, and his stepfather Edward Murdstone use to trash him and finally sent him to a boarding school, Salem House.
At the school, David got a ruthless headmaster Mr. Creakle.
After sometimes his mother gave birth to a baby boy but when David returned to Salem House after celebrating holidays at home, his mother and her baby dies.
When he again returns home he is sent to work under a wine merchant by his stepfather Murdstone in London.
As David grows he comes in contact with variety of characters including his landlord daughter Agnes Wickfield, who becomes his confidant.
He remarries the beautiful Dora Spenlow but she also died of a miscarriage.
He remarries Agnes Wickfield who always loved him and had four children including a daughter Betsy.
The great aunt of David renamed him as "Trotwood Copperfield".
The character 'Dora' is modeled on Dickens' first love 'Maria'.
The arbitrary suffering of innocents is the main theme of the novel.
David is born and later suffers under his stepfather Mr Murdstone.
He is sent to work in a factory, then runs away to Aunt Betsey.
He studies, loves little Emily's circle, and trusts the charming Steerforth.
He marries Dora, while Uriah Heep plots against Mr Wickfield.
Dora dies.
Steerforth ruins Emily.
David later marries Agnes and becomes a novelist.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Shirley

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1849 (Sort Year: 1849)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two Yorkshire women face love, work, and a mill conflict in wartime.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1849 is correct. Smith, Elder published Shirley, A Tale, by Currer Bell, on 26 October 1849. Britannica says it appeared in October, after Anne Bronte's death in May 1849. The name Shirley was then mainly a boy's name.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Shirley Keeldar (A rich heiress who runs her estate and chooses her own husband); Caroline Helstone (A quiet young woman with little money, in love with Robert); Robert Moore (A mill owner who installs new machines during the trade crisis); Louis Moore (Robert's poorer brother, who becomes Shirley's husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in Yorkshire in 1811 and 1812, during the cloth crisis.
Mill owner Robert Moore brings in machines, and workers attack the mill.
His cousin Caroline Helstone loves him, but she has little money or work.
Heiress Shirley Keeldar manages her land and befriends Caroline.
Caroline marries Robert, and Shirley marries his brother Louis.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Captive Ladie

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1849 (Sort Year: 1849)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Michael Madhusudan Dutt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An English verse tale of a captive Rajput princess and of Prithviraj's love and defeat.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1849 is correct. The book was printed at the Advertiser Press in Madras and signed M M S Dutt. The same volume also includes Visions of the Past. The database marks the work as a translation. That flag is a catalog error. This is an original English poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prithviraj (The king of Delhi, the poem's active hero and the princess's lover); The captive princess (A princess of Kanauj, imprisoned so that Prithviraj cannot claim her); Jayachandra (The king of Kanauj, who confines the princess and withholds help)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem retells a legend from just before Mahmud of Ghazni's attack.
The king of Kanauj holds a Feast of Victory and expects other princes to attend.
The king of Delhi, Prithviraj, refuses, because he will not accept a rival overlord.
A princess is shut in a lonely fort so Prithviraj cannot reach her.
Prithviraj disguises himself as a bhat (a bard) and carries her away.
A Muslim army later besieges his capital.
He is defeated and dies.

items.title: "The Seven Lamps of Architecture" (1849) — John Ruskin

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Seven Lamps of Architecture

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1849 (Sort Year: 1849)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Ruskin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book that tests architecture by seven moral lamps, from Sacrifice to Obedience.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Encyclopedia.com both date the book to 1849.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Ruskin (The critic who turns architecture into a moral lesson)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
6. Unto This Last: Four essays on the first principals of political economy (1860) 7. Fors Clavigera: letters to the workmen and labourers of Great Britain (vol 1-4) (1871-1880)
Ruskin sets seven moral tests for good building.
The lamps are Sacrifice, Truth, Power, Beauty, Life, Memory, and Obedience.
Sacrifice means real labour, not cheap show.
Truth means honest materials, not fake stone or wood.
Memory means a building should respect the work of the past.
The book helped the Gothic Revival in Britain.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Strayed Reveller

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1849 (Sort Year: 1849)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young reveler sees the gods and the pain of human life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems was published anonymously in 1849, signed By A. The database year 1849 is correct. The exact date of composition is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Strayed Reveller (A youth whose vision comes from Circe's cup); Circe (The enchantress who questions the youth); Ulysses (The hero who enters and talks with Circe)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Circe finds a youth who has drunk from her enchanted cup.
The youth, the Strayed Reveller, sings of what the gods see.
The gods look down on heroes, poets, and suffering people.
Ulysses arrives and speaks with Circe.
The youth asks for more of the cup and sings again.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Alton Locke

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Kingsley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tailor-poet joins the Chartists and sees the cost of sweated work.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1850 is correct. Chapman and Hall published Alton Locke, Tailor and Poet: An Autobiography in two volumes in 1850. Victorian Web lists it under 1850. The exact months of writing are not fixed here. The poem The Sands of Dee appears inside the novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alton Locke (A tailor and poet who narrates his own life); Sandy Mackaye (A Scottish bookseller who mentors Alton)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Alton Locke, a poor tailor, teaches himself poetry in London.
He sees tailors crowded into filthy rooms for tiny pay.
He joins the Chartists (workers who demanded political rights).
Sandy Mackaye, a Scottish bookseller, guides his reading and his anger.
The novel asks why desperate workers turned to the Charter.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: In Memoriam A.H.H

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long elegy for Arthur Henry Hallam, moving from grief toward a hard won faith.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written between 1833 and 1850 and published anonymously in 1850. Hallam had died in 1833. The poem is not posthumous. The same year Tennyson became Poet Laureate. The database year 1850 is correct. Its anonymous flag fits this poem only.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Tennyson mourning, though the 1850 book did not print his name); Arthur Henry Hallam (The dead friend, named in the title initials A.H.H.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hallam, Tennyson's closest friend, dies suddenly in 1833.
Tennyson writes short lyrics of mourning for seventeen years.
The speaker moves through despair, doubt, and slow acceptance.
Geology and the struggle of nature shake his trust in a loving God.
The poem ends with a marriage song for his sister Cecilia.

items.title: "Sonnets from the Portuguese" (1850) — Elizabeth Barrett Browning

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sonnets from the Portuguese

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Forty four love sonnets about her courtship, first printed in 1850.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written from 1845, during the courtship, and given to Robert in July 1849. First published in November 1850 in the new edition of Poems. Database year 1850 is the print year. The database posthumous flag is wrong. She lived until 29 June 1861.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A woman who moves from doubt to full love); The Beloved (The man she addresses, standing for Robert Browning)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
She began the sonnets in 1845, during the secret courtship.
She kept all 44 in a notebook and did not show them at once.
She gave them to Robert Browning in July 1849.
He urged her to print them in the new Poems of November 1850.
The title pretends they are translations, so they seem less personal.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Prelude

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Wordsworth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An epic autobiographical poem in blank verse tracing the spiritual and intellectual growth of the poet's mind.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database correctly notes published posthumously in 1850. Wordsworth called it the Poem to Coleridge. His widow Mary named it The Prelude after his death in 1850.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Wordsworth (The poet-narrator who traces his growth from childhood in the Lake District); Samuel Taylor Coleridge (Wordsworth's friend and intellectual partner to whom the poem is addressed); Dorothy Wordsworth (The poet's sister whose love and observation steady his troubled spirit)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1850)
The Prelude or Growth of a Poets Minds: An Autobiographical Poem is a conversation poem in blank verse.
It is an extremely personal and riveling work on the details of Wordsworth's life.
He began to work on 'The Prelude' in 1798 and continued to work on it throughout his life.
On a letter to Dorothy he referred to it as "The poem on the growth of my own mind."
Initially Wordsworth titled it - Poem to Coleridge.
It contains 14 books. The first version appeared in 1805.
Book 1 is about "Introduction: Childhood and School Time", Book 2 - "School Time" (contd); Book 3 'Residence at Cambridge', Book 4 - Summer Vacation, Book 5 - 'Books', Book 6 - Cambridge and the Alps, Book 7 - Residence in London, Book 8 - Retrospect: Love of Nature Leading to Love of Man, Book 9 - Residence in France, Book 10 - The Residence in France (contd), Book 11 - France (concluded), Book 12 - Imagination and Taste: How impaired and restored, Book 13- Imagination … (concluded), Book 14 - Conclusion.
In the Prelude, there is a description of Cambridge university.
Famous Quote "Bliss was in it that down to be alive, but to be young was very heaven".
Wordsworth coined the famous phrase "Spots of time" in The Prelude (in Book 12) as "There are in our existence spots of time that with distinct pre-eminence retain a renovating virtue, whence, depressed…"
In Prelude there is an appearance of Boy of Winander who is affected by Muteness in Book 5, 'Books' "There was a boy; ye know him well, ye Cliffs And Island of Winander"! - many a time At evening, when the earliest star began… Blew mimic hootings to the silent owls.
In the above lines it is clear that the boy of Winander is suffering of muteness. This boy is actually a dwarf (tiny) man.
First version of Prelude in 2 books - 1799 Second version in 13 books - 1805 Third version in 14 books - 1850 Lines Composed a Few Miles Above Tindern Abbey "For nature then The Curser pleasures of my boyish days And their glad animal movements all gone by to me was all in all."
In the above lines Wordsworth is talking about both first and second stage in his relationship with nature.
Full title - "Lines Written a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey, on Revisiting the Banks of the Wye during a tour, July 13, 1798"
Wordsworth worked on this autobiographical epic for over forty years.
He completed major versions in two parts in 1799 and thirteen books in 1805.
He addressed the entire poem to his close friend Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
He kept revising it until his death, expanding it to fourteen books.
His widow Mary published it in July 1850 and gave it the title The Prelude.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Scarlet Letter

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1850 (Sort Year: 1850)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Nathaniel Hawthorne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In Puritan Boston, Hester Prynne is forced to wear a scarlet A for adultery.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1850. The database year is correct. Hawthorne wrote the novel after losing his Custom House post. The preface recalls that job.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hester Prynne (The woman punished for adultery, who wears the scarlet letter A); Arthur Dimmesdale (The minister who is Pearl's father and hides his guilt); Roger Chillingworth (Hester's husband, who studies Dimmesdale in order to take revenge); Pearl (Hester's child, a living sign of the broken law)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hester stands on the scaffold with her child, Pearl, and a scarlet A.
She will not name the father, the minister Arthur Dimmesdale.
Her husband arrives, calls himself Roger Chillingworth, and hunts the secret.
Dimmesdale's hidden guilt destroys him, while Hester's skill earns some respect.
He confesses on the scaffold, and later one gravestone covers both lovers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Cranford

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Gaskell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Gentle village ladies keep up appearances with elegant economy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first paper appeared in Household Words on 13 December 1851. Further papers followed into 1853. Chapman and Hall issued the book in June 1853. Database span 1851-53 matches the serial. The book year is 1853. Britannica and Victorian Web both treat Cranford as the 1853 volume drawn from that serial.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Smith (The narrator who visits and reports on Cranford); Miss Deborah Jenkyns (The elder sister who defends old genteel rules); Miss Matty Jenkyns (The gentler sister whose losses draw the town together); Captain Brown (A frank newcomer whose manners disturb Cranford habits)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Cranford is a town ruled socially by its women.
The Jenkyns sisters guard old genteel habits and rank.
Captain Brown's plain ways clash with their sense of dignity.
Losses test Miss Matty, and her friends quietly help her.
The humor is kind, and the village recalls Knutsford.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Moby-Dick

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1851 (Sort Year: 1851)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herman Melville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ishmael sails with Captain Ahab, who hunts the white whale that took his leg.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the Brigham Young University catalogue date the book to 1851. Melville dedicated it to Nathaniel Hawthorne.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ishmael (The narrator and sole survivor of the Pequod); Captain Ahab (The captain obsessed with killing Moby Dick); Moby Dick (The white whale that Ahab hunts); Queequeg (A tattooed harpooner and Ishmael's friend); Starbuck (The first mate who fears Ahab's revenge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ishmael goes to sea and joins the whaler Pequod.
He befriends the harpooner Queequeg.
Captain Ahab reveals his hunt for the white whale.
Ahab lost his leg to Moby Dick and wants revenge.
The ship sails the world, and the whale becomes a vast symbol.
Moby Dick destroys the Pequod, and only Ishmael survives.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Social Statics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1851 (Sort Year: 1851)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herbert Spencer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose book on the rights people need for happiness, and on a very small state.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: John Chapman published the book in London in 1851. Britannica and Stanford both use 1851. He was writing it around 1850. A later reprint calls one text the 1850 edition. The exam year is 1851. The database year is correct. The database genre Poetry is wrong, because this is prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Herbert Spencer (The author arguing for equal freedom and a small state)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Spencer asks what rules a society needs if people are to be happy.
He says each person should be free, so long as others stay equally free.
Government should guard rights, and it does harm when it goes further.
He expects people to adapt to social life, so the state can shrink.
Most of his later politics is already present in this early book.

items.title: "The House of the Seven Gables" (1851) — Nathaniel Hawthorne

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The House of the Seven Gables

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1851 (Sort Year: 1851)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Nathaniel Hawthorne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Salem family lives for generations under a curse until love breaks it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1851, while Hawthorne lived in Lenox. The database year is correct. It is a novel of the Pyncheon curse, not a second name for The Scarlet Letter.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hepzibah Pyncheon (An elderly cousin who opens a small shop in the cursed house); Clifford Pyncheon (Hepzibah's brother, home after a long imprisonment); Phoebe Pyncheon (A young country cousin whose kindness revives the house); Holgrave (A lodger descended from the Maules, who loves Phoebe); Judge Jaffrey Pyncheon (A smiling, powerful cousin who repeats the family's old greed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Colonel Pyncheon once seized Matthew Maule's land, and Maule cursed him.
The old house of seven gables still holds that guilt.
Poor Hepzibah and her broken brother Clifford keep the house.
Young Phoebe and the lodger Holgrave bring new life into it.
Judge Pyncheon's death ends the grip of the old wrong, and love lifts the curse.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Stones of Venice

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1851 (Sort Year: 1851)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Ruskin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A three-volume history of Venice that reads its buildings as a record of its society.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database span 1851-53 is correct. Britannica says the three volumes appeared in 1851 and 1853. Volume one is 1851. Volumes two and three are 1853.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Ruskin (The writer who reads Venice as a moral history)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ruskin studies the buildings of Venice across three volumes.
He links Byzantine, Gothic, and Renaissance styles to social life.
The chapter The Nature of Gothic praises free craftsmen.
He says a society's art shows the justice of its labour.
Venice declines when craft becomes mechanical and proud.
The book later shaped the Arts and Crafts movement.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Uncle Tom’s Cabin

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1851 (Sort Year: 1851)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Harriet Beecher Stowe

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel that follows enslaved families sold, hunted, and torn apart in America.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1851 matches the serial start. Britannica says the National Era ran it in 1851 and 1852, and the book appeared in 1852. The full title adds or Life Among the Lowly.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Uncle Tom (An enslaved Christian man who is sold south and killed by Legree); Eliza (An enslaved mother who flees to save her child Harry); Evangeline St. Clare (The child called Eva, whose death is a famous scene); Simon Legree (The brutal owner who beats Tom to death); Topsy (An enslaved child who says she just grew and was never made)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an anti-slavery novel "helped by the groundwork for the civil war", according to Will Kaufman. It is based on the life of an Afro-American writer….
This sentimental novel depicts the reality of slavery while also asserting that Christian love can overcome something as destructive as enslavement of fellow human things.
Main characters: Uncle Tom Eliza Slave 2. A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin (1851): Non- fiction 3. Dred: A Tale of the Great Dismal Swamp (1856) 4. The Minister's Weeing 5. Old Two Town Folks (1869)
In Maine she began a long tale of slavery, after years near the Ohio River.
The National Era in Washington printed the tale in parts during 1851 and 1852.
Mr. Shelby agrees to sell Uncle Tom and the child Harry to pay a debt.
Eliza runs with her child, while Tom is sold south.
Little Eva dies, and Simon Legree beats Tom to death.
The 1852 book sold in huge numbers and split North from South.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Bleak House

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge lawsuit eats a family fortune, while fog and disease spread through London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from March 1852 to September 1853. The book came out in 1853. Database range 1852-53 matches the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Esther Summerson (A modest young woman who narrates half the novel); John Jarndyce (Esther's kind guardian at Bleak House); Lady Dedlock (A proud lady with a hidden past); Jo (A homeless boy who sweeps a street crossing); Inspector Bucket (A detective who follows the mystery)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel was published in 1852-1853. It's a romantic novel.
The novel is a vigorous satire on the abuses of the old court of chancery.
The delays and costs of it brought misery and ruin on its suitors.
The tale centers in the fortunes of an uninteresting couple Richard Carstone, and his amiable cousin Ada Clare.
They are wards of the court in the case of Jarndyce.
They fell in love and secretly marry.
The case of Jarndyce comes to an end due to sudden death of Richard.
When Ada goes to live with John Jarndyce. She is accompanied by Esther Summerson, a supposed orphan.
The case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce drags on in the Court of Chancery.
Esther Summerson tells part of the story, and a cool narrator tells the rest.
Lady Dedlock hides a secret tied to Esther's birth.
Jo, a poor crossing sweeper, carries disease from the slum to the rich.
Inspector Bucket tracks the mystery.
Legal costs swallow the whole estate.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Empedocles on Etna

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1852 (Sort Year: 1852)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Greek philosopher Empedocles, sick of the world, leaps into Etna.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Empedocles on Etna, and Other Poems appeared in 1852. Arnold left the title poem out of Poems (1853) because the suffering finds no vent in action. New Poems (1867) restored it. The database year 1852 is the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Empedocles (The philosopher who chooses death in the volcano); Callicles (The young harp player whose songs answer Empedocles); Pausanias (The physician who climbs part of the way with Empedocles)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Empedocles climbs Mount Etna with his harp, weary of public life.
The poet Callicles sings from the woods below the mountain.
Empedocles laments the loss of joy, youth, and belief.
He throws himself into the crater of the volcano.
Callicles keeps singing after the philosopher's death.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Blithedale Romance

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1852 (Sort Year: 1852)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Nathaniel Hawthorne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poet tells how a utopian farm fails and how Zenobia is destroyed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1852. The database year is correct. Hawthorne drew it from his disappointment with Brook Farm, a real utopian community.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Miles Coverdale (The poet who narrates and watches the community from a distance); Zenobia (A brilliant, passionate woman whose defeat ends in drowning); Hollingsworth (A reformer who loves one plan more than the people around him); Priscilla (A frail young woman tied to Zenobia by a hidden family bond)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Miles Coverdale joins Blithedale, a farm community that hopes to remake life.
The reformer Hollingsworth wants the group to serve his one project.
Zenobia, a proud woman, and pale Priscilla are rivals in love and power.
The community's ideals crack under ego, secrecy, and sexual jealousy.
Zenobia drowns, and Coverdale later admits he loved Priscilla.

items.title: "The History of Henry Esmond" (1852) — William Makepeace Thackeray

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The History of Henry Esmond

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1852 (Sort Year: 1852)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Makepeace Thackeray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A historical novel about Henry Esmond in the reign of Queen Anne.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in three volumes by Smith, Elder in 1852. It was not issued in monthly parts. The database year 1852 is correct. The full title adds Esq., a Colonel in the Service of Her Majesty Queen Anne.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Henry Esmond (The narrator, a colonel who tells his own youth); Rachel, Lady Castlewood (The woman who protects Henry and later shares his life); Beatrix Esmond (Rachel's brilliant daughter, hungry for rank)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a historical fiction of Henry Esmond, a colonel in the service of Queen.
It is a sequel to his novel The Virginians (1857-1859).
Henry Esmond grows up in the Castlewood family and is told he is illegitimate.
He serves in the wars and stays loyal to Lady Castlewood.
He loves her proud daughter Beatrix, who wants power at court.
He learns that he is the true heir, but he gives the title away.
The book ends with his choice of a quieter, truer love.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Bartleby, the Scrivener

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herman Melville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Wall Street copyist answers every request by saying he would prefer not to.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Brigham Young University date the first printing to Putnam's Monthly Magazine in 1853. It was collected in The Piazza Tales in 1856.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bartleby (A scrivener (a law copyist) who withdraws from every demand); The Lawyer (The narrator who employs Bartleby and cannot save him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Wall Street lawyer hires Bartleby as a copyist.
Bartleby works well at first.
He then refuses each task with a quiet sentence.
He stops copying and will not leave the office.
The lawyer cannot force him and cannot understand him.
Bartleby is jailed and dies, having refused every offer of help.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hypatia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Kingsley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A historical novel about Hypatia and faith in ancient Alexandria.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial began in Fraser's Magazine in 1852. The two-volume book appeared in 1853. Database year 1853 matches the book. The subtitle is New Foes with an Old Face. Victorian Web and the Circulating Library agree on the 1853 volumes.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hypatia (A pagan philosopher and teacher in Alexandria); Philammon (A young monk who enters the city and meets her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Philammon, a young monk, leaves the desert for Alexandria.
He meets Hypatia, a pagan teacher admired for her learning.
Christians, Goths, and Romans struggle for power in the city.
A mob murders Hypatia during the religious conflict.
Kingsley uses that past to warn against dangers he saw in his own church.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Arnold's 1853 collection, under his own name, with a famous preface.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poems, a new edition, was published by Longman in 1853. This is the first volume under Arnold's own name. The database year 1853 is correct. Do not confuse this book with New Poems of 1867.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sohrab (The young warrior in the new poem Sohrab and Rustum); Rustum (The father who kills Sohrab without knowing him); The Scholar-Gipsy (The Oxford wanderer of the new title poem in this book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book reprints some poems from 1849 and 1852.
It leaves out Empedocles on Etna.
It adds Sohrab and Rustum and The Scholar-Gipsy.
The preface says a poem needs action, not only suffering.
It holds up classical models for an age short of moral grandeur.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ruth

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Gaskell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A seduced young woman is given a chance at a moral new life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1853 is correct. Victorian Web says Ruth was published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in January 1853. Britannica also dates Ruth to 1853. The exact start of composition is not fixed here. Gaskell had outlined the story to Charlotte Bronte in 1852.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ruth Hilton (A seduced seamstress who tries to build an honest life); Mr. Bellingham (The gentleman who seduces Ruth and then leaves her); Thurstan Benson (A dissenting minister who shelters Ruth); Faith Benson (Thurstan's sister, who helps keep Ruth's secret)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ruth Hilton, a young seamstress, is deserted by her lover.
The minister Thurstan Benson takes her into his home.
She is presented as a widow so her child will be spared shame.
The lie is exposed, and much of the town turns against her.
She nurses the sick in a fever and dies after that service.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Newcomes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Makepeace Thackeray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A story of the Newcome family, and of Colonel Newcome's love for his son Clive.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from October 1853 to August 1855. The Bradbury and Evans book is dated 1855. The database span 1853-55 is the serial. The subtitle is Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Colonel Thomas Newcome (An honest soldier whose goodness cannot master London society); Clive Newcome (The Colonel's son, an artist who loves Ethel); Ethel Newcome (Clive's cousin, pressed by her family toward a rich marriage); Barnes Newcome (Ethel's cold brother, who intrigues against Clive)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a sequel to Pendennis.
Colonel Thomas Newcomes and his son Clive are the central figures.
Colonel Thomas Newcome comes home from India to be with his son Clive.
Clive loves his cousin Ethel, but family pride blocks the match.
Barnes Newcome schemes to keep money and rank in his own hands.
The Colonel loses his fortune and ends his days in a poor house.
His death is told with deep feeling, and a short epilogue plays with a happy ending.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Villette

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1853 (Sort Year: 1853)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charlotte Brontë

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lonely English teacher builds a life at a foreign school.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1853 is correct. Britannica says the novel was published in January 1853. A Morning Post notice of 27 January 1853 advertises it as published that day. The city of Villette stands for Brussels.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucy Snowe (The quiet narrator, a teacher who remakes her life); Madame Beck (The watchful mistress of the school in Villette); Dr. John Graham Bretton (The English doctor whom Lucy first loves); Paul Emanuel (The professor who becomes Lucy's deeper love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lucy Snowe leaves England and finds work in the city of Villette.
She teaches at Madame Beck's school, where the mistress spies on everyone.
She cares first for Dr. John, then more deeply for Paul Emanuel.
Loneliness and a breakdown test her, and she recovers her will.
She gains her own school, while Paul's return is left uncertain.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hard Times

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1854 (Sort Year: 1854)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mill town run on facts and profit breaks the people who live by feeling.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Weekly parts in Household Words ran from 1 April to 12 August 1854. The book came out the same year. Database year 1854 is correct. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Gradgrind (A school owner who worships facts); Louisa Gradgrind (His daughter, starved of feeling); Josiah Bounderby (A rich mill owner who boasts of a false past); Stephen Blackpool (An honest worker ruined by the system); Sissy Jupe (A circus girl who stands for warmth and imagination)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
"Hard Times for these Times" is the complete title.
It highlights the social and economic pressure of that time.
It appeared in a weekly installment in a periodical "House Hold Woods".
The expression 'Hard Times' means a period of depression when food is scanty or when wages are low or when unemployment is widespread.
The major characters of the novel are- Thomas Gradgrind, Josiah Bounderby, Louisa, Sissy, Hart House, and Stephen, etc.
The novel is divided into three parts which are headed as.
Sowing.
Reaping, and.
Garnering.
The novel takes a hard, unsympathetic look at utilitarianism.
The novel suggests that the 19th century England's overzealous of Industrialization and threatens to turn human beings into machine by thwarting the development of their emotions and imaginations.
Thomas Gradgrind teaches children that only hard facts matter.
His daughter Louisa is pushed into marriage with the boastful manufacturer Bounderby.
Sissy Jupe, from a circus family, keeps human kindness alive.
The worker Stephen Blackpool is trapped by an unjust marriage law and a false charge.
Louisa's collapse shows that a life of facts alone cannot sustain a soul.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: North and South

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Gaskell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A southern clergyman's daughter learns the life of a mill town.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Victorian Web dates the Household Words serial from 2 September 1854 to 27 January 1855. The two-volume book is 1855. Britannica gives the span 1854-1855. The database calls the work Poetry. That label is wrong. North and South is a novel. She began it in the winter of 1853-1854.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Margaret Hale (A clergyman's daughter who moves from south to north); John Thornton (A Milton mill owner who argues with Margaret, then loves her); Nicholas Higgins (A factory worker and union man whom Margaret comes to know); Mr. Hale (Margaret's father, a clergyman who leaves his pulpit)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Margaret Hale leaves the rural south for the mill town of Milton.
She clashes with the mill owner John Thornton.
A strike sets her between Thornton and the worker Nicholas Higgins.
She sees pain on both the masters' side and the workers' side.
Respect grows into love as north and south learn from each other.

items.title: "Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects" (1854) — Frances E. W. Harper

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1854 (Sort Year: 1854)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Frances E. W. Harper

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short book of poems on slavery, faith, drink, and a mother's pain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1854 is correct. Poetry Foundation and Lehigh University both give 1854. Lehigh prints The Slave Mother from this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The enslaved mother (The woman in The Slave Mother, whose child is taken from her); The child (The boy who clings to his mother and is torn away)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Harper gathered poems she used in talks against slavery.
The Slave Mother shows a boy pulled from an enslaved mother's arms.
The mother loves the child, but the law says he is not hers.
Other poems attack slavery and also warn against strong drink.
A Boston printing appeared in 1854, and the book was reprinted many times.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Benito Cereno

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herman Melville

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An American captain misreads a slave-ship revolt until the truth breaks open.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Brigham Young University date Putnam's Monthly Magazine to 1855. The story was reprinted in The Piazza Tales in 1856.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amasa Delano (An American captain whose kindness hides a blind reading); Benito Cereno (The Spanish captain, held hostage by the revolt); Babo (The leader of the enslaved revolt, posing as a servant)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Captain Amasa Delano meets a Spanish slave ship in trouble.
Its captain, Benito Cereno, seems weak and terrified.
The servant Babo never leaves Cereno's side.
Delano thinks he sees loyalty, not a revolt.
The enslaved people have already seized the ship.
Delano's men retake it, and the leaders of the revolt are killed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Leaves of Grass

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walt Whitman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A growing book of free verse that Whitman revised from 1855 until his death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Project Gutenberg date the first edition to 1855. The Whitman Archive lists editions through 1891-1892. That last printing reprints the 1881-1882 text and adds annexes. Annexes are extra sections placed at the end. The database year 1855 is correct for the first edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A large first person voice who says he contains multitudes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1855 Whitman paid to print a thin book in Brooklyn.
The title page gave no author name, but his picture was in the book.
The poems use long lines and a bold voice saying I.
Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote him a letter of strong praise.
Later editions added poems and changed the order.
The 1891-1892 printing is called the deathbed edition.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Maud

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A monodrama about a lover driven into madness and then toward war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in July 1855 by Edward Moxon as Maud, and Other Poems. The Poetry Foundation dates Maud 1855. It appeared in Tennyson's lifetime under his name. It is not posthumous. The database year 1855 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A single unstable voice who loves Maud and tells the whole poem); Maud (The beloved, heard through the speaker's desire and fear)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker hates a corrupt rich world and loves Maud.
Her brother scorns him, and a duel brings death and horror.
The speaker loses his mind and imagines he is buried.
A garden lyric calls Maud into the night.
He seeks healing by going out to war.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Men and Women

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A two volume collection of 1855 that holds his finest dramatic monologues.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in two volumes in 1855. Database year 1855 is correct. It contains fifty one poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fra Lippo Lippi (A Florentine painter monk who praises the real world); Andrea del Sarto (A painter who has skill but lacks a higher reach); Bishop Blougram (A worldly bishop who argues with a doubting journalist)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Fifty one poems appeared in two volumes in 1855.
Fra Lippo Lippi defends a painter's love of real bodies and streets.
Andrea del Sarto, called the faultless painter, mourns a perfect but cold art.
Other speakers include Bishop Blougram and the lover in Love Among the Ruins.
A few poems, such as One Word More, speak more directly of Browning's own love.

items.title: "My Bondage and My Freedom" (1855) — Frederick Douglass

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: My Bondage and My Freedom

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Frederick Douglass

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His second autobiography, longer and more independent than the 1845 book.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1855 is correct. It was published in New York in 1855. The database genre label Fiction is wrong. This book is an autobiography.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
