fields.value: Frederick Douglass (The autobiographer, now a famous lecturer and editor); James McCune Smith (The Black physician who introduces the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He retells childhood, literacy, the fight with Covey, and the escape.
He adds a fuller account of life after slavery.
He describes lecturing for the antislavery movement.
He shows his break with Garrison's control of his public voice.
He argues from human nature, not only from his own suffering.
James McCune Smith introduces this edition.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Warden

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anthony Trollope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A gentle clergyman gives up a comfortable post when a reformer says the charity is misused.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1855 is correct. Britannica calls it his first novel of distinction in the Barsetshire series.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Septimus Harding (A kind clergyman and warden who chooses a clear conscience); Eleanor Harding (Harding's daughter, loved by the reformer John Bold); John Bold (A young reformer who questions the hospital income); Archdeacon Grantly (Married to Harding's daughter, and eager to fight the attack)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Septimus Harding is warden of Hiram's Hospital, a home for old men.
His pay looks too large for the old men's share of the charity.
John Bold, who loves Harding's daughter Eleanor, starts a public attack.
The newspaper The Jupiter joins the attack on Harding.
Harding resigns, though he could have fought and kept the post.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Westward Ho!

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1855 (Sort Year: 1855)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Kingsley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An adventure novel about Devon sailors in Elizabethan England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1855 is correct. Macmillan published the novel in three volumes in 1855. The story is set in the reign of Elizabeth I. A Devon resort was later named from the title. The slug keeps westward-ho without the exclamation mark.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amyas Leigh (A Devon adventurer and the hero of the voyage); Rose Salterne (The woman loved by Amyas and by his rivals); Salvation Yeo (An older sailor fierce in his Protestant faith)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Amyas Leigh of Devon dreams of sea fights and the New World.
He loves Rose Salterne, who is also loved by rival men.
The tale follows privateers (licensed raiders) against Spain.
Salvation Yeo and other sailors share Amyas's Protestant zeal.
The action belongs to the reign of Elizabeth I.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Aurora Leigh

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1856 (Sort Year: 1856)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Barrett Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse novel about a woman poet who chooses both art and love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: She was at work on it by 1853. The EBB Archive dates publication to November 1856. The title page reads 1857, so Britannica and the Poetry Foundation often say 1857. Further impressions came in January and March 1857. Database year 1856 matches the month of issue. The 1857 date is the imprint year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aurora Leigh (The woman poet who narrates the story); Romney Leigh (Her cousin, a philanthropist who learns his social plan has failed); Marian Erle (A poor woman betrayed and then sheltered by Aurora)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aurora tells her own life, from Italy to a strict English aunt.
She educates herself in her father's hidden books and starts to write.
At 20 she refuses Romney, who wants a helper, not a poet.
In London she wins a name, then meets the wronged Marian Erle.
Romney, later blind and humbled, and Aurora choose a shared life.

items.title: "It Is Never Too Late to Mend" (1856) — Charles Reade

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: It Is Never Too Late to Mend

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1856 (Sort Year: 1856)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Reade

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A ruined farmer seeks his fortune abroad while a thief suffers in a cruel prison.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Richard Bentley published the three volume novel in London in 1856. The database year 1856 is correct. The prison story is modern. It is not set in the Middle Ages.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: George Fielding (The honest farmer who goes to Australia); Susan Merton (The woman George hopes to marry); John Meadows (The country gentleman who schemes to win Susan); Tom Robinson (The thief who suffers under the new prison system); Governor Hawes (The cruel prison governor)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
George Fielding must earn money before he can marry Susan Merton.
John Meadows, a rich country gentleman, wants Susan and works against George.
George leaves for Australia.
Tom Robinson, a thief, is arrested and shut in a silent prison.
Governor Hawes uses cruel labour and punishment on the prisoners.
The novel uses these scenes to attack real abuses in English jails.

items.title: "The Young Fur Traders" (1856) — R. M. Ballantyne

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Young Fur Traders

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1856 (Sort Year: 1856)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: R. M. Ballantyne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A restless boy leaves settlement life for the northern fur trade.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1856 is correct. The full title is Snowflakes and Sunbeams, or The Young Fur Traders. Nelson of Edinburgh published it in 1856.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charley Kennedy (The restless young hero who wants adventure.); Kate Kennedy (His sister, who accepts work at home.); Frank Kennedy (Their father, once a fur trader himself.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Charley Kennedy lives at the Red River Settlement.
His father, Frank Kennedy, wants him to take a quiet post.
Charley wants the hard, free life of the fur traders.
His sister Kate listens, and she stays with home duties.
The tale follows his training and dangers in the wild.
Ballantyne drew the setting from his Hudson's Bay Company years.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Barchester Towers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1857 (Sort Year: 1857)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anthony Trollope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about a power struggle in Barchester after a new bishop arrives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1857 is correct. The database genre label Poetry is wrong. This is a novel. Gutenberg's text also says first published in 1857.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mrs Proudie (The new bishop's wife, who tries to rule the diocese); Mr Slope (The bishop's chaplain, oily, ambitious, and finally defeated); Dr Proudie (The weak new bishop of Barchester); Eleanor Bold (Harding's widowed daughter, courted by several men); Mr Arabin (The clergyman who wins Eleanor)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Old Bishop Grantly dies, and the city asks who will replace him.
The new bishop, Dr Proudie, is ruled by his wife and his chaplain.
Mrs Proudie and Mr Slope push a Low Church plan on the cathedral.
They clash with Archdeacon Grantly and the older clerical party.
Eleanor Bold, now a widow, marries Mr Arabin, and Slope is driven out.

items.title: "Scenes of Clerical Life" (1857) — George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Scenes of Clerical Life

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1857 (Sort Year: 1857)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three stories about Church of England clergymen in the Midlands. It is her first published fiction.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database says 1857, which is the serial year in Blackwood's Magazine. The two volume book came out in 1858. This is the first use of the name George Eliot.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amos Barton (A poor and plain curate (junior priest) in the first story); Maynard Gilfil (A clergyman in the second story); Janet Dempster (A wife with a cruel husband in the third story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book has three stories: Amos Barton, Mr Gilfil's Love Story and Janet's Repentance.
Each story is about a different clergyman and his village.
They are set in and around the made up town of Milby.
The stories look at poverty, drink and the troubles of ordinary people.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Coral Island

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1858 (Sort Year: 1858)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: R. M. Ballantyne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three boys are wrecked on a Pacific island and must survive.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the book to 1858. A Victorian fiction list also gives Nelson of Edinburgh in 1858. The database year 1857 is one year early. The database calls the book a drama, but it is a novel. The Gutenberg text checked here is an 1884 reprint.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph Rover (The narrator, a boy who loves to roam.); Jack Martin (The older, steady friend.); Peterkin Gay (The younger, quick, funny friend.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ralph Rover tells the story, and he loves to roam.
He goes to sea with Jack Martin and Peterkin Gay.
A storm wrecks their ship in the Pacific.
The three boys must live on a coral island.
They later see a pirate ship coming through the reef.
Ballantyne offers the tale to boys as both fun and a lesson.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Doctor Thorne

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1858 (Sort Year: 1858)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anthony Trollope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young heir must marry money, but he loves a girl the county thinks is poor.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1858 is correct. It is the third Barsetshire novel. Gutenberg's text says first published in 1858.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frank Gresham (The squire's son, pressed to marry a rich woman); Mary Thorne (The doctor's niece, heroine of the novel); Doctor Thomas Thorne (Mary's uncle, who protects her family secret); Sir Roger Scatcherd (A rough, rich contractor whose will changes Mary's fate)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Gresham estate is in debt, so Frank is told to marry wealth.
Frank loves Mary Thorne, niece of the country doctor.
The county sees Mary as too poor and too obscure for the heir.
Sir Roger Scatcherd's will leaves a fortune that reaches Mary.
Frank can then marry her with both love and money.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Our American Cousin

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1858 (Sort Year: 1858)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Tom Taylor

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A three act comedy about a plain American among proud English relatives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1858 is the first performance, at Laura Keene's Theatre in New York on 15 October. Taylor wrote the farce in 1851. London saw it in 1861. A known printing is 1869. Some accounts wrongly say the first opening was in London.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Asa Trenchard (The blunt American cousin who comes to claim family land); Florence Trenchard (The lively English cousin, first played by Laura Keene); Lord Dundreary (A silly lord whose jokes stole the show); Coyle (The greedy agent who threatens the family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Asa Trenchard, a plain American, comes to England to claim family land.
He meets proud relatives, including Florence Trenchard and Lord Dundreary.
He saves the family from Coyle, a greedy money agent.
Laura Keene first staged it in New York on 15 October 1858.
Sothern's silly Lord Dundreary became the part audiences loved.
On 14 April 1865, Booth shot Lincoln during the third act.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Phantastes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1858 (Sort Year: 1858)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George MacDonald

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young man steps from his dead father's desk into a fairy dream world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1858 is correct. Britannica dates Phantastes 1858. The London book was published by Smith, Elder in 1858.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anodos (The young man who tells the story and enters the fairy world); The tiny woman (A fairy figure who comes out of the old desk)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Anodos wakes on the morning after his twenty first birthday.
He opens an old desk and finds papers, rose leaves, and a tiny woman.
The woman grants him a wish and sends him toward fairy country.
Flowers, shadows, and strange beings test him on the way.
The tale works like a dream that also teaches the soul.

items.title: "A Tale of Two Cities" (1859) — Charles Dickens

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Tale of Two Cities

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: During the French Revolution, a wasted lawyer dies so that a lookalike can live.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Weekly parts in All the Year Round ran from 30 April to 26 November 1859. The book came out in 1859. Database year 1859 is correct. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sydney Carton (A brilliant, wasted lawyer who dies for Darnay); Charles Darnay (A Frenchman who looks like Carton and marries Lucie); Lucie Manette (Dr Manette's daughter, loved by both men); Dr Alexandre Manette (A doctor freed from the Bastille); Madame Defarge (A revolutionary who knits a record of the condemned)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The opening lines of the novel is "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair…"
The novel was published in 1859 and it is connected to French Revolution.
The two cities in the novel are London and Paris.
It appeared in the Dickens' journal "All the Year Round" in 31 installments.
The scene shifts from one city to other.
The chief characters of the novel are Dr. Manette who suffered for many years in Bastille.
Lucie Manette is his daughter who married Charles Darnay.
Sidney Carton, the young lawyer, who was in love with Lucy, sacrificed his life in order to save the life of Charles Darnay.
Madame Defarge, the hard-hearted revolutionary leader and Miss Pross, the protecting angel of Lucie and Evermonde brothers are villainous characters.
Darnay was in relation with theses villainous characters and so was captured by the revolutionaries and only saved at the last moment by Sydney Carton.
The novel presents a vivid picture of the city of Paris during The French Revolution.
The story moves between London and Paris before and during the Revolution.
Dr Manette is released from the Bastille and joins his daughter Lucie.
Charles Darnay, a French noble who rejects his family, is tried in London.
Sydney Carton, who looks like Darnay, loves Lucie but seems to waste his life.
In Paris, Carton takes Darnay's place at the guillotine.

items.title: "Adam Bede" (1859) — George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Adam Bede

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A village carpenter loves a girl who is led astray by a rich young man.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database 1859 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Adam Bede (The honest carpenter and hero); Hetty Sorrel (A pretty, vain village girl); Arthur Donnithorne (The young squire who misleads Hetty); Dinah Morris (A Methodist preacher, Hetty's cousin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the first novel of Eliot and it is a pastoral novel set in a rural community of Hayslope, England in summer 1799.
The novel revolves around a love rectangle between beautiful but thoughtless Hetty Sorrel, Captain Arthur Donnithorne, young squire who seduces her, Adam Bede (Hetty's unacknowledged suitor), and Dinah Morris, Hetty's cousin.
It is written in 3 volumes.
The real village where Adam Bede was set is 'Ellastone'.
Adam is a local carpenter, admired for his integrity and intelligence. He is in love with Hetty.
The plot of Adam Bede is founded on a story told to George Eliot by her aunt Elizabeth Evans.
Jonathan Burges is Adam's employer at carpentry shop.
It is called a "novel of seduction" Plot:.
Adam is a local carpenter falls in love with Hetty but she is attracted to Arthur.
When Adam interrupts between them, Arthur and Adam fights.
Arthur agrees to leave Hetty.
Hetty Sorrel also agreed to marry with Adam but shortly before marriage it is discovered that she is pregnant.
In desperation, Hetty leaves in search of Arthur but could not find him.
She delivers the baby but abandons the infant in a field but retrieves the infant again because she could not bear child cries, but till the time the child is dead of exposure.
Hetty is caught and tried for child murder.
She is found guilty and sentenced to hang.
Dinah enters the prison and pledges to stay with Hetty until the end. Dinah is a Methodist preacher girl.
When Arthur hears of her impending execution he rushes to court and asked the sentence commuted to transportation. Hetty dies just before she is set to return to Hayslope.
Ultimately Dinah and Adam became aware of their love and gets married and live peacefully with their families.
Quote: "It has been a hard day for thee."
Adam Bede is a good carpenter in the village of Hayslope.
He loves Hetty Sorrel, but she loves Arthur Donnithorne, the squire's grandson.
Hetty is left pregnant and alone.
She harms her baby and is tried.
Adam later finds a quiet love with Dinah Morris, a woman preacher.

items.title: "Idylls of the King" (1859) — Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Idylls of the King

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A set of Arthurian poems on the rise of Camelot and its ruin through guilt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first book appeared in 1859. Britannica Scholars notes new idylls in The Holy Grail, and Other Poems in 1869, dated 1870. The cycle grew after 1859. The database phrase 1859, expanded later, is right. The poems are not posthumous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: King Arthur (The ideal king whose realm fails when faith inside it fails); Guinevere (Arthur's queen, whose love for Lancelot helps ruin the court); Lancelot (Arthur's greatest knight and Guinevere's lover); Vivien (The woman who ensnares Merlin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King Arthur founds the Round Table as a fellowship of duty.
Lancelot's love for Queen Guinevere brings deceit into the court.
Separate idylls tell of Enid, Vivien, Elaine, and others.
The hope of the Table fades as rumour and betrayal spread.
Arthur's kingdom ends, and the old order gives way.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: On Liberty

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Stuart Mill

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay on how far society may limit the freedom of an individual.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Project Gutenberg, the Stanford Encyclopedia, and Wikipedia all date the essay to 1859.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Stuart Mill (The essayist who states the harm principle); Harriet Taylor Mill (His wife, who helped form the argument)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mill asks when society may limit a person's freedom.
He warns against the tyranny of the majority.
Power over an adult is just only to prevent harm to others.
Thought, speech, and private life should stay free.
Odd or new ideas help a society find truth.
Harriet Taylor Mill helped shape the argument.

items.title: "On the Origin of Species" (1859) — Charles Darwin

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: On the Origin of Species

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Darwin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A science book arguing that species change by natural selection.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1859 is correct. John Murray published the book on 24 November 1859. The full title is On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection. A joint paper with Alfred Russel Wallace appeared in 1858. Britannica dates the private theory to 1837-1839, after the Beagle voyage of 1831-1836.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Darwin returned from the Beagle with notes on plants and animals.
He worked in private for years on how species might change.
Alfred Russel Wallace reached a similar idea, so both men published in 1858.
The 1859 book shows how small useful changes can build new species.
He closes by praising the grandeur in this view of life.

items.title: "The Ordeal of Richard Feverel" (1859) — George Meredith

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1859 (Sort Year: 1859)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Meredith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A father tests a strict system of education on his son, and it fails.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in 1859. Britannica and the Victorian circulating library list agree. Database year 1859 is correct. It is a novel. Mudie's library refused it. It is not his first book. The Shaving of Shagpat came in 1856.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Austin Feverel (The proud baronet who tries to educate his son by a system); Richard Feverel (The son who loves Lucy and is put through an ordeal); Lucy (The girl of lower rank whom Richard loves)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sir Austin Feverel raises his son Richard by a private System.
Richard falls in love with Lucy, a girl below his rank.
Pride in father and son blocks a simple marriage.
The book is a romantic comedy that ends in tragedy.
Mudie's circulating library cancelled a large order, calling it improper.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Woman in White

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1860 (Sort Year: 1860)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Wilkie Collins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Walter Hartright uncovers a plot that swaps Laura Fairlie for a double.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial began in All the Year Round on 26 November 1859 and ended in August 1860. Sampson Low published the three volume book in August 1860. Britannica labels the novel 1860. The database span 1859-60 matches the serial, not a different book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Walter Hartright (A drawing master who narrates much of the case and loves Laura); Laura Fairlie (The heiress whose identity is stolen); Anne Catherick (The woman in white, Laura's double, who knows a dangerous secret); Marian Halcombe (Laura's brave half sister and a main investigator); Sir Percival Glyde (Laura's husband, who hides the secret of his birth); Count Fosco (Percival's brilliant and ruthless helper)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Walter meets a frightened woman in white on a dark road.
He then falls in love with Laura Fairlie, who looks like that woman.
Laura marries Sir Percival Glyde, who wants her money.
Percival and Count Fosco lock Laura away under Anne's name.
Marian Halcombe and Walter expose the crime and restore Laura.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Framley Parsonage

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anthony Trollope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young vicar slides into debt through fashionable friends, while his sister wins a difficult love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Cornhill ran it from January 1860 to April 1861. Smith, Elder published the book in April 1861. Britannica dates the book 1861.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mark Robarts (Vicar of Framley, led into debt by grand friends); Lucy Robarts (Mark's sister, who loves Lord Lufton); Lady Lufton (The local patroness, proud at first, then won over); Lord Lufton (Lady Lufton's son, who wants to marry Lucy); Nathaniel Sowerby (A spendthrift MP who draws Mark into bills of debt)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mark Robarts is the young vicar of Framley, backed by Lady Lufton.
He signs bills for the fashionable MP Nathaniel Sowerby.
The debt threatens Mark's home and his good name.
His sister Lucy loves Lord Lufton, but his mother resists the match.
Lady Lufton learns Lucy's worth, and the parsonage is saved.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Great Expectations

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Pip receives money, becomes a gentleman, and learns that his hopes were built on shame.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Weekly parts in All the Year Round ran from 1 December 1860 to 3 August 1861. The three volume book came out in 1861. Database range 1860-61 matches the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pip (The narrator, a blacksmith's boy who becomes a gentleman); Joe Gargery (The kind blacksmith who raises Pip); Mrs Joe (Pip's harsh sister and one mother figure); Miss Havisham (A rich woman who stopped her life on her wedding day); Estella (Miss Havisham's beautiful adopted daughter); Abel Magwitch (The convict who secretly funds Pip)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pip (Phillip Pirrip) is the protagonist of this novel, who is a young orphan living with his sister and her husband (Mr. Joe) in Kent.
While Pip was sitting in a cemetery on one evening looking at his parent's tombstone, he was grabbed by an escaped convict Magwitch.
Magwitch asked Pip to bring food for him and also a file to cut his irons in the leg.
Pip obeys but the convict is recaptured.
One day Pip makes a visit to Satis house with his uncle Pumblechook. At Satis House lives Miss Havisham. There Pip meets a young girl name Estella who treats him well.
He falls in love with Estella and dreamed of becoming a wealthy man to become worthy of Estella.
With Miss Havisham's guidance Pip is apprenticed to his brother in law Mr. Joe, a village blacksmith and Pip works in the forge unhappily.
Orlick was a malicious labourer of Mr. Joe, attacks Mrs. Joe and makes her dumb.
One day Mr. Jaggers comes with news that a secret benefactor (actually the convict Magwitch) has given Pip a large fortune to go to London immediately to start his education as a gentleman.
Pip misinterprets Miss Havisham as a secret benefactor.
In London, Pip befriends Herbert Pocket and Wemmick (Jaggers' clerk).
He furthers his education by studying with the tutor Matthew Pocket, Herbert's father.
Herbert and Pip started leading an undisciplined life in London, enjoying themselves and increasing debts.
Pip again confronts Orlick but was promptly fired by Mr. Jaggers.
Mrs. Joe dies and Pip goes home to attend the funeral.
One night Magwitch appears and reveals that he is his benefactor.
Pip learns that Compeyson (former partner of Magwitch) is the man who abandoned Miss Havisham and Estella is the daughter of Magwitch.
Miss Havisham has raised Estella to break men's heart as a revenge for the pain of her own broken heart.
Pip begins to care for Magwitch.
Estella is married to Bentley Drummle.
Pip makes a visit to Satis House and Miss Havisham asks for forgiveness and Pip forgives her.
Pip and Herbert tries to let Magwitch escape to London but in the meantime Pip is attacked by Orlick, but Herbert saved him.
While Pip and Herbert were trying to make Magwitch escape through the river on a rowboat they are caught by the police.
Magwitch and Compeyson fight in the river in which Compeyson is drowned.
Magwitch in sentenced to death and thus Pip loses his fortune.
Magwitch died and Pip falls ill.
Joe comes to London to care for Pip and they are reconciled.
Pip learns that after robbing Uncle Pumblechook, Orlick is in jail and his brother-in-law Joe is married to Biddy.
Pip goes abroad with Herbert to work.
After many years when he returns he finds Estella in a ruined garden at Satis House.
Her husband had treated her badly but was now dead.
Pip and Estella departs from the garden hand in hand believing they will never part again.
As a boy, Pip helps an escaped convict on the Kent marshes.
He visits Satis House, loves Estella, and is ashamed of his home.
A secret fortune lets him train as a London gentleman.
He learns that the convict Magwitch, not Miss Havisham, is his benefactor.
The fortune is lost.
Pip returns humbled, and the ending with Estella is quiet.

items.title: "The Mill on the Floss" (1860) — George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Mill on the Floss

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1860 (Sort Year: 1860)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A brother and sister grow up at a mill. Their love and quarrels end in a flood.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database 1860 is correct. Wikipedia gives 4 April 1860 for the three volume book. The other database record (george-eliot-the-mill-on-the-floss) wrongly shows 1914.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Maggie Tulliver (The clever, warm hearted heroine); Tom Tulliver (Her stern brother); Philip Wakem (A kind young man Maggie befriends); Stephen Guest (A suitor who leads Maggie into scandal)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tom and Maggie Tulliver grow up at Dorlcote Mill by the River Floss.
Their father loses the mill after a lawsuit.
Maggie is clever and loving.
Tom is stern and proud.
Maggie is judged by the town after a scandal.
A flood comes and the two die together.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Unto This Last

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1860 (Sort Year: 1860)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Ruskin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four essays on political economy that say there is no wealth but life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Project Gutenberg dates the Cornhill essays from August to December 1860. Encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia date the book edition to 1862. The database year is the essay year, not the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Ruskin (The essayist who redefines wealth as human well-being)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Four essays attack the political economy of Ruskin's day.
They first appeared in Cornhill Magazine in 1860.
Ruskin says wealth is life, not a pile of money.
He defends fair wages and the honour of labour.
Angry readers made the magazine stop the series.
The book edition came out in 1862.
Mahatma Gandhi later took the book as a guide.

items.title: "Considerations on Representative Government" (1861) — John Stuart Mill

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Considerations on Representative Government

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Stuart Mill

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A treatise arguing that representative government is the best form for a capable people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and the Toronto Collected Works listing both date the book to 1861. The database genre Poetry is a catalog error. The book is political prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Stuart Mill (The philosopher arguing for representative government)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mill asks which form of government does the most good.
He says representative government is the best ideal.
Citizens grow by voting, speaking, and holding office.
A people must be willing and able to sustain that government.
He supports a wider vote and seats matched to vote share.
The book is political prose, not a poem.

items.title: "East Lynne" (1861) — Mrs Henry Wood / Ellen Wood

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: East Lynne

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mrs Henry Wood / Ellen Wood

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lady Isabel leaves her husband, is thought dead, and returns in disguise as a governess.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1861 is correct for the novel. Britannica and Project Gutenberg both date the book to 1861. It was later dramatized with great success. A stage date is not the novel's date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lady Isabel Vane (The wife who elopes, is thought dead, and comes back disguised); Archibald Carlyle (The hard-working lawyer Isabel marries and then leaves); Francis Levison (The man who persuades Isabel to run away and then deserts her); Madame Vine (The false name Isabel uses as governess in her old home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lady Isabel Vane is left poor after her father dies.
She marries the lawyer Archibald Carlyle, then runs away with Francis Levison.
Levison deserts her, and people come to think that she has died.
She returns in disguise as a governess (a home teacher) to her own children.
Carlyle has married again.
She hides under the name Madame Vine.
The tale moralizes about a wife's fall, and it became a famous stage piece.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lady Audley’s Secret

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mary Elizabeth Braddon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A beautiful wife hides a past life, and a lazy barrister hunts the truth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A weekly serial began in Robin Goodfellow on 6 July 1861 and stopped unfinished that September. Sixpenny Magazine then ran it from February 1862 to January 1863. Tinsley Brothers published the three-volume book in 1862. Database span 1861-62 covers the start and the book. The magazine serial also reaches January 1863.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucy Graham (Lady Audley) (Helen Talboys under a new name, Sir Michael's bigamous wife); Sir Michael Audley (The older rich landowner who marries the young governess); Robert Audley (Sir Michael's nephew, who investigates George's disappearance); George Talboys (Helen's first husband, who vanishes after seeing her portrait); Alicia Audley (Sir Michael's daughter, who resents her new stepmother)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lucy Graham, a governess (a teacher in a private home), marries Sir Michael Audley.
She is really Helen Talboys, and she has let people think she died.
George Talboys returns from Australia and then vanishes at Audley Court.
His friend Robert Audley, a barrister (a court lawyer), traces her past.
Robert proves the bigamy.
She tries to burn the inn where he sleeps.
She confesses.
He sends her to an asylum (a hospital for mental illness) abroad.
George is found alive.

items.title: "Silas Marner" (1861) — George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Silas Marner

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lonely weaver loses his gold but gains a little girl who changes his life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database 1861 is correct. Wikipedia gives 2 April 1861.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Silas Marner (The weaver); Eppie (The orphan girl he adopts); Godfrey Cass (The squire's son and Eppie's secret father); Dunstan Cass (Godfrey's brother, who steals the gold)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe is the third novel of Eliot.
It is a realistic novel centering on a humble weaver Silas who renounces religion after members of his church blame him for the theft of a pouch of coins.
The novel is set in 19th century.
Silas Marner, a weaver is accused of stealing the congregation's funds.
Silas is proclaimed guilty.
He married William Dane.
Chief characters are:.
Silas Marner : a weaver.
Godfrey Cass : eldest son of the local squire.
Dunstan Cass : second eldest son of squire Romola (1863)
It is a historical novel set in Florence during 1490's renaissance of Italy.
It is about a deep study of life in the city of Florence from an intellectual, artistic, religious, and social point of view.
It first published in fourteen parts published in Cornhill Magazine.
It explores the Florentine religion and politics through the eyes of beautiful and highly educated Romola and her husband Tito.
Silas Marner is a weaver who was falsely accused and left his old town.
He lives alone in the village of Raveloe and loves his gold.
His gold is stolen.
A small girl wanders into his house, and he raises her as his own.
Her love brings him back into the community.

items.title: "The Cloister and the Hearth" (1861) — Charles Reade

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Cloister and the Hearth

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Reade

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Dutch artist loves Margaret, becomes a monk, and is the father of Erasmus.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1861 is correct. The fifteenth century is the setting, not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gerard Eliason (The artist who becomes a monk); Margaret Brandt (The woman he loves, and the mother of his son); Erasmus (Their son, the famous scholar)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gerard Eliason, a young Dutch artist, gives up the idea of the priesthood for love.
He loves Margaret Brandt, but his father has him imprisoned.
The lovers part, and enemies tell Gerard that Margaret is dead.
Wild with grief, he becomes a monk.
They meet again, and he learns that they have a son.
His vows keep him from marriage.
The son grows up to be Erasmus.

items.title: "The Early Italian Poets" (1861) — Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Early Italian Poets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1861 (Sort Year: 1861)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English verse translations of Dante and other early Italian poets.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1861 is correct for the book. The Rossetti Archive dates The Early Italian Poets to 1861 and the revised edition, Dante and His Circle, to 1874. The database genre Fiction is wrong. This is a book of verse translations, not a novel. He had begun Italian translation work in the 1840s, but the book year is 1861.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dante Alighieri (The poet whose Vita Nuova Rossetti translates); Beatrice (The beloved at the center of Dante's New Life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rossetti translates poems of the dolce stil novo (sweet new style).
The book includes a full version of Dante's Vita Nuova (New Life).
His preface says a good poem must not become a bad one.
Notes explain the poets and the history around them.
A later edition in 1874 was retitled Dante and His Circle.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Aurora Floyd

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1863 (Sort Year: 1863)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mary Elizabeth Braddon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A banker's daughter hides a past marriage, and a murder follows her to her new home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Temple Bar serialized it monthly from January 1862 to January 1863. Tinsley Brothers published the three-volume book in 1863. Database span 1862-63 matches that history. The book year to memorize is 1863.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aurora Floyd (A passionate heiress with a hidden marriage in her past); John Mellish (The devoted country gentleman Aurora marries); Talbot Bulstrode (A proud suitor who cannot accept Aurora's secret); Steeve Hargraves (A stable hand called the Softy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aurora Floyd is the high-spirited daughter of a rich banker.
She hides a long absence and a secret earlier marriage.
Talbot Bulstrode and John Mellish both court her.
She marries John Mellish, but a man from her past arrives.
That man is a horse trainer.
He is murdered, and Aurora is suspected.
The book turns on bigamy and extortion (threats made in order to get money).

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Chronicles of Carlingford

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Margaret Oliphant

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A linked set of stories about clergy, chapel folk, and society in the town of Carlingford.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The 1911 Britannica dates the early magazine run to 1862-1865. Miss Marjoribanks then appeared as a book in 1866. Modern Britannica dates the anonymous books 1863-1866. The database span 1862-66 fits that early cluster. Phoebe Junior, a last chronicle of Carlingford, was published in 1876.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucilla Marjoribanks (The heroine of one chronicle, who tries to organise Carlingford society); The Carlingford clergy (Ministers and curates whose chapel and church quarrels fill the series)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The tales first appeared in Blackwood's Magazine in the early 1860s.
Salem Chapel follows a minister outside the Church of England and his narrow congregation.
The Perpetual Curate and other tales add more clergy and family plots.
Miss Marjoribanks, in 1866, shows a young woman trying to rule the town's social life.
Phoebe Junior in 1876 is the last chronicle, later than the database end year 1866.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: First Principles

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herbert Spencer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: It opens his Synthetic Philosophy, his plan to unite the sciences.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A prospectus went out in 1860. Britannica and Stanford date the book to 1862, from Williams and Norgate. A Gutenberg text marked second thousand is dated 1863. The database year 1862 is the first publication. The database genre Poetry is wrong, because this is prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Herbert Spencer (The author setting out the base laws of his system)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is the first volume of a long series called the Synthetic Philosophy.
Part one discusses the Unknowable, a reality beyond science and beyond religion.
Part two states laws he thinks hold for every kind of change.
He defines evolution as a move from a loose sameness to a joined complexity.
He then applies that pattern to life, mind, and society in later volumes.

items.title: "Goblin Market and Other Poems" (1862) — Christina Rossetti

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Goblin Market and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christina Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first major book, led by Goblin Market and filled with lyrics of love, loss, and faith.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First published by Macmillan in 1862. Database year 1862 is correct. A revised edition followed in 1876.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Macmillan published the book in 1862 under her own name.
Goblin Market is the long opening poem.
Shorter lyrics such as Remember sit beside it.
Devotional poems close the volume.
Dante Gabriel Rossetti designed the frontispiece and decorations.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: No Name

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Wilkie Collins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two sisters lose name and fortune, and Magdalen fights the law in disguise.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: All the Year Round serialized it from 15 March 1862 to 17 January 1863. Sampson Low published the three volume book on 14 December 1862. Britannica dates the novel 1862. The database year 1862 matches the book, not the serial's last part.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Magdalen Vanstone (The daring sister who uses disguise to recover the family money); Norah Vanstone (Magdalen's quieter sister, who suffers the loss with patience); Captain Wragge (A cunning trickster who helps Magdalen and watches his own profit)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Vanstone daughters learn that the law does not recognize them.
A sudden death and a cancelled will give the money to a relative.
Norah bears the loss quietly, but Magdalen refuses to submit.
Magdalen uses acting and false names to get near the fortune.
The struggle breaks her health, and a kinder ending follows.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Romola

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A historical novel set in 1490s Florence. A woman loses faith in the men she trusted.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Serial in Cornhill Magazine from July 1862 to August 1863. The three volume book came out in 1863. Database says 1862-63, which is correct for the serial. Archive and Wikisource date the book 1863.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Romola de' Bardi (The heroine); Tito Melema (Her false husband); Savonarola (A real preacher in Florence)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Romola is the daughter of a blind scholar in Renaissance Florence.
She marries Tito Melema, a charming Greek, who turns out to be false.
She is guided for a time by the preacher Savonarola.
She loses trust in both men and finds her own sense of duty.

items.title: "The Channings" (1862) — Mrs Henry Wood / Ellen Wood

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Channings

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1862 (Sort Year: 1862)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mrs Henry Wood / Ellen Wood

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A cathedral-town family suffers when a son is blamed for a clerk's stolen bank note.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1862 is correct. Britannica dates the novel to 1862. It is a family story, not a second edition of East Lynne.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Arthur Channing (The son who is blamed for the missing note); Roland Yorke (The clerk who takes Galloway's note and later explains); Mr Galloway (The lawyer whose bank note vanishes from a letter); Charley Channing (A younger brother and cathedral chorister); Constance Channing (A daughter of the Channing family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Channings are a middle-class family in the cathedral city of Helstonleigh.
A twenty-pound note disappears from a letter in Mr Galloway's office.
Suspicion falls on Arthur Channing, a son of the family.
Roland Yorke, another clerk, had taken the note and meant to replace it.
The family must endure shame, school trouble, and money worries.
The worst crime is this small theft.
A schoolboy ghost supplies a comic fright.

items.title: "Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature" (1863) — Thomas Henry Huxley

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1863 (Sort Year: 1863)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Henry Huxley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three essays that place humans beside apes, using bodies and fossils.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1863 is correct. Clark University records the first three essays as published in January 1863.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Henry Huxley (The scientist speaker who sets out the evidence)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book has three essays, issued together in January 1863.
The first traces how people discovered gibbons, orangs, chimpanzees, and gorillas.
Those apes have no tails, and adults share the human number of teeth.
The second essay compares the human body with other animal bodies.
He says humans differ less from gorillas than gorillas differ from lower apes.
The third essay studies old human bones, including Neanderthal fossils.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Ticket-of-Leave Man

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1863 (Sort Year: 1863)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Tom Taylor

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A melodrama about an innocent convict, a detective, and a return to crime.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1863 is correct. It opened at the Olympic Theatre in London in 1863 and ran for 407 nights. It is founded on Le Retour de Melun by Brisebarre and Nus.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Robert Brierly (Bob, the innocent man who returns on a ticket of leave); Jack Hawkshaw (A detective who uses disguise and more than one voice); Jem Dalton (Tiger, the criminal leader of the gang); Joe Skirritt (Hawkshaw's friend, harmed by Dalton)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bob Brierly, a young countryman, is caught in a fake money plot in London.
Detective Hawkshaw arrests him, though Bob is innocent.
Years later Bob returns from prison as a ticket of leave man (a convict let out early).
The old gang, led by Tiger Dalton, tries to drag Bob back to crime.
Hawkshaw hunts Dalton, who had harmed Hawkshaw's friend Joe Skirritt.
Bob and Hawkshaw then work together to stop the gang.
Taylor took the story from the French play Le Retour de Melun.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Water-Babies

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1863 (Sort Year: 1863)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Kingsley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A chimney boy becomes a water baby and learns moral lessons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial ran in Macmillan's Magazine in 1862-1863. The book appeared in 1863. Database year 1863 matches the volume. Victorian Web lists the serial under 1862 and the volume under 1863. The subtitle is A Fairy Tale for a Land Baby.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tom (A chimney sweep who becomes a water baby); Ellie (A little girl who enters the water world with him); Grimes (Tom's harsh master, a chimney sweep); Mrs. Doasyouwouldbedoneby (A fairy who teaches the golden rule of kindness); Mrs. Bedonebyasyoudid (A fairy who pays Tom back for his own deeds)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tom, a chimney sweep, runs away after cruel treatment.
He falls into a river and is changed into a water baby.
He meets water creatures and two stern, kind fairy teachers.
Mrs. Bedonebyasyoudid punishes him as he has treated others.
The tale teaches kindness and also jokes about bad science.

items.title: "Apologia Pro Vita Sua" (1864) — John Henry Newman

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Apologia Pro Vita Sua

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1864 (Sort Year: 1864)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Henry Newman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Newman defends his honesty by telling how he moved from Anglican life to Rome.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Newman wrote it in 1864 as a reply to Kingsley. It first appeared in parts and then as a book in 1864. A revised text followed in 1865. The database year 1864 is the first publication. The famous doubt sentence is in that history of his opinions.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Henry Newman (The writer, speaking in his own voice about his life and faith); Charles Kingsley (The Anglican clergyman and novelist whose charge provoked the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Charles Kingsley publicly attacked Newman's honesty about religious truth.
Newman answers by telling the history of his religious opinions.
He recalls his Anglican years and his part in the Oxford Movement.
He explains why he entered the Roman Catholic Church in 1845.
He argues that many hard questions still do not add up to doubt.
The book restored his public name far beyond Catholic readers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Armadale

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Wilkie Collins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two men named Allan Armadale face an old crime, a dream, and Lydia Gwilt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Cornhill Magazine serialized it from November 1864 to June 1866. Smith, Elder published the book on 15 May 1866. Britannica dates Armadale 1866. The database span 1864-66 is the serial period. The book year is 1866.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Allan Armadale (The rich, friendly heir who bears the family name); Ozias Midwinter (The other Allan Armadale, a darker friend who fears the dream); Lydia Gwilt (A beautiful schemer who tries to take the fortune by fraud and murder)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A dying confession tells how one Allan Armadale killed another.
Their sons share the name, and one lives as Ozias Midwinter.
A dream seems to warn that Midwinter will harm his friend.
Lydia Gwilt plots marriage and murder to seize the Armadale fortune.
Midwinter refuses to act out the dream, and Gwilt's plot fails.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Enoch Arden

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1864 (Sort Year: 1864)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tale of a sailor who returns after years away and will not break his wife's new home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1864 by Moxon in the volume Enoch Arden. The Poetry Foundation links it to his wish to voice common feeling. It is not posthumous. The database year 1864 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Enoch Arden (The sailor who sacrifices his claim so his wife can keep her new peace); Annie (Enoch's wife, who remarries after long silence); Philip (The patient friend who marries Annie)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Enoch Arden, Annie, and Philip grow up together in a little port.
Annie marries Enoch, and he sails away to earn money.
Years pass with no news, and Annie at last marries Philip.
Enoch comes home, sees their happiness, and refuses to reveal himself.
He dies without reclaiming his place, and the town gives him a costly funeral.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Our Mutual Friend

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1865 (Sort Year: 1865)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A drowned heir returns in disguise, and a fortune in dust heaps tests love and greed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts ran from May 1864 to November 1865. The book came out in 1865. Database range 1864-65 matches the serial. The unfinished flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Harmon (The heir who is thought dead and returns in disguise); Bella Wilfer (The young woman named in the father's will); Lizzie Hexam (A boatman's daughter who can read the river); Bradley Headstone (A schoolmaster driven by jealous rage); Noddy Boffin (The kind dustman who inherits when Harmon seems dead)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gaffer Hexam finds a body in the Thames, thought to be John Harmon.
Harmon is alive and watches, under another name, the woman he was meant to marry.
The dust heaps of old Harmon hold a great fortune.
Bradley Headstone's jealousy leads to violence on the river.
Bella Wilfer learns to value love above money, and Harmon reveals himself.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Rajmohan’s Wife

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1864 (Sort Year: 1864)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young wife warns the man she loves that robbers plan to attack his house.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1864 is the serial year, and the serial trap flag is right. It ran in the Indian Field, edited by Kishori Chand Mitra. A book reprint came later, after the magazine issues were hard to find.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Matangini (Rajmohan's wife, who risks her life to warn Madhav); Rajmohan (Her abusive husband, who joins the robbers); Madhav Ghose (The educated cousin she loves, and her sister's husband); Mathur Ghose (Madhav's cousin, who plots for the property and for Matangini)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Matangini is the young wife of the harsh Rajmohan in a Bengal village.
She loves Madhav Ghose, who has married her sister, but she still protects him.
She overhears Rajmohan planning a dacoity (an armed robbery) at Madhav's house.
She crosses the night to warn Madhav, and the attack fails.
Mathur, a cruel cousin, locks her away because he wants her.
The serial ends suddenly.
Rajmohan is jailed, Mathur dies, and Matangini dies young.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Wives and Daughters

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Gaskell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished story of Molly Gibson, her new sister, and two families.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the work 1864-1866 and says it was unfinished at her death on 12 November 1865. Victorian Web dates the two-volume book to 1866 and calls it unfinished and posthumous. Database span 1864-66 matches the serial history. The subtitle is An Everyday Story. The serial ran in The Cornhill Magazine.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Molly Gibson (The doctor's daughter whose quiet goodness holds the story); Cynthia Kirkpatrick (Molly's beautiful stepsister, charming and restless); Roger Hamley (The younger Hamley son, a scientist who comes to love Molly); Mr. Gibson (Molly's father, the country doctor who remarries); Squire Hamley (The proud father of the neighboring Hamley family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Molly Gibson's father marries Hyacinth, a charming but shallow widow.
Molly gains a stepsister, the beautiful and restless Cynthia.
The two young women are drawn toward the Hamley brothers.
Secrets and village talk test Molly's steady goodness.
Gaskell died before the last chapter, so the novel is unfinished.

items.title: "Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland" (1865) — Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1865 (Sort Year: 1865)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A child falls down a rabbit hole into a rude, dreamlike world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1865 is the withdrawn Macmillan printing. Britannica says only about 21 copies survive. The reprint was ready by Christmas 1865 and is dated 1866. The early handwritten gift is Alice's Adventures Underground, published in 1886. The book is a prose tale, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alice (A curious girl whose dream journey the book follows); The Queen of Hearts (A furious queen who orders heads to be cut off); The Mad Hatter (A rude host at a tea party that never ends); The Cheshire Cat (A grinning cat who says everyone there is mad)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
On 4 July 1862 Dodgson told the tale on a boat trip to Godstow.
Alice Liddell asked him to write her adventures down.
Alice follows a rabbit and falls into a world of odd creatures.
She meets the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, and the Queen of Hearts.
John Tenniel drew the pictures for the Macmillan book of 1865.
Tenniel disliked the printing, so that first issue was withdrawn.
A new printing was ready by Christmas 1865, but dated 1866.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Drum-Taps

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1865 (Sort Year: 1865)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walt Whitman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Civil War poems that move from the call to arms to grief for the dead.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the book to May 1865. The Whitman Archive agrees, and dates the sequel to autumn 1865. In 1867 both were added to Leaves of Grass. The database year 1865 is correct for the separate book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A poet who moves from war fever to mourning); Abraham Lincoln (The dead president mourned in the sequel poems)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Whitman nursed wounded soldiers in Washington hospitals.
Drum-Taps was published as its own book in May 1865.
Early poems call young men into the war.
Later poems watch the wounded and the dead at night.
A sequel in autumn 1865 added poems on Lincoln's death.
In 1867 the war poems were attached to Leaves of Grass.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Durgeshnandini

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1865 (Sort Year: 1865)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Rajput prince and a chieftain's daughter love each other while Pathan war surrounds them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1865 is correct. The Bengali title means daughter of the fort's lord. An English translation appeared in 1880. The database marks the book as a translated text because the original is Bengali.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jagat Singha (The Rajput prince and hero); Tilottama (The Bengali chieftain's daughter whom he loves); Aesha (The Pathan leader's daughter, who nurses the wounded prince); Bimala (A woman of the household who warns Jagat of danger)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The romance is set when Mughal power and Pathan chiefs clash in Bengal.
Prince Jagat Singha loves Tilottama, the chieftain's daughter.
Pathan fighters wound the prince in a sudden attack.
Aesha, daughter of the Pathan leader, nurses him and comes to love him.
Love and loyalty pull against the war.
The book showed readers that a full novel could be written in Bengali.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Essays in Criticism

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1865 (Sort Year: 1865)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1865 book of essays on the job of the critic.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Function of Criticism was given as a lecture in 1864 and printed in the 1865 book. That book is the First Series. The Second Series came out in 1888, after his death. The database year 1865 matches the First Series.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Matthew Arnold (The critic speaking in his own essays)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The opening essay is The Function of Criticism at the Present Time.
Arnold says criticism should see the object as it really is.
He attacks narrow English habits and praises wider European ideas.
Later essays treat European writers and moral thinkers.
A second series came out in 1888, after Arnold died.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Sesame and Lilies

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1865 (Sort Year: 1865)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Ruskin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two lectures on reading and on women's education, published together in 1865.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia says the lectures were given in December 1864 and published in 1865. Encyclopedia.com also dates the volume to 1865. Project Gutenberg reprints a later 1894 edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Ruskin (The lecturer on books and on the education of women)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Two lectures from 1864 were published as a book in 1865.
Of Kings' Treasuries is about how to read books.
Ruskin splits books of the hour from books of all time.
Of Queens' Gardens discusses women's education and moral power.
He asks readers to choose wisdom over fashion and rank.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Miss Marjoribanks

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Margaret Oliphant

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lucilla Marjoribanks comes home and tries to manage Carlingford society.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Serialised in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine from February 1865 to May 1866. The first book edition was published by Blackwood in 1866. The database year 1866 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucilla Marjoribanks (A confident young woman who wants to organise Carlingford); Dr. Marjoribanks (Her father, a doctor who likes a quiet and orderly house); Nancy (The cook whose dinners give the house its local fame)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
At fifteen, Lucilla loses her mother and offers to stay and comfort her father.
Dr. Marjoribanks sends her back to school.
Years later she returns, keeps the cook Nancy, and sets out to lead the town's evenings.
She steers guests, rivals, and possible husbands with calm confidence.
The comedy asks how far a clever woman can rule a small town.

items.title: "The Crown of Wild Olive" (1866) — John Ruskin

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Crown of Wild Olive

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Ruskin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three lectures on work, traffic, and war, published as a prose book in 1866.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1866 is correct for the book. Encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia date it to 1866 and describe three lectures: Work, Traffic, and War. The database genre Poetry is a catalog error. It is prose. A later edition added a fourth lecture.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Ruskin (The lecturer on work, taste, and war)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This book collects lectures on work, traffic, and war.
Work asks what kind of labour is worthy.
Traffic links public taste with moral life.
War asks when fighting can be just.
The 1866 book is prose, not a poem.
A later edition added a fourth lecture.

items.title: "The Prince’s Progress and Other Poems" (1866) — Christina Rossetti

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Prince’s Progress and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christina Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her second major book, led by a tale of a prince who arrives too late.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Macmillan published The Prince's Progress and Other Poems in 1866. Database year 1866 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The prince (A slow bridegroom who wastes the years of his journey); The princess (The bride who dies before he arrives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A princess waits while her prince delays the journey.
He lingers with pleasures and with people he meets.
Years pass before he reaches her gate.
He finds the princess dead and the bridal too late.
Other lyrics and devotional poems fill the rest of the 1866 book.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: New Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1867 (Sort Year: 1867)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Arnold's 1867 volume, his last major book of new verse.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: New Poems was published in 1867. It is virtually his last book of new verse. Dover Beach's first printing is in this volume. The database year 1867 is correct. This is not the 1853 volume called Poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Empedocles (The philosopher restored to print in this volume); Thyrsis (The shepherd name for Arthur Hugh Clough in the elegy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book restores Empedocles on Etna, dropped from Poems in 1853.
It prints Dover Beach for the first time.
Thyrsis, an elegy for the poet Clough, is included.
Rugby Chapel remembers his father, Thomas Arnold.
After this book he wrote little new verse.

items.title: "Under Two Flags" (1867) — Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Under Two Flags

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1867 (Sort Year: 1867)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An English officer flees a false charge and serves in Algeria.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1867 matches the first book publication. Project Gutenberg and the 1911 Britannica both give 1867.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bertie Cecil (An English guards officer who accepts shame to protect others.); Cigarette (A bold camp girl. Her sharp talk is compared to Voltaire, a French writer.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bertie Cecil is a charming officer in a rich London guards regiment.
He is accused of forgery, which means signing a false paper.
He stays silent, because the truth would hurt his brother and a lady.
He lets people think he is dead and goes to Algeria.
He joins a French regiment under another name.
Cigarette, a bold girl of the army camp, shares his dangers.
The story turns on honor, exile, and sacrifice.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: “Dover Beach”

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1867 (Sort Year: 1867)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lover by the sea mourns the retreat of religious faith.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem was first printed in New Poems (1867). Scholars often suggest composition near 1851, and some notes may go back to about 1849. Those writing dates are not certain. The sure date is publication in 1867. The database phrase first published 1867 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A lover looking out from Dover toward France); The Loved One (The person asked to stay true in a faithless world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
2. Scholar Gypsy 3. Rugby Chapel (elegy poem on the death of his father; 1867) 4. Culture and Anarchy (1869); An essay in political and social criticism 5. Thyrsis (1867); It was written on the death of his friend Arthur Hugh Clough 6. On the Study of Celtic Literature (1867) 7. Essays in Criticism (Prose)
It is a short lyric poem published in 1867.
It was first published in collection of new poems.
The poem is about the shore of English ferry port Dover, Kent, facing Calais, France at the Strait of Dover, the narrowest part (21 miles) of the English Channel. At this place Arnold honeymooned.
Opening Lines: "The sea is calm tonight The tide is full, the moon lies fair Upon the straits; -on the French coast the light"
In Fahrenheit 451; author Ray Bradbury imposed his protagonist Guy Montag to read part of Dover Beach to his wife Mildred and her friends to show them what literature is about and why books should not be burned.
The speaker looks at the calm moonlit sea from Dover.
The sound of pebbles brings in the eternal note of sadness.
He recalls Sophocles hearing human misery on the Aegean.
The Sea of Faith, once full, now withdraws from the shore.
He asks his love to be true on a dark plain of battle.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Little Women

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1868 (Sort Year: 1868)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Louisa May Alcott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four March sisters grow up in New England while their father is away at war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Part one appeared in 1868. Part two, sometimes called Good Wives, appeared in 1869. The database span 1868-69 is correct. Her sister May illustrated the first edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jo March (The restless sister who writes, based on Alcott herself); Meg March (The eldest sister, who longs for pretty things and then marries); Beth March (The shy, musical sister who becomes gravely ill and dies); Amy March (The youngest sister, who loves art and later marries Laurie); Marmee (Mrs. March, the mother who guides the four sisters); Laurie (Theodore Laurence, the rich boy next door and Jo's close friend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy complain about a Christmas with no presents.
Marmee asks them to give their breakfast to a poor family.
Jo befriends Laurie, the boy next door, and the sisters face work and love.
Beth grows very ill.
Father returns from the American Civil War.
In the second part Meg marries, Beth dies, Amy marries Laurie, and Jo marries Professor Bhaer.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Earthly Paradise

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1868 (Sort Year: 1868)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Morris

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem in which wanderers and their hosts trade tales from Greece and the North.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The University of Maryland guide says he began the poem in the early 1860s. The first volumes appeared between 1868 and 1870. The Iowa Morris Archive says parts 1 and 2 came in 1868 and parts 3 and 4 in 1870. The database span 1868-70 matches publication, not a single year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
