fields.value: The idle singer (The poet's voice in the opening apology); The wanderers (Medieval travelers who never find a deathless land)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A band of medieval wanderers seeks a land where no one dies.
They fail, and they settle with a surviving group of Greeks.
For a year the two groups tell each other stories.
The tales come in pairs, month by month, in verse.
The poet calls himself an idle singer of an empty day.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Moonstone

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1868 (Sort Year: 1868)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Wilkie Collins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A stolen Indian diamond is traced through many narrators to a hidden thief.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: All the Year Round serialized it from 4 January to 8 August 1868. Tinsley published the three volume book in July 1868. Britannica dates The Moonstone 1868. The database year 1868 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rachel Verinder (The young woman who inherits the diamond and guards a painful secret); Franklin Blake (Rachel's cousin, who removes the diamond without knowing he has done it); Sergeant Cuff (The detective who studies the theft with patience and roses as his hobby); Gabriel Betteredge (The house steward and the first narrator); Godfrey Ablewhite (The respectable man who is the real thief)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A British officer seizes a sacred diamond in India and brings the curse home.
Rachel Verinder receives the Moonstone on her birthday, and it vanishes.
Sergeant Cuff investigates, and several witnesses tell the story in turn.
Franklin Blake learns that he took the diamond in an opium sleep.
Godfrey Ablewhite is exposed, and the diamond returns to India.

items.title: "The Ring and the Book" (1868) — Robert Browning

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Ring and the Book

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1868 (Sort Year: 1868)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Browning

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse novel in twelve books retells a Roman murder from ten conflicting points of view.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He found the source book, later called the Old Yellow Book, in Florence in 1860. The poem was issued in four volumes from November 1868 to February 1869. Database span 1868-1869 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Count Guido Franceschini (The husband accused of the murders); Pompilia (His young wife, who speaks near death); Giuseppe Caponsacchi (The priest who helped Pompilia flee); The Pope (The judge who decides Guido's fate)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
16. My Last Duchess (dramatic lyric poem)
Browning found an old Roman trial book in Florence and later built the poem on it.
Count Guido Franceschini is accused of murdering his wife Pompilia and her parents.
Each book gives one speaker's version of the crime.
Pompilia, the pope, the lawyers, and Rome itself all speak.
The pope judges Guido.
The poem asks how any human telling can reach truth.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Culture and Anarchy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1869 (Sort Year: 1869)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose book that sets culture against the disorder of modern England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The book appeared in 1869. Britannica, the University of Texas chronology, and the Academy of American Poets agree on that year. The database year 1869 is correct. This is prose, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Matthew Arnold (The critic who defines culture and names the three classes); Barbarians (His name for the aristocracy); Philistines (His name for the commercial middle class); The Populace (His name for the working class when it acts without standards)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is Arnold's philosophical essay arguing for restructuring England's social ideology.
Arnold contrasts culture as "the study of perfection" with anarchy "the prevalent mood of English's new democracy".
Culture is inspired by "Right Reason".
He divides human society into three main classes: i) Barbarians : represents aristocrats ii) Philistines : represents middle class iii) The Populace : represents working class.
The Barbarians are confident about their place and characterized by individualism, but they have lost touch with society.
Philistines are associated with business and are obvious to culture.
The third class Populace is raw and still not developed, and this class is mostly fully exploited by Barbarians and Philistines.
Culture and Anarchy is also famous for its popularization of the phrase "sweetness and light".
The term 'sweetness and light' was coined by Jonathan Swift in his Battle of The Books.
'Sweetness and light' stands for beauty and wisdom that culture adds to life.
Chapters of Culture and Anarchy i) Sweetness and Light ii) Doing as One Likes iii) Barbarians, Philistines, and Populace iv) Hebraism and Hellenism v) Porro Unum est Necessarium vi) Our Liberal Practitioners.
Culture and Anarchy was the result of restlessness in mid-19th century which arouse from rapid industrialization in the country.
Arnold defines culture as the study of perfection.
Culture seeks sweetness and light, not only money or force.
He splits society into Barbarians, Philistines, and the Populace.
Barbarians are the aristocracy.
Philistines are the commercial middle class.
Doing as one likes, without standards, leads toward anarchy.

items.title: "The Subjection of Women" (1869) — John Stuart Mill

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Subjection of Women

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1869 (Sort Year: 1869)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Stuart Mill

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay arguing that the legal rule of men over women is wrong.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Project Gutenberg and Wikipedia both date the book to 1869. Mill says the opinion itself was much older, and Harriet Taylor Mill shared the work.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Stuart Mill (The author of the argument for women's legal equality); Harriet Taylor Mill (The collaborator who shaped the essay)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mill argues that the legal rule of men over women is wrong.
He developed the case with Harriet Taylor Mill.
Custom, not nature, has kept women in the home.
No one can know women's powers until the law sets them free.
He defends education, work, and an equal vote for women.
Free women would also improve men and the whole society.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: God's Grandeur

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1918 (Sort Year: 1918)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Gerard Manley Hopkins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sonnet that says God's glory still charges the world, even after trade has smeared it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Autograph copies are dated 23 February 1877 and March 1877. Robert Bridges printed it in Poems in 1918.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A priest poet praising God in the natural world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker says the world is charged with God's grandeur.
That glory can flame out like light from shaken foil.
Generations have trodden the earth and smeared it with toil.
Even so, nature is never spent.
The Holy Ghost broods over the world like a bird with bright wings.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Jude the Obscure

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hardy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A stonemason fails in love and in his dream of university study.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial ran in Harper's New Monthly Magazine from December 1894 to November 1895. Early parts used the titles The Simpletons and Hearts Insurgent. The book came out in November 1895. Hardy finished the writing in March 1895. It is not the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jude Fawley (A poor mason who longs to study at Christminster); Sue Bridehead (His cousin, a teacher who fears a legal marriage); Arabella Donn (The barmaid Jude marries, then leaves, then meets again); Richard Phillotson (The schoolmaster who marries Sue); Little Father Time (Jude's son, who leaves the note about too many children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the last completed novel of Hardy.
The protagonist is Jude Fawley, a working-class young man as a stonemason (a village boy fired by academic aspirations educated himself in cloves) but fails to get admitted in the university.
He is trapped into marriage by Arabella Donn, and she bears him a baby boy and goes off to Australia.
Then he falls in love with his cousin Sue Bridehead, she marries a middle-aged schoolmaster Phillotson. Physical attraction soon drives her to Jude and they live together for several years.
Arabella comes back and Sue takes charge of her boy Little Father Time.
In the end, Jude meets wretches at the age of 30.
The novel was originally printed in Harper's New Monthly Magazine in 1894 and then in 1895 in Hardy volume.
Jude Fawley, a poor orphan, dreams of study at Christminster.
He teaches himself Greek and Latin while he works as a mason.
He marries Arabella Donn, then loves his cousin Sue Bridehead.
Sue leaves her husband and lives with Jude, but society shames them.
Their children die, Sue returns to her husband, and Jude dies alone.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Kim

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1901 (Sort Year: 1901)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An Irish orphan in Lahore joins the spy game on India's roads.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The book was published in 1901. Britannica, the Poetry Foundation, and the Nobel bibliography agree. It is not the year of Kim.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kimball O'Hara (An Irish orphan in Lahore, called Little Friend of all the World); Teshoo Lama (The Tibetan priest searching for a river of healing); Mahbub Ali (The horse trader who draws Kim into secret work); Colonel Creighton (The British officer who trains Kim for the Game); Hurree Babu (The Bengali agent who works beside Kim)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kimball O'Hara grows up on the streets of Lahore.
He meets a Tibetan lama who is searching for a sacred river.
Kim is drawn into the Great Game (the spy contest of Britain and Russia).
He travels India with the lama while he carries secret papers.
The lama finds his river, and Kim is torn between two lives.

items.title: "Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews" (1870) — Thomas Henry Huxley

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1870 (Sort Year: 1870)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Henry Huxley

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1870 collection of talks and reviews on science, schooling, and Darwin.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1870 is correct for the Macmillan book. The oldest piece inside it was an 1854 address. London, June 1870, is the date of the opening letter.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Henry Huxley (The lecturer and reviewer whose pieces are collected here); John Tyndall (The scientist friend addressed in the opening letter)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Huxley gathered talks and reviews that he had already given or printed.
A lay sermon of 1866 urges people to improve natural knowledge (science learned by observation).
A talk of 1868, called A Liberal Education, asks what real schooling is.
Another 1868 talk, On the Physical Basis of Life, is about protoplasm (the living stuff in cells).
The volume also reprints his review of Darwin's On the Origin of Species.
A letter to John Tyndall, dated June 1870, opens the book.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lothair

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1870 (Sort Year: 1870)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Benjamin Disraeli

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rich young lord is pulled between the Roman Catholic Church, the English Church, and Italy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1870 is correct. Disraeli wrote it after his short first term as prime minister in 1868. It is not part of Coningsby, Sybil, and Tancred.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lothair (A rich young nobleman courted by rival churches); Cardinal Grandison (A Roman Catholic prince of the church who seeks Lothair); Theodora (A woman who draws Lothair toward the Italian cause)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lothair is a young Englishman with a vast inheritance.
Catholic teachers and English churchmen both compete for him.
He is also drawn toward the Italian fight for unity.
The novel tests where faith, nation, and love should lead him.
It was a bestseller by a man who had already been prime minister.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1870 (Sort Year: 1870)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book of original poems, including early sonnets and ballads.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1870 is correct for the public book. Poems were recovered from Elizabeth Siddal's grave in 1869. Poetry Foundation notes a 1869 printing history, while the Rossetti Archive dates the public volume Poems to 1870. The book sold several editions in 1870. Buchanan's attack, The Fleshly School of Poetry, followed in 1871-1872.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sister Helen (The speaker of a ballad who melts a wax figure); Jenny (A young woman addressed in the dramatic poem Jenny)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After his wife's death he buried a manuscript in her grave.
In 1869 that manuscript was recovered and prepared for print.
The 1870 volume holds a revised Blessed Damozel and other poems.
It also holds an early group of House of Life sonnets.
Robert Buchanan attacked the book as fleshly, or too sensual.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems and Ballads

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1866 (Sort Year: 1866)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Algernon Charles Swinburne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1866 book of lyrics that made Swinburne famous and shocked many readers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year starts a literary period. It is not the book year. Britannica and the Poetry Foundation both date Poems and Ballads to 1866. A less sensual second series appeared in 1878. The dedication inside later printings is marked 1865, but the book year is 1866.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of Hymn to Proserpine (A pagan voice who says the pale Galilean has conquered); The speaker of The Garden of Proserpine (A tired voice who thanks the gods that no life lasts forever)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is a collection, not one story.
Hymn to Proserpine mourns the old gods after Christianity wins.
The Garden of Proserpine welcomes rest, sleep, and the end of desire.
Dolores and other poems treat pain and desire without apology.
Critics attacked the book, while many young readers praised it.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Tess of the d'Urbervilles

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1891 (Sort Year: 1891)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hardy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor country woman is ruined by two men and a harsh moral code.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial ran in The Graphic from 4 July to 26 December 1891. The book came out in December 1891. The exact start of composition is not fixed here. It is not the novel's year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tess Durbeyfield (A poor village woman whom Hardy calls a pure woman); Alec d'Urberville (The rich man who seduces Tess and later pursues her); Angel Clare (The clergyman's son who marries Tess and then abandons her); Joan Durbeyfield (Tess's mother, who pushes her toward the d'Urberville family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tess Durbeyfield learns that her family claims an old noble name.
Alec d'Urberville seduces her, and she bears a child who dies.
She works as a dairymaid and falls in love with Angel Clare.
On their wedding night Angel rejects her when she tells the truth.
Alec returns, Tess kills him, and the law hangs her.

items.title: "The Man from Snowy River" (1890) — Banjo Paterson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Man from Snowy River

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Banjo Paterson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young mountain rider catches a runaway colt after the famous horsemen fail.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That number is the period, not the poem. The Bulletin printed it in April 1890. The State Library dates that issue 26 April 1890. Angus and Robertson published the book in October 1895.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Man from Snowy River (The small unnamed rider who finishes the mountain chase); Clancy of the Overflow (A famous horseman who joins the muster)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A valuable colt escapes from a station yard and joins the wild horses.
Noted riders, including Clancy of the Overflow, gather for the chase.
The country turns too rough, and most of the men give up.
A small unnamed rider from Snowy River goes on alone.
His ride brings the colt back, and the bush retells the story.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Mayor of Casterbridge

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thomas Hardy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A man sells his wife, rises to mayor, and then loses everything.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Hardy was at work on the novel in 1884 and finished it in April 1885. The Graphic serial ran from 2 January to 15 May 1886. Smith, Elder published the two-volume book on 10 May 1886. It is not this novel's year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michael Henchard (A hay-trusser who becomes mayor and then loses all); Donald Farfrae (The young Scot who replaces Henchard in work and in love); Susan Henchard (The wife Henchard sells, who later returns); Elizabeth-Jane (The daughter who stays with Henchard and then learns the truth); Lucetta Templeman (Henchard's former love, who marries Farfrae)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sub-title: The Life and Death of a Man of Character (1886)
It is a tragic masterpiece of Hardy.
It is set in the fictional town of Casterbridge (Dorchester).
Michael Henchard, a hay trusser get drunk in fair and sells his wife, Susan, and child, Elizabeth Jane, for 5 guineas to Newson, a sailor.
Returning to his senses, he takes a solemn vow not to touch and drink for 21 years, and he rises to be the mayor of Casterbridge.
Donald Farfrae becomes his successful rival in business as well as love.
Donald Farfrae married Lucetta, the woman whom Henchard loves.
Henchard met his wife and child again after 18 years.
Newson returns and take Elizabeth back (his daughter).
Newson had married Susan and Elizabeth Jane is their daughter however another Elizabeth Jane, i.e. the daughter of Henchard and Susan had died.
Henchard learns this secret from a letter of Susan which he finds on her death bed that Susan marked to be opened only after Elizabeth Jane's marriage.
Thus Henchard goes cruel towards Jane.
Lucetta takes Elizabeth into her household to attract the attention of Henchard.
Elizabeth is married to Donald Farfrae.
Henchard dies.
'Abel Whittle' is a worker in Henchard's hay yard, a man who is constantly late for his job.
Skimmington-ride has been shown in this novel.
Lucetta Templeman is also a character of this novel.
Quote: "Happiness was but the occasional episode in a general drama of pain."
Drunk at a fair, Michael Henchard sells his wife and child.
Years later he is the rich mayor of Casterbridge.
Susan returns with Elizabeth-Jane, and Henchard hires Donald Farfrae.
Farfrae gains wealth and love while Henchard falls.
Henchard dies alone, and his will asks for no mourning.

items.title: "The Mystery of Edwin Drood" (1870) — Charles Dickens

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Mystery of Edwin Drood

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1870 (Sort Year: 1870)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Dickens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A choirmaster's obsession and a young man's disappearance end in an unsolved mystery.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Monthly parts began in April 1870. Only six numbers appeared. Dickens died on 9 June 1870.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Jasper (The choirmaster who desires Rosa and hates Edwin's claim); Edwin Drood (Jasper's nephew, who vanishes); Rosa Bud (Edwin's fiancee, frightened by Jasper); Neville Landless (A hot tempered young man suspected of the crime); Dick Datchery (A white haired stranger whose real identity is never told)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
John Jasper, a cathedral choirmaster, leads a double life and uses opium.
He desires Rosa Bud, who is engaged to his nephew Edwin Drood.
Neville Landless quarrels with Edwin, so suspicion can fall on Neville.
Edwin disappears after a storm, and the town hunts for a body.
Dickens died after six of twelve parts.
No ending was written.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Waltzing Matilda

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Banjo Paterson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A swagman steals a sheep, then jumps into a billabong when the police arrive.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He wrote the words at Dagworth station, near Winton, in 1895. Some accounts date word sheets to 1902. The famous Billy Tea song sheet is dated 1903. Do not treat one print year as settled.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The swagman (The wandering worker who steals the sheep and drowns); The squatter (The station boss who comes with the police); The policemen (Three officers who demand the stolen sheep)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A swagman (a walker who carries his bundle) camps by a billabong, a bush waterhole.
A jumbuck, which is a sheep, comes to drink, and he grabs it.
He hides the sheep in his tucker bag, his food bag.
The squatter (the station boss) and three policemen ask whose sheep it is.
The swagman jumps into the waterhole and drowns.
His ghost sings beside the coolibah, a kind of gum tree.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Little Men

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1871 (Sort Year: 1871)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Louisa May Alcott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jo and Professor Bhaer run a school for boys at Plumfield.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1871 as Little Men: Life at Plumfield with Jo's Boys. The database year 1871 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jo Bhaer (Jo March, now married, who runs Plumfield with her husband); Professor Bhaer (Jo's husband and the teacher at the school); Nat Blake (A shy new boy who arrives with a letter from Laurie); Tommy Bangs (A lively Plumfield boy who greets Nat on the stairs)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nat Blake, a poor boy sent by Laurie, arrives at the gate.
Jo, now Mrs. Bhaer, takes him into a noisy, kind school.
The boys learn lessons, play pranks, and tend gardens and pets.
Daisy and Demi, Meg's twins, live among the boys.
The school puts kindness and useful work beside book learning.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Middlemarch

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of life in a Midlands town in 1829 to 1832, told through several linked stories.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Eight paper bound parts from December 1871 to December 1872. A four volume book came out in parallel, with volume one dated 1871 and the other three dated 1872. Database 1871-72 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dorothea Brooke (The idealistic heroine); Edward Casaubon (Her older husband, a dry scholar); Tertius Lydgate (A young doctor with new ideas); Rosamond Vincy (Lydgate's vain wife); Will Ladislaw (Casaubon's young cousin); Nicholas Bulstrode (A banker with a hidden past)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Complete title: Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life.
It was first published in eight installments during 1871-1872.
The novel is set in the fictitious Midlands town of Middlemarch during 1829-1832.
It consists of several distinct stories and a large cast of characters.
Middlemarch is a work of realism that refers to many historical events: the 1832 Reform Act, the beginnings of the railways, the death of King George IV.
It originated in two unfinished pieces.
During the years 1869-1870, the novel "Middlemarch" which focused the character of Lydgate and the long story "Miss Brooke", which focused on the character of Dorothea.
The heroine of the novel Dorothea Brooke, an exclusively religious and pious girl who married a man Mr. Casaubon who can not satisfy her emotionally or mentally. Dorothea finally married Mr. Casaubon.
Virginia Woolf called "Middlemarch"- "The magnificent book which with all its imperfections is one of the few English books written for grown up people.
The character Will Ladislaw is the cousin of Mr. Casaubon.
About Dorothea: "With all the eagerness to know the truths of life, she retained very childlike ideas about marriage… the really delightful marriage must be that when your husband was a sort of a father and could even teach you Hebrew, if you wished it."
Celia Brooke is the sister of Dorothea Brooke.
Dorothea Brooke marries the old scholar Casaubon, hoping to do great work.
The young doctor Lydgate marries Rosamond Vincy, and money troubles harm them.
Casaubon dies.
His will keeps Dorothea from marrying his cousin Will Ladislaw.
The banker Bulstrode is shamed when his past is exposed.
Dorothea marries Will and lives a quiet but useful life.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Descent of Man

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1871 (Sort Year: 1871)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Darwin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A science book on human origins and on sexual selection.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1871 is correct. The Cambridge Darwin timeline dates publication to February and March 1871. The full title is The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex. The exact year he began this volume is not fixed here. Human evolution had been in his notes for decades.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Darwin applies evolution to the human body and the human mind.
He argues that people share ancestors with other animals.
He explains sexual selection (mate choice by beauty or strength).
The book also discusses races, morals, and the two sexes.
Cartoons then pictured Darwin himself as an ape.

items.title: "Through the Looking-Glass" (1871) — Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Through the Looking-Glass

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1871 (Sort Year: 1871)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Alice enters a mirror world that moves like a game of chess.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1871 matches Britannica. The book was published in December 1871. The title page is dated 1872, which is the year the Poetry Foundation cites. Both years are right if you say which one you mean. He was already planning the sequel in the year after 1865. The full title adds and What Alice Found There.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alice (The same girl, now walking through a mirror into a chess world); The Red Queen (A strict chess queen who hurries Alice from square to square); Humpty Dumpty (An egg shaped speaker who explains the hard words in Jabberwocky); The Walrus (A smooth talker in the poem who invites the oysters to a feast)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Its complete title is- Through the Looking Glass, and what Alice Found There.
It is a sequel to Alice's Adventure in Wonderland.
In this novel Alice again enters into a fantastical world by climbing through a mirror into the world that she can see beyond it.
It includes the verses Jabberwocky The Walrus and The Carpenter And the episode, Tweedledum and Tweedledee.
Characters: i)
This sequel sends Alice through a mirror into another unreal land.
The land is laid out like a chessboard, and Alice moves as a pawn.
She meets the Red Queen, Tweedledum, Tweedledee, and Humpty Dumpty.
The poems include Jabberwocky and The Walrus and the Carpenter.
The book is dated 1872, but it was published in December 1871.
Britannica rates it as good as the first Alice book, or better.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Erewhon

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1872 (Sort Year: 1872)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A traveler finds a strange land that mocks Victorian faith in progress.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1872 is correct. Britannica says it first appeared without his name. He claimed it after readers liked it. It is not posthumous. The posthumous flag in the database belongs to The Way of All Flesh.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (An unnamed traveler who enters Erewhon and reports its laws); The Erewhonians (People whose reversed rules mock Victorian England)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A traveler crosses mountains like those Butler saw in New Zealand.
He enters Erewhon, a name made by rearranging nowhere.
An anagram is a word made by reordering the letters of another word.
The country jails sick people and sends criminals to hospital.
It has banned machines, fearing they may replace human beings.
The Musical Banks stand for a church people do not truly use.
The pretty land turns out to be a satire, not a perfect world.

items.title: "The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals" (1872) — Charles Darwin

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1872 (Sort Year: 1872)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Charles Darwin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of how people and animals show feelings on the body.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1872 is correct. The Cambridge timeline dates publication to November 1872. Project Gutenberg also dates the book 1872. Darwin first meant to place this material inside Descent of Man. Notes on expression began after the Beagle voyage, so the research span is long. The exact start year is not fixed here.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Darwin collected notes on faces and gestures for many years.
The material grew too large for The Descent of Man.
He names serviceable habits as one cause of expression.
He compares crying, anger, and fear in humans and animals.
The book uses drawings and early photographs of faces.

items.title: "The Princess and the Goblin" (1872) — George MacDonald

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Princess and the Goblin

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1872 (Sort Year: 1872)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George MacDonald

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Princess Irene and the miner boy Curdie face goblins under a mountain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1872 is correct. Britannica and Project Gutenberg both date the book 1872. The database genre label says poetry, which is a mistake.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Princess Irene (The child who lives in the mountain castle); Curdie (A miner boy who is not afraid of the goblins); The old queen (The shining woman in the tower who cares for Irene)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Princess Irene, about eight, lives in a lonely castle on a mountain.
Goblins in the mines below plot harm against the kingdom.
Irene finds an old queen in a high room of the castle.
The old queen spins a thread that can guide Irene.
Curdie, a brave miner boy, helps her stop the goblin plan.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Autobiography

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1873 (Sort Year: 1873)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Stuart Mill

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Mill's life story, published in 1873 after his death, from a severe education to public reform.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He drafted the book in the 1850s and revised it later. The Liberty Fund text of the Collected Works dates publication to 17 October 1873, after his death in May 1873. Wikipedia also dates the book to 1873.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Stuart Mill (The narrator of his own education and mental crisis); James Mill (His father and severe teacher); Harriet Taylor Mill (The companion who changed his feelings and his feminism); Jeremy Bentham (The utilitarian thinker who shaped his youth)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mill tells the story of his strict education.
His father, James Mill, taught him Greek as a small child.
He met the ideas of Jeremy Bentham and became a reformer.
A mental crisis in his twenties shook his faith in logic alone.
Poetry and Harriet Taylor helped him recover feeling.
The book was published in October 1873, after he had died.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Literature and Dogma

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1873 (Sort Year: 1873)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Matthew Arnold

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A religious essay that reads the Bible as literature, not as hard dogma.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Smith, Elder published the book in London in 1873. A University of Texas chronology also dates it 1873. The database year 1873 is correct. God and the Bible (1875) is a later reply to critics, not this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Matthew Arnold (The critic reading the Bible as literature and as conduct)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Arnold asks readers to take the Bible as literature about conduct.
He ties religion to right conduct warmed by feeling.
Dogma (fixed church doctrine) has hidden the Bible's real power.
He speaks of a power, not ourselves, that makes for righteousness.
The book angered many believers and shaped later liberal reading.

items.title: "Studies in the History of the Renaissance" (1873) — Walter Pater

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Studies in the History of the Renaissance

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1873 (Sort Year: 1873)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walter Pater

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of essays on Renaissance art, ending with a bold claim for beauty and intense life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the Gutenberg chronology date the Macmillan book to 1873. The 1877 second edition is retitled The Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry, and its listed contents omit the Conclusion. The 1888 third edition restores the Conclusion and adds The School of Giorgione. The database year 1873 is the first edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Walter Pater (The critic whose voice guides each essay)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
2. Marius the Epicurean: His Sensations and Ideas.
It is a historical and philosophical novel written between 1881 and 1884 and published in 1885 set in 161-177 AD in the Rome of the Antonines.
It is one and only novel by Pater. 3. Appreciations: An Essay on Style. 4. Coleridge's Writing (1866).
Pater gathers essays on Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo, and others.
He treats the Renaissance as a rebirth of the senses and of art.
He asks the reader to know a work by its personal effect.
The Conclusion says success is to burn with a hard, gemlike flame.
He ends by praising the love of art for art's sake.

items.title: "The Idea of a University" (1873) — John Henry Newman

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Idea of a University

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1873 (Sort Year: 1873)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: John Henry Newman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Newman argues that a university should teach knowledge as a good in itself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Newman gave the first Dublin lectures in May 1852. Ten discourses were published in 1852. Later papers appeared in 1859 as lectures and essays on university subjects. The two parts were heavily edited and joined in 1873 under the title The Idea of a University. The database year 1873 is that collected book. The database calls it poetry. It is prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Henry Newman (The lecturer and rector speaking to Dublin Catholics about education)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Newman was asked to lead a new Catholic university in Dublin.
In 1852 he lectured on what a university is for.
He says a university teaches universal knowledge across many fields.
Liberal knowledge is its own end, even before it becomes useful.
Later essays on university subjects were gathered with the lectures.
The combined book of 1873 carries the title students now use.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Study of Sociology

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1873 (Sort Year: 1873)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herbert Spencer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A guide to sociology as a science, and to the biases that block fair study.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Stanford lists the book as 1873. Thomson says Spencer contributed it to the International Scientific Series in 1873. The database year 1873 is correct. It is not the multi volume Principles of Sociology, which runs from 1876 to 1896. The database genre Poetry is wrong, because this is prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Herbert Spencer (The author explaining how to study society without bias)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Spencer argues that society can be studied in a scientific way.
He lists obstacles, including patriotism, class feeling, and party bias.
He says religious and educational habits also twist what people notice.
He asks the student to prepare in biology and in the study of mind.
The book helped make sociology a subject people could teach.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Govinda Samanta

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1874 (Sort Year: 1874)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Lal Behari Day

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prize novel about the hard life of a Bengal peasant.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1874 is correct. Macmillan published two volumes that year under the title Govinda Samanta. The preface says the prize book lacked the last three chapters, which were added later. The 1878 edition is titled Bengal Peasant Life. The motto on the title page is a line by Thomas Gray.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Govinda Samanta (The peasant hero, a Bengal raiyat whose life the novel follows); Sambhu's mother (An old village woman who tells stories to the boy Govinda)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1871 Joy Kissen Mookerjea of Uttarpara offered a prize for a rural novel.
Day's English story won that prize in the middle of 1874.
It follows Govinda Samanta, a raiyat, from birth through village life.
Readers see his cottage, his school, marriage, and a Hindu widow's pain.
Landlords, a famine, and an indigo planter press the poor.
Macmillan of London printed the first edition in two volumes in 1874.
In 1878 the same book was reissued as Bengal Peasant Life.

items.title: "Recollections of a Tour Made in Scotland" (1874) — Dorothy Wordsworth

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Recollections of a Tour Made in Scotland

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1874 (Sort Year: 1874)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dorothy Wordsworth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose account of the 1803 walking tour through Scotland with William.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The tour took place in 1803. Principal Shairp published the full text at Edinburgh in 1874. The Library of Congress records that Edmonston and Douglas edition. The database year 1874 is the print year, not the year of the walk. Knight's preface confirms the 1874 edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dorothy Wordsworth (The narrator of the 1803 Scottish tour); William Wordsworth (Her brother and fellow traveller)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1803 Dorothy toured Scotland with her brother William.
She wrote the recollections as a prose narrative of that journey.
She describes roads, lochs, cottages, and people they meet.
Her descriptions show the same eye that shaped his poems.
The full book was first published in 1874, after her death.

items.title: "The City of Dreadful Night" (1874) — James Thomson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The City of Dreadful Night

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1874 (Sort Year: 1874)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: James Thomson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A bleak night poem by the later James Thomson, not by the poet of The Seasons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It does not fit this author. James Thomson of The Seasons died in 1748. The City of Dreadful Night is by James Thomson (Bysshe Vanolis), born in 1834. It ran in the National Reformer in 1874 and in a book in 1880.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A wanderer in a city and a desert of despair); The woman with the lamp (A figure in the desert whose lamp is her burning heart)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The database files this poem under the wrong James Thomson.
The real author is James Thomson, pen name Bysshe Vanolis, born in 1834.
A speaker moves through a city that feels like endless night.
A desert passage repeats despair, with no comfort from hope.
A woman appears whose lamp is her own burning heart.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Queen Mary

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1875 (Sort Year: 1875)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A historical verse play on Mary Tudor and her troubled reign.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Henry S. King published Queen Mary in 1875. Henry Irving produced it in 1876, and it was withdrawn after 23 performances. The database year 1875 is the book year, not the first night.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Queen Mary (Mary Tudor, the queen at the centre of the play); Philip (The Spanish prince whose marriage to Mary is a political storm)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mary Tudor comes to the throne and hopes to restore the old Catholic faith.
Her marriage and her harsh religious policy divide the people.
The play follows fear, rebellion, and the queen's lonely end.
Tennyson wrote it as a kind of sequel to Shakespeare's history plays.
Henry Irving staged a shortened version, and it soon closed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Arian Witness

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1875 (Sort Year: 1875)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Krishna Mohan Banerjee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A scholarly book arguing that old Aryan scriptures point toward the Bible and Christ.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Thacker, Spink and Company of Calcutta published the book in 1875. It is a work of religious scholarship. The database lists it under drama. Readers should class it as prose. Two supplementary essays followed in 1880. The database year 1875 is correct for this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Krishna Mohan Banerjee (The scholar-priest arguing the case in his own prose)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is a published book of religious scholarship.
Banerjee reads Vedic and related Aryan texts beside the Bible.
He says early Hindu sacrifice resembles the Christian idea of a saviour.
He identifies Jesus as the true Prajapati, the self-giving lord of creatures.
The aim is a positive link between Hinduism and Christianity.
Two shorter essays in 1880 continued the same argument.

items.title: "The Way We Live Now" (1875) — Anthony Trollope

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Way We Live Now

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1875 (Sort Year: 1875)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anthony Trollope

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A satire of London greed, as the financier Melmotte rises on a false railway and then falls.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1875 is the book year. Monthly parts ran from February 1874 to September 1875. Chapman and Hall issued the book in 1875. The Trollope Society dates the book June 1875.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Augustus Melmotte (A financier whose great railway company is a fraud); Lady Carbury (A widow who writes and schemes for social success); Sir Felix Carbury (Her selfish son, hunting Marie Melmotte's fortune); Marie Melmotte (Melmotte's daughter, wanted for her money); Roger Carbury (An honest country cousin who stands apart from the fraud)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Augustus Melmotte dazzles London with money, parties, and bold talk.
His scheme is a railway from Salt Lake City into Mexico.
Lady Carbury and her son Felix chase rank and Melmotte's money.
Melmotte enters high society and even reaches Parliament.
The fraud breaks, Melmotte falls, and empty fashion is exposed.

items.title: "The Wreck of the Deutschland" (1918) — Gerard Manley Hopkins

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Wreck of the Deutschland

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1918 (Sort Year: 1918)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Gerard Manley Hopkins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long religious ode on the 1875 wreck of the Deutschland and on God's hard mercy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He wrote it after the December 1875 wreck. The Month rejected it in 1876. First book publication is in Poems, 1918.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (Hopkins, addressing God and recalling the wreck); The tall nun (One of five Franciscan nuns who die in the wreck)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In December 1875 the German ship Deutschland is wrecked in a storm.
Five Franciscan nuns are among those who die.
The speaker asks how a loving God allows such terror.
He comes to call God both lightning and love.
The Jesuit magazine The Month rejected the poem in 1876.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Trial by Jury

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1875 (Sort Year: 1875)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: W. S. Gilbert

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short comic opera in which a bride sues the man who broke his promise.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the piece to 1875. MIT dates the opening to 25 March 1875 at the Royalty Theatre. Rochester records the Walter Smith libretto of 1875. The database year 1875 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Angelina (The plaintiff, the woman who brings the case); Edwin (The defendant, the man who broke the promise); The Learned Judge (A foolish judge who ends the trial by a comic marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Angelina sues Edwin for breach of promise (breaking a pledge to marry).
The judge, the jury, and the lawyers treat the case as a joke.
Everyone sings.
There is no separate spoken scene.
The judge settles the muddle by offering to marry Angelina himself.
The piece opened at the Royalty Theatre on 25 March 1875.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Trial by Jury

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1875 (Sort Year: 1875)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Sullivan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Angelina sues Edwin for a broken promise, and the Judge marries her himself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First performed at the Royalty Theatre, London, on 25 March 1875. The vocal score also appeared in 1875. The database year 1875 is correct. It is a comic opera, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Angelina (The plaintiff, who sues for a broken engagement); Edwin (The defendant, who has fallen in love with someone else); The Judge (A vain judge who ends the case by marrying Angelina)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edwin leaves Angelina, so she sues him for breach of promise.
The jury and the Judge side with her because she looks charming.
Edwin says love changes, and he even offers to marry two women.
Her lawyer blocks every clever way out.
The Judge is in a hurry, so he marries Angelina himself.

items.title: "A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields" (1876) — Toru Dutt

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1876 (Sort Year: 1876)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Toru Dutt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English translations of French poems, printed in Calcutta in 1876.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: University of Toronto dates the first edition to March 1876 at Bhowanipore. Gosse saw that book in August 1876. It was the only book printed in her lifetime. The database year 1876 is correct.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Toru and her sister Aru turned French poems into English verse.
The 1876 book has 165 poems and no preface.
Aru translated eight poems, and Toru translated the rest.
It was printed at Bhowanipore by the Saptahik Sambad Press.
Edmund Gosse found a copy in London in August 1876.
A second edition, prepared by her father, appeared in 1878.

items.title: "Daniel Deronda" (1876) — George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Daniel Deronda

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1876 (Sort Year: 1876)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her last novel, about a spoilt young woman and a man who discovers his Jewish roots.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Eight monthly parts from February to September 1876. Database 1876 is correct. It was her last completed novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gwendolen Harleth (A proud young woman in an unhappy marriage); Daniel Deronda (The title hero, a kind young man); Henleigh Grandcourt (Gwendolen's cruel husband); Mirah Lapidoth (A Jewish singer Daniel rescues); Mordecai (Mirah's brother, a dreamer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It was the most controversial novel of Eliot.
Because it dealt with the position of Jews in British and European society.
The novel begins with the meeting of Daniel Deronda and Gwendolen Harleth in the fictional town of Leubronn, Germany.
It is the last novel of Eliot.
Daniel finds himself attracted to the beautiful, stubborn, and selfish Gwendolen.
Gwendolen Harleth marries the cold Grandcourt for money and security.
Daniel Deronda saves her from despair and becomes her guide.
Daniel meets Mirah and Mordecai and learns he is Jewish.
He marries Mirah and leaves for the East to support a Jewish homeland.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Harold

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1877 (Sort Year: 1877)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse play on King Harold and the fall of Saxon England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Poetry Foundation dates Harold 1876 and says it found no producer in Tennyson's life. The Shepherd bibliography and Tennysoniana date the King title page 1877. The database year 1876 matches the Poetry Foundation year. This file uses 1877 for the title page.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harold (The English king who falls in the Norman conquest)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Harold holds England in the last days before the Norman invasion.
Claims, oaths, and rival armies close in on him.
The play ends with his defeat and the end of the old English kingship.
Tennyson tried to make this play tighter than Queen Mary.
No producer staged it while he was alive.

items.title: "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" (1876) — Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1876 (Sort Year: 1876)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A boy's mischief, a murder, a cave, and hidden gold in a river town.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the UC Berkeley guide both date the book to 1876. The American Publishing Company issued it in Hartford. The database year 1876 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tom Sawyer (A clever, restless boy who longs for adventure); Aunt Polly (Tom's guardian, who scolds him and loves him); Huckleberry Finn (Tom's ragged friend, freer than the town boys); Becky Thatcher (The girl Tom loves, and his partner in the cave); Injun Joe (The murderer whom Tom fears and finally escapes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel by Twain is about a young boy Tom Sawyer who is growing up along the Mississippi river. It is set in the fictional town of St. Petersburg.
Tom Sawyer lives with his aunt Polly and his half-brother 'Sid'. He falls in love with Becky Thatcher, a new girl in the town.
Tom Sawyer accompanies Huckleberry Finn to the graveyard at night where they witness a trio of grave robbers, Dr. Robinson, Muff Potter and Injun Joe, getting into fight.
In the fight Potter is knocked unconscious and Injun Joe stabs Doctor Robinson and puts the murder blame on Potter, who is arrested and charged with murder.
When Potter's trial begins, Tom testifies against Injun Joe and Potter is acquitted but Injun Joe flees from the window.
Tom fears for his life as Injun Joe can easily find him.
While Tom and Huck were on hunting, they saw Injun Joe and his companion planning to bury some stolen treasure.
Huck overhears their plan to attack the widow Douglas, Huck prevents the crime and becomes an anonymous hero.
Injun Joe is starved to death in a sealed cave. Tom and Huck takes the box of gold that was hidden by Injun Joe (carrying 12000$).
Douglas adopts Huck.
Tom Sawyer lives with Aunt Polly in a Mississippi town.
He tricks other boys into whitewashing a fence for him.
He and Huck see Injun Joe commit a murder in a graveyard.
The boys run off, are thought dead, and return to their own funeral.
Tom and Becky are lost in a cave, and Injun Joe dies there.
Tom and Huck find the robber's gold and become rich.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Black Beauty

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1877 (Sort Year: 1877)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Anna Sewell

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A horse tells his life, from a kind home through cruel work to final rest.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1877 is correct. Britannica Kids says she began the book in 1871 and finished it in 1877. The full title is Black Beauty: The Autobiography of a Horse. The database lists it under poetry, but it is a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Black Beauty (The horse who tells his own life from birth to old rest); Ginger (A mare whose bad treatment has made her angry and ill); Merrylegs (A lively pony who is Beauty's companion in a kind stable); John Manly (A good coachman who handles Beauty with care)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Black Beauty is born in a meadow and learns gentle manners from his mother.
Kind masters train him, and the coachman John Manly treats him well.
In London a tight bearing rein and hard cab work damage his body.
He shares the pain of Ginger, a mare made angry by cruelty.
Overwork breaks him, until a kind owner buys him and he recovers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Daisy Miller

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1878 (Sort Year: 1878)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry James

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short novel about a free spoken American girl whose manners shock Americans in Europe.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica Students dates Daisy Miller 1878. Project Gutenberg says its text is the first American book appearance of 1879. The database year 1878 matches the earlier date. Keep both years: 1878, then the American book in 1879.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daisy Miller (A young American woman whose frank manners are misread); Winterbourne (An American who has lived in Europe and watches Daisy); Giovanelli (The Italian gentleman who accompanies Daisy in Rome)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a novella by Henry James.
It portrays the courtship of the beautiful American girl Daisy Miller by Winterbourne a sophisticated compatriot of hers.
Daisy is 9 years old.
In Vevey, Winterbourne meets Daisy Miller, a lively American girl.
She walks and talks with men more freely than European custom allows.
In Rome she is seen with an Italian companion named Giovanelli.
American residents snub her and call her a flirt.
She visits the Colosseum at night, falls ill, and dies.
Winterbourne understands her innocence only when it is too late.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: H.M.S. Pinafore

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1878 (Sort Year: 1878)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: W. S. Gilbert

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic sea opera about love, rank, and a muddled baby swap.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates H.M.S. Pinafore to 1878. MIT dates the opening to 25 May 1878 at the Opera Comique in London. The database year 1878 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Joseph Porter (A proud First Lord of the Admiralty who knows little of the sea); Captain Corcoran (The captain of the ship H.M.S. Pinafore); Ralph Rackstraw (A common sailor who loves Josephine); Josephine (The captain's daughter); Little Buttercup (A seller on the ship who knows the baby secret)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sailor Ralph loves Josephine, the captain's daughter.
Sir Joseph Porter, a grand official, also wants to marry her.
Rank on the ship blocks the young lovers.
Little Buttercup reveals that two babies were swapped long ago.
The ranks reverse, and the right couples can marry.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: H.M.S. Pinafore

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1878 (Sort Year: 1878)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Sullivan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sailor loves his captain's daughter, until a baby mix-up changes their rank.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First performed at the Opera Comique on 25 May 1878. The full title is HMS Pinafore, or The Lass that Loved a Sailor. The Savoy Theatre opened in 1881, so this opening was not at the Savoy. The database year 1878 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph Rackstraw (A common sailor who loves the captain's daughter); Josephine (Captain Corcoran's daughter, promised to Sir Joseph); Captain Corcoran (Captain of the ship, proud of his rank); Sir Joseph Porter (First Lord of the Admiralty, who rose without going to sea); Little Buttercup (A seller on the ship who reveals the baby mix-up)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ralph, a sailor, loves Josephine, daughter of Captain Corcoran.
The Captain wants her to marry Sir Joseph Porter, First Lord of the Admiralty.
Sir Joseph says rank should not block love, which secretly helps Ralph.
Buttercup admits she mixed up Ralph and the Captain when they were babies.
The ranks are swapped, so Josephine may marry Ralph.

items.title: "Le Journal de Mademoiselle d’Arvers" (1879) — Toru Dutt

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Le Journal de Mademoiselle d’Arvers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1879 (Sort Year: 1879)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Toru Dutt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A French novel of love, murder, and madness, published in Paris after her death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: She died in 1877. Gosse says it was published in 1879 under Clarisse Bader's care. University of Toronto also dates the Paris edition to 1879. It is her own French prose, not a translation. The database year 1879 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mademoiselle d'Arvers (The young woman at the center of the diary story); The two brothers (Rivals whose love leads to murder and madness)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is told as a journal, which means a private diary.
Toru wrote the novel in French.
It is not a translation.
Two brothers fall in love with the same quiet young woman.
That rivalry leads to fratricide, the killing of a brother.
The tale also ends in madness, but it stays controlled.
Clarisse Bader saw it published in Paris in 1879.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Egoist

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1879 (Sort Year: 1879)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Meredith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about a vain gentleman who must be cured of self love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in three volumes by Kegan Paul in 1879. Britannica and the Victorian circulating library list agree on 1879. Database year 1879 is correct. It is a novel, not a poem and not the modernist magazine The Egoist.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Willoughby Patterne (The egoist whose pride the plot tests); Clara Middleton (The witty fiancée who tries to escape the match); Laetitia Dale (The woman who has watched his vanity for years)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sir Willoughby Patterne is a rich man in love with his own image.
One bride, Constantia, leaves him before the wedding.
He then engages Clara Middleton, who struggles to get free.
Laetitia Dale has loved him long and sees him clearly.
Comedy forces the egoist to face a humbler place among people.

items.title: "The Pirates of Penzance" (1879) — W. S. Gilbert

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Pirates of Penzance

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1879 (Sort Year: 1879)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: W. S. Gilbert

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic opera about a pirate apprentice trapped by a too strict sense of duty.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: MIT dates the New York premiere to 31 December 1879 and the London premiere to 3 April 1880. Rochester says a rough British performance came the night before New York, to guard the copyright. Britannica dates it 1879 in New York and 1880 in London. The database year 1879 is the first performance year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frederic (A young man apprenticed to pirates by a mistake); Mabel (The major-general's daughter whom Frederic loves); Major-General Stanley (A modern model officer who boasts of useless knowledge); The Pirate King (Leader of the soft-hearted pirates); Ruth (The pirate maid who first bound Frederic to the crew)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Frederic turns twenty-one and thinks his pirate apprenticeship is over.
He loves Mabel, a daughter of Major-General Stanley.
The Pirate King says Frederic was born on 29 February.
Duty then binds him, because that birthday comes only in leap years.
The pirates and the police end in a comic peace.

items.title: "Moths" (1880) — Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Moths

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1880 (Sort Year: 1880)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young woman is pushed into a cruel fashionable marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1880 matches the first publication. Britannica and a modern scholarly edition both give 1880.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Vere Herbert (The young heroine, hurt by her mother and her husband.); Vere's mother (A harsh mother who forces the marriage.); Vere's husband (A wasteful and cruel husband.); The opera singer (The man Vere loves.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is a novel of rich European society.
Vere Herbert is the young heroine.
Her harsh mother pushes her into a bad marriage.
Her husband is wasteful and cruel.
The book speaks of divorce, a legal end to marriage.
Vere is at last united with an opera singer she loves.
The title compares careless society to moths drawn into a flame.

items.title: "The Portrait of a Lady" (1881) — Henry James

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Portrait of a Lady

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1881 (Sort Year: 1881)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry James

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Isabel Archer, a free American woman, inherits money and marries the wrong man in Europe.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the book 1881. The database records a serial in 1880-1881 and the book in 1881. This file keeps 1881 as the book year. Later novels such as The Ambassadors belong to 1903, not to this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Isabel Archer (A young American who values her liberty and misjudges a husband); Gilbert Osmond (An American collector in Italy who marries Isabel for her money); Madame Merle (A polished friend who helps arrange the marriage); Ralph Touchett (Isabel's cousin, who wants her to live freely)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the story of a spirited young American woman Isabel Archer, who in "affronting her destiny" finds it overwhelming.
She inherits a large amount of money and subsequently becomes the victim of Machiavellian scheming by two American expatriates.
It is set in Europe and regarded the masterpiece of James.
The other characters are Ralph Touchett, Gilbert Osmand, Casper Goodwood and Lord Warburton.
Isabel Archer comes to England and refuses early offers of marriage.
A large inheritance gives her the freedom she thinks she wants.
Madame Merle helps steer her toward Gilbert Osmond in Italy.
Isabel marries Osmond and finds his fine taste hides a cold will.
She sees how she was used, and she must choose what to do next.

items.title: "A Pageant and Other Poems" (1881) — Christina Rossetti

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Pageant and Other Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1881 (Sort Year: 1881)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Christina Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1881 collection that includes a verse pageant and the sonnet sequence Monna Innominata.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: London Macmillan and the Boston Roberts Brothers edition are both dated 1881. Database year 1881 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of Monna Innominata (A woman poet who loves and also chooses faith over that love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title piece is a pageant of the months of the year.
Monna Innominata speaks as a woman whose love stays unnamed.
The sonnets weigh love against a higher religious claim.
Shorter lyrics continue her themes of time and renunciation.
Macmillan issued the London book in 1881.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ballads and Sonnets

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1881 (Sort Year: 1881)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Dante Gabriel Rossetti

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His 1881 book of ballads plus the finished House of Life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1881 is correct. The Rossetti Archive dates Ballads and Sonnets to 1881, and Poetry Foundation places the last surge of poems in 1880-1881. He died on 9 April 1882, so the book is not posthumous. It contains the finished House of Life. The King's Tragedy tells the murder of King James I.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of The King's Tragedy (The narrator of the historical ballad); King James (The Scottish king whose murder the ballad tells)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
New narrative poems were too many for a mere reprint.
He split the work into a new Poems and this second book.
The ballads include The White Ship and The King's Tragedy.
The King's Tragedy tells the murder of King James I.
The House of Life appears here in its long final form.

items.title: "Life and Times of Frederick Douglass" (1881) — Frederick Douglass

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1881 (Sort Year: 1881)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Frederick Douglass

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His last autobiography, from slavery through the Civil War and public office.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first book appeared at Hartford in 1881. An enlarged edition appeared in 1892.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frederick Douglass (The older autobiographer looking back over his whole public life); Abraham Lincoln (The president Douglass meets and later rejudges)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He again tells his early life, then continues far past 1855.
He describes work with John Brown's circle and meetings with Lincoln.
He records the Civil War, Black soldiers, and the failure of Reconstruction.
He includes later offices, including marshal and minister to Haiti.
The 1892 edition adds the Haiti years and his last public battles.
He calls the whole record several lives in one.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1881 (Sort Year: 1881)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Wilde's 1881 book of lyrics, paid for by himself, in the manner of Keats, Rossetti, and Swinburne.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published at Wilde's own expense in 1881. Database year 1881 is correct.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Wilde gathered early poems and published them at his own expense.
Many pieces echo the music and imagery of older poets he admired.
Impression du Matin paints the Thames at dawn like a picture.
Other poems take up classical myth, politics, and the theatre.
The book helped his public pose as an aesthete before the famous plays.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Treasure Island

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1883 (Sort Year: 1883)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Louis Stevenson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jim Hawkins finds a pirate map and sails with Long John Silver.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Young Folks serialized it from 1 October 1881 under the name Captain George North. The book appeared late in 1883. Britannica sometimes dates it 1881, the serial start. It is a novel, not a drama.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jim Hawkins (The boy who tells most of the story and outwits the mutineers); Long John Silver (The charming ship's cook who is also the pirate leader); Ben Gunn (A marooned sailor who has already moved Flint's gold); Doctor Livesey (The steady doctor who stands with the honest party)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jim Hawkins keeps a map from the dead pirate Billy Bones.
Squire Trelawney and Doctor Livesey fit out the Hispaniola.
The one-legged cook, Long John Silver, leads a secret mutiny.
On the island, Jim meets Ben Gunn and slips between both camps.
The loyal party survives, and Flint's treasure is found and shared.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Anandamath

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1882 (Sort Year: 1882)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Rebel monks shelter a landlord in a famine and sing praise to the motherland.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1882 is the right exam year. The 1911 Britannica and the Vande Mataram article both say 1882. One older arts note prints 1892, and that year should not replace 1882. The book is Bengali, so the database marks it as a translated text.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mahendra (A rich landlord separated from his family by the famine); Satyananda (Leader of the rebel children of the Mother); The sannyasis (Hindu ascetic fighters who chant Vande Mataram)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story uses the Bengal famine of 1770 and the Sannyasi rising.
Mahendra, a rich landlord, is driven from home and loses his family.
Sannyasis (Hindu ascetic rebels) give him shelter.
They worship the country as a mother goddess.
They chant Vande Mataram, meaning I revere the Mother.
A mysterious physician later tells their leader, Satyananda, to pause the fight.

items.title: "Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan" (1882) — Toru Dutt

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1882 (Sort Year: 1882)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Toru Dutt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English poems on Hindu legends and on her own garden, published after her death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: University of Toronto dates the first London edition to 1882, with Gosse's memoir. She died in 1877, so the book is posthumous. A Project Gutenberg copy prints a title page dated 1885. That is a later printing. The database year 1882 is right for first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Savitri (A wife in a Hindu legend who wins her husband back from death); Sita (The exiled wife in the Ramayana, a long Hindu heroic poem); Lakshman (Rama's brother, who guards Sita in the forest)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After returning to Calcutta, Toru studied Sanskrit.
She retold legends such as Savitri, Lakshman, and Sita.
She also wrote personal poems, including Our Casuarina Tree.
She died before every planned legend poem was written.
