Her father filled two gaps with Vishnu Purana stories from magazines.
Edmund Gosse introduced the London edition.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Silver King

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1882 (Sort Year: 1882)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Arthur Jones

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1882 melodrama, written with Henry Herman, about a gambler blamed for murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1882 is right. The first night was 16 November 1882 at the Princess's Theatre, London. Henry Herman was the writing partner.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Wilfred Denver (A ruined gambler who becomes the Silver King); Nellie Denver (His loyal wife); Geoffrey Ware (The man whose murder Denver is blamed for); Captain Herbert Skinner (A criminal who helps trap Denver)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Wilfred Denver, a gambler, is tied to the murder of Geoffrey Ware.
Ware had once admired Denver's wife, Nellie.
Denver flees, reads a report of his own death, and escapes abroad.
He grows rich in the silver mines of Nevada.
He returns in disguise as the Silver King to save his family.
The real criminals are exposed, and Denver's name is cleared.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Folk-Tales of Bengal

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1883 (Sort Year: 1883)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Lal Behari Day

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English retellings of old Bengali tales heard from village speakers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1883 is correct. Macmillan published the first edition in 1883. The Project Gutenberg text is the 1912 reprint with pictures by Warwick Goble. Its title page calls Day the author of Bengal Peasant Life.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sambhu's mother (The old village woman whose tales Day heard as a boy); The storytellers (A Christian woman, Brahmans, a barber, and a servant who spoke the tales)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Captain R. C. Temple asked Day to collect unwritten Bengali stories.
As a boy, Day had heard hundreds of tales from Sambhu's mother.
He later heard more from a Christian woman, two Brahmans, a barber, and a servant.
None of them knew English, so he translated their Bengali at home.
He rejected tales that did not match the old stories he remembered.
An orthodox teller ends each story with a short verse about a thorn.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hester

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1883 (Sort Year: 1883)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Margaret Oliphant

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two strong women clash around a family bank in the town of Redborough.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published by Macmillan in three volumes in 1883. The 1911 Britannica lists Hester in 1883. The database year 1883 is correct. It is not one of the Carlingford books.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hester Vernon (A proud young cousin who wants useful work and resents charity); Catherine Vernon (The older woman who saved the bank and now controls it); Edward Vernon (A young banker in Catherine's house who draws near to Hester)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Catherine Vernon saves Vernon's bank after her cousin John flees with its money.
Years later, John's widow returns with their daughter Hester, who is proud and poor.
Catherine houses the poor relations and brings young men into the bank.
Hester and Catherine distrust each other, though both are able and proud.
A new crisis at the bank forces the two women toward a harder understanding.

items.title: "The Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays" (1883) — Elizabeth Lynn Linton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1883 (Sort Year: 1883)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Lynn Linton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A collection of sharp essays attacking the manners of the modern girl.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The title essay first appeared in the Saturday Review in March 1868. Richard Bentley published this two-volume collection in 1883. The database year 1883 is the book, not the first printing of the essay. Gutenberg shows the 1883 Bentley title page and her signed preface.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: E. Lynn Linton (The essayist, speaking in a severe public voice); The Girl of the Period (Her name for the fashionable modern young woman she attacks)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title essay first appeared in the Saturday Review in 1868.
It contrasts an older modest English girl with a new fashionable one.
Linton attacks dyed hair, paint, slang, and the hunger for luxury.
She argues that this girl copies scandalous women and displeases men.
In 1883 Bentley reprinted the essays in two volumes under her name.

items.title: "The Story of an African Farm" (1883) — Olive Schreiner

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Story of an African Farm

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1883 (Sort Year: 1883)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Olive Schreiner

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: On a lonely South African farm, Lyndall fights for a free life and dies after childbirth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1883 is correct. She wrote the novel while working as a governess, before she left for England in 1881. It was published in 1883 under the pen name Ralph Iron.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lyndall (The young woman who rejects conventional marriage and dies in childbirth); Waldo (Lyndall's suitor, a seeker of spiritual and intellectual freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel draws on Schreiner's childhood on the isolated South African veld (open grassland).
Lyndall grows up on an ostrich farm under strict Boer (Dutch settler) rules.
She wants the freedom to choose her own life and refuses an ordinary marriage.
She decides to have a child, and she dies in childbirth.
Waldo, who loves her, longs for spiritual and intellectual freedom.
The book was praised and attacked for feminist and anti-Christian views.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Towards Democracy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1883 (Sort Year: 1883)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edward Carpenter

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long free verse poem calling for a freer and more equal human life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database phrase 1883; expanded editions is right. Part I came in 1883. Parts I and II came in 1885. Parts I to III came in 1892. Part IV came in 1902. The complete edition came in 1905. A library edition followed in 1908.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A prophetic voice that calls readers toward a freer common life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Part I appeared in 1883 from John Heywood in Manchester.
The speaker looks toward a democracy of the spirit, not only of votes.
Long unrhymed lines follow the model of Walt Whitman.
The Bhagavad Gita also feeds the poem's religious hope.
Later parts grew the book until a complete edition in 1905.

items.title: "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn" (1884) — Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1884 (Sort Year: 1884)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Huck and Jim raft the Mississippi, and Huck rejects the slave law.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatto and Windus published it in London in December 1884. Webster published it in New York in February 1885. The title on those editions has no The.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Huckleberry Finn (The narrator, a boy who trusts friendship more than the law); Jim (Miss Watson's enslaved man, seeking freedom down the river); Tom Sawyer (Huck's friend, who complicates Jim's escape); The duke and the king (Two cheats who sell Jim and fool the river towns)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel was first published in United Kingdom in Dec 1884 and in United States in Feb 1885.
It is the sequel to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.
The novel is told in first person, by Huckleberry 'Huck' Finn, a friend of Tom Sawyer and narrator of two other novels of Mark Twain, i.e. Tom Sawyer Abroad and Tom Sawyer, Detective.
The novel has a colorful description of people and places along the Mississippi River.
The novel is set in Southern Antibellum Society.
It became controversial because of its coarse language and use of racial stereotypes.
It consists of 43 chapters.
Huck fakes his death to escape his drunken father.
He joins Jim, who is running from slavery.
A raft carries them past feuding families and cheating actors.
Huck decides he will help Jim even if the town calls it a sin.
Tom Sawyer delays the escape with foolish storybook plans.
Jim is freed, and Huck plans to light out for the territory.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Becket

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1884 (Sort Year: 1884)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Alfred, Lord Tennyson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse tragedy on Thomas Becket's clash with the king and his death in the cathedral.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Macmillan published Becket in 1884. The Poetry Foundation lists it with the late plays and says only The Cup had real stage success among them. The database year 1884 is the publication year. A first night is not given here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Becket (The archbishop who chooses the Church over the king's will); King Henry (The king and former friend whose anger leads to the murder)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Becket, once the king's close servant, becomes Archbishop of Canterbury.
He defends the Church against the king's demands.
Friendship turns into a public quarrel.
Knights kill Becket in the cathedral.
The play leaves the stage world of Shakespeare further behind than Queen Mary did.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Diana of the Crossways

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Meredith

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about a brilliant woman writer trapped in a bad marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in 1885. Britannica, Wikipedia, and the Victorian circulating library list agree. Database year 1885 is correct. Database genre Poetry is wrong. The subtitle on the title page is A Novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Diana Warwick (The heroine, a novelist in an unhappy marriage); Caroline Norton (The real woman whose troubles suggested parts of Diana's story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Diana Warwick is a witty woman and a novelist.
Her marriage is unhappy, and scandal follows her name.
Readers linked her story to the real Caroline Norton.
The book watches how a woman reads the inner life and the public one.
It was his first great popular success, including in America.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: King Solomon’s Mines

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. Rider Haggard

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Allan Quatermain leads two Englishmen to King Solomon's diamond mines in Africa.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1885 is correct. Britannica and Project Gutenberg both date the book 1885.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Allan Quatermain (The hunter who tells the story); Sir Henry Curtis (The Englishman who is searching for his brother); Captain Good (A companion on the journey); Umbopa (An African companion on the journey); Gagool (The old woman he calls a fiend (an evil spirit))

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Allan Quatermain, a hunter, agrees to guide Sir Henry Curtis.
They seek Curtis's missing brother and the old diamond mines.
The party crosses a deadly desert and enters a hidden kingdom.
They survive a tribal war and meet the old woman Gagool.
They escape with some diamonds and find the brother alive.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Marius the Epicurean

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walter Pater

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A philosophical romance about a young Roman who tests ways of living under Marcus Aurelius.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates Marius the Epicurean to 1885. The Gutenberg chronology says Macmillan published two volumes in 1885, after work from 1880 to 1885. Leeds describes an 1885 copy as the second edition. The database year 1885 is correct for first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marius (A young Roman who searches for a worthy way to live); Marcus Aurelius (The emperor whose Stoic court Marius enters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Marius grows up in the Roman countryside and loses his childhood faith.
He tests Epicureanism (a search for calm, refined pleasure) and other schools.
He serves the Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius.
With a friend he reads the tale of Cupid and Psyche in Apuleius.
He moves toward Christian ritual, but the book stays a quiet inner story.

items.title: "The Autobiography of Christopher Kirkland" (1885) — Elizabeth Lynn Linton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Autobiography of Christopher Kirkland

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elizabeth Lynn Linton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel that tells her own life story through a male narrator.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Bentley published three volumes in 1885. The 1911 Britannica calls it a veiled autobiography. Victorian Web explains the sex reversal. The database genre label Poetry is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Christopher Kirkland (The male narrator, a mask for Eliza Lynn Linton herself); Esther Lambert (The wife in the novel, a mask for Linton's husband W. J. Linton)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Christopher Kirkland narrates a life that closely follows Linton's own.
She changes her sex to male, and she changes her husband's sex to female.
The story moves from a religious childhood toward freethought (belief without church dogma).
It shows her work as a writer and the strain of her marriage.
Readers should treat it as a novel, not as a straight autobiography.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Mikado

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: W. S. Gilbert

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic opera, set in a made-up Japanese town, about love, law, and a hidden prince.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates The Mikado to 1885. MIT dates the opening to 14 March 1885 at the Savoy Theatre in London. The database year 1885 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nanki-Poo (The Mikado's son, disguised as a minstrel); Yum-Yum (The young woman loved by Nanki-Poo and claimed by Ko-Ko); Ko-Ko (The Lord High Executioner of Titipu); Katisha (An older woman who claims Nanki-Poo as her own); The Mikado (The ruler who arrives in search of his son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nanki-Poo, the Mikado's son, hides as a wandering singer.
He loves Yum-Yum, who is promised to Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner.
A foolish law says that flirting is punished by death.
Ko-Ko must produce an execution or lose his own head.
The truth comes out, and Nanki-Poo wins Yum-Yum.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Mikado

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1885 (Sort Year: 1885)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Sullivan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In the town of Titipu, a fake execution hides the Mikado's runaway son.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First performed at the Savoy Theatre on 14 March 1885. The full title is The Mikado, or The Town of Titipu. The vocal score also dates from 1885. The database year 1885 is correct. It is a comic opera, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nanki-Poo (The Mikado's son, disguised as a wandering musician); Yum-Yum (Ko-Ko's ward, whom Nanki-Poo loves and marries); Ko-Ko (Lord High Executioner, a former tailor condemned for flirting); Katisha (An older lady of the court who claims Nanki-Poo); Pooh-Bah (A proud official who holds many paid posts at once); The Mikado (The ruler who comes to Titipu looking for his son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nanki-Poo flees his father, the Mikado, to escape marriage with Katisha.
Disguised as a musician, he loves Yum-Yum, ward of Ko-Ko.
Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner, must behead someone or lose his post.
He files a false report that Nanki-Poo has been executed.
To escape blame, Ko-Ko marries Katisha, and Nanki-Poo is revealed as the son.

items.title: "A Romance of Two Worlds" (1886) — Marie Corelli

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Romance of Two Worlds

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Marie Corelli

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A first novel about illness, visions, and an electric creed of God.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1886 is correct. Britannica calls this her first book and says it deals with psychic experience. The Electric Creed chapter describes God as electric radiance.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A young woman musician who tells what happened to her); Raffaello Cellini (An Italian painter at her hotel in Cannes); Heliobas (A Chaldean teacher who explains the Electric Creed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A young woman musician in London falls ill with sleepless gloom.
Friends take her to Cannes, where she meets the painter Raffaello Cellini.
Cellini leads her to Heliobas, who says he is a Chaldean.
A Chaldean here means a descendant of the wise men of the East.
Heliobas gives her a strange drink and guides her through visions.
His Electric Creed calls God a shape of pure electric radiance.
This first book appeared in 1886 and treats psychic experience.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Departmental Ditties

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Light comic poems about British officials and station life in India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Departmental Ditties appeared in 1886, while Kipling worked on the Civil and Military Gazette in Lahore. Britannica and the Nobel bibliography date the book 1886. The database year 1886 is correct.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems joke about clerks, love affairs, and government files.
They grew from verses he wrote for Anglo-Indian newspapers.
Names, promotions, and Simla gossip fill the scenes.
The tone is witty, but the daily work of empire is the setting.
The book made his verse known before he left India.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Jo’s Boys

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Louisa May Alcott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten years later, the Plumfield boys return as young adults.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1886. The full title is Jo's Boys, and How They Turned Out. The database year 1886 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jo Bhaer (Now a famous author and the friend of the grown students); Nan (A determined young woman who studies medicine); Dan (A restless former Plumfield boy who keeps wandering); Tom Bangs (The faithful young man who studies medicine to stay near Nan)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Plumfield has become a college, helped by Mr. Laurence's gift.
Jo is a famous writer and a guide to the young men and women.
Nan studies medicine.
Dan still wanders, and Tom still follows Nan.
The original boys come back from many jobs and many countries.
The book closes the March family story as the children choose their work.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Kidnapped

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Louis Stevenson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: David Balfour is kidnapped, shipwrecked, and hunted across the Highlands with Alan Breck.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It ran in Young Folks in 1886 and was published as a book the same year. The database year 1886 is correct. Poetry Foundation places the Highland wandering in 1751.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David Balfour (The Lowland youth who tells the story and claims his inheritance); Alan Breck Stewart (A proud Jacobite fugitive who becomes David's companion); Ebenezer Balfour (David's miser uncle, who tries to keep the estate by kidnapping him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Young David Balfour goes to his uncle Ebenezer after his father dies.
Ebenezer has him kidnapped onto a ship so he cannot claim the estate.
The ship wrecks, and David meets the Jacobite Alan Breck Stewart.
They flee across the Highlands after the Appin murder.
David returns to claim his right, and the uncle's plot is exposed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: She

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. Rider Haggard

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two men find Ayesha, the queen of Kor who does not die.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year is 1886. Project Gutenberg prints First Published 1886. Britannica dates the book 1887. Keep 1886 as the earlier mark and 1887 as the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ayesha (The beautiful queen of Kor, called She who must be obeyed); Leo Vincey (The young man she takes for her lost lover's descendant); Holly (The older man who travels with Leo); Job (The man Holly sends to fetch his box)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Holly and Leo Vincey travel to find a white queen in Africa.
Ayesha is called She who must be obeyed.
She has waited two thousand years for her lover to return.
She killed that lover long ago, and she sees him again in Leo.
She enters a magic fire so she can live forever, and then she falls into dust.

items.title: "Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde" (1886) — Robert Louis Stevenson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Louis Stevenson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Doctor Jekyll uses a drug to release Edward Hyde, the evil side of himself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Stevenson dreamed the change, drafted the tale, and rewrote it as an allegory. It was published in 1886. The database year is correct. Poetry Foundation says the first draft was burned after Fanny objected.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dr Henry Jekyll (A respected scientist who splits off his evil desires as Hyde); Mr Edward Hyde (Jekyll's violent second self, smaller, cruel, and free of shame); Mr Gabriel Utterson (Jekyll's lawyer, who pieces the mystery together); Dr Hastie Lanyon (A rational friend who sees the transformation and is shattered)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mr Utterson, a lawyer, is troubled by a brutal man named Edward Hyde.
Hyde is tied to the respectable Doctor Henry Jekyll by a strange will.
Jekyll has a drug that lets him become Hyde and then return.
Hyde grows stronger, and the drug stops obeying Jekyll.
Jekyll's last statement explains the split, and Hyde dies in the locked room.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Bostonians

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1886 (Sort Year: 1886)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry James

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A struggle in Boston between a reformer and a Southern conservative for a young woman speaker.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A Project Gutenberg text of the Macmillan edition says it was first published in 1886. Britannica Students also dates The Bostonians 1886. The database year 1886 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Olive Chancellor (A Boston reformer who loves the cause of women and loves Verena); Verena Tarrant (A young speaker whom Olive and Basil both try to claim); Basil Ransom (Olive's cousin from Mississippi, who opposes the reformers)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Basil Ransom, a conservative from Mississippi, visits his cousin in Boston.
Olive Chancellor wants to devote her life to the cause of women.
Both of them are drawn to Verena Tarrant, a gifted young speaker.
Olive trains Verena for public reform and fears losing her.
Ransom wants Verena to leave the platform for a private life.

items.title: "A Study in Scarlet" (1887) — Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Study in Scarlet

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1887 (Sort Year: 1887)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first Holmes novel, in which Watson meets Holmes and they solve a London revenge murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1887 is the first publication, in Beeton's Christmas Annual. Ward, Lock issued a separate book in 1888. These sources do not fix the writing year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sherlock Holmes (A consulting detective who reads tiny clues); Dr John Watson (An army doctor who shares the rooms and tells the story); Jefferson Hope (The avenger who crosses the ocean to punish the killers); Inspector Lestrade (A Scotland Yard officer who works beside Holmes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dr Watson, wounded in Afghanistan, needs a cheap place to live.
He meets Sherlock Holmes, and they share rooms at 221B Baker Street.
Holmes investigates the murder of Enoch Drebber in London.
The killer is Jefferson Hope, avenging a forced marriage in Utah.
A long American flashback explains the Mormon settlement and Lucy Ferrier.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Allan Quatermain

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1887 (Sort Year: 1887)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. Rider Haggard

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sequel in which Quatermain enters Zu Vendis and dies after a civil war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1887 is correct. Britannica and Project Gutenberg both date Allan Quatermain 1887.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Allan Quatermain (The ageing hunter who narrates this last journey); Umslopogaas (The axe warrior who fights beside him); Sir Henry Curtis (Quatermain's English friend from the earlier quest); The sister queens (The rival rulers of Zu Vendis)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Quatermain has just buried his only son, and his heart is broken.
He sets out again with old companions, including Umslopogaas.
They find the hidden kingdom of Zu Vendis.
Two sister queens rule there, and their rivalry becomes war.
Quatermain's own story ends in that war.

items.title: "Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life" (1887) — Krupabai Satthianadhan

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1887 (Sort Year: 1887)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Krupabai Satthianadhan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young Indian Christian woman fights for schooling and a life of her own.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Serialised in the Madras Christian College Magazine in 1887-1888. The database book year 1895 is the surviving Madras edition. That 1895 printing is marked a second edition. One university study says a lost first book appeared in 1892. This file dates first publication from the 1887 serial.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Saguna (The narrator, a young Indian Christian woman based on the author); Bhasker (Her elder brother, who encourages her reading and then dies young); Saguna's mother (A practical woman who wants her daughter trained for housework)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Saguna grows up in a convert family that still argues about a girl's place.
Her mother wants her at the cooking fire, but her brother Bhasker shares his books.
She studies hard and enters Madras Medical College to help women.
Illness and overwork force her to leave the medical course.
The story follows her own early life and ends in a marriage of equals.

items.title: "Plain Tales from the Hills" (1888) — Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Plain Tales from the Hills

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1888 (Sort Year: 1888)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short stories of British and Indian lives in the hills and the plains.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The book appeared in 1888. Many stories had already run in the Civil and Military Gazette. Britannica and the Nobel bibliography date the book 1888. The database year 1888 is correct. The Man Who Would Be King is not in this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lispeth (A hill woman in the opening story, hurt by an Englishman); Trejago (The Englishman in Beyond the Pale who loves an Indian widow)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Most of the stories first appeared in the Civil and Military Gazette.
They show love, shame, and sudden death in Simla and the plains.
Soldiers, civilians, and Indian characters share the book.
The tales are brief, sharp, and often end with a twist.
The newspaper stories were collected as a book in 1888.

items.title: "The Happy Prince and Other Tales" (1888) — Oscar Wilde

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Happy Prince and Other Tales

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1888 (Sort Year: 1888)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of fairy tales in which beauty and kindness give themselves away for the poor.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1888. Database year 1888 is correct. It is fiction, not a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Happy Prince (A statue who gives away his gold and jewels); The Swallow (A bird who serves the prince until winter kills him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A gilded statue, the Happy Prince, sees the suffering of his city.
He asks a swallow to strip his gold and jewels and carry them to the poor.
The swallow stays past the time to migrate and dies in the cold.
The prince's lead heart cracks.
The town pulls the statue down.
An angel carries the heart and the dead bird to God as the most precious things.

items.title: "A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court" (1889) — Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1889 (Sort Year: 1889)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A modern factory boss wakes in King Arthur's Britain and tries to remake it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Project Gutenberg and the UC Berkeley guide both date the novel to 1889. Charles Webster issued it in New York. The database year 1889 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hank Morgan (A practical Yankee who tries to modernize Arthur's Britain); King Arthur (The legendary king, whom Hank both serves and challenges); Merlin (The court magician and Hank's enemy); Clarence (A young courtier who helps Hank's reforms)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hank Morgan, a Connecticut boss, is struck on the head.
He wakes in the England of King Arthur.
He uses modern knowledge and is taken for a great magician.
He tries to bring schools, machines, and rule by the people.
Merlin, the nobles, and the Church fight his new order.
His experiment ends in war and ruin, not in a happy progress.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Appreciations

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1889 (Sort Year: 1889)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Walter Pater

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A set of critical essays on English writers, opened by an essay on style.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates Appreciations to 1889. The Gutenberg chronology says Macmillan published it in 1889. Style had appeared in the Fortnightly Review in December 1888. The 1889 contents include Aesthetic Poetry. A later edition adds Feuillet's La Morte. The database year 1889 is the first book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Walter Pater (The critic speaking in each essay)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens with Style, first printed in a review in 1888.
Pater says good style cuts away surplusage (extra words that add nothing).
He then writes on Wordsworth, Coleridge, Lamb, and Browne.
Essays on Shakespeare and on Rossetti follow.
A postscript looks back at romance and classicism.

items.title: "The Master of Ballantrae" (1889) — Robert Louis Stevenson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Master of Ballantrae

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1889 (Sort Year: 1889)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Robert Louis Stevenson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two brothers split by the Jacobite rising pursue each other across years and seas.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the novel 1889. The database year 1889 matches that publication. The story opens on the Jacobite rising of 1745.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: James Durie (The Master of Ballantrae, the glamorous older brother); Henry Durie (The younger brother who keeps the estate and is eaten by resentment); Ephraim Mackellar (The steward who narrates and sides with Henry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1745 the Durie family sends one son to the Jacobites and keeps one at home.
James, the elder, called the Master, is the charming and cruel brother.
Henry, the younger, stays, inherits, and is blamed for playing safe.
The Master returns from supposed death and drains Henry's life and name.
Their hatred follows them abroad and ends with both brothers destroyed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Nether World

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1889 (Sort Year: 1889)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gissing

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel of Clerkenwell poverty, where a plan to use money for the poor collapses.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1889 is correct. Smith, Elder published it in three volumes in 1889.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jane Snowdon (A poor young woman her grandfather hopes to make a helper of the poor); Michael Snowdon (Jane's grandfather, who brings money back from abroad); Sidney Kirkwood (A jeweller caught between love and poverty); Clara Hewett (An ambitious young woman whose hopes are ruined)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set among poor workers in Clerkenwell, London.
Michael Snowdon returns with money and finds his granddaughter Jane.
He wants Jane to spend that money on helping the poor.
Sidney Kirkwood, a workman, is tied to both Jane and Clara Hewett.
Clara is attacked and disfigured, and the hopeful plan fails.
Jane and Sidney remain inside the same hard world.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Dreams

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Olive Schreiner

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eleven short allegories about truth, love, and a woman's hard road to freedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1890 is correct for the book. Some pieces were begun years earlier. Her note, dated November 1890 at Matjesfontein, says each dream is placed by the date of its first part. One printed date cannot cover every piece.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Hunter (A seeker who leaves comfortable beliefs to search for Truth); Wisdom (An old man, also called Knowledge, who guides the hunter); Truth (The white bird the hunter longs to see and cannot yet hold)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book holds eleven dreams, printed in the order she wrote them.
A note at the front is dated November 1890, at Matjesfontein in the Cape.
In The Hunter, a man gives up easy beliefs and climbs after Truth.
Wisdom tells him that Truth may be caught only by Truth itself.
Three Dreams in a Desert shows a woman struggling toward freedom.
Other dreams, such as The Lost Joy, turn love and pain into pictures.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: News from Nowhere

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Morris

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A utopian romance in which a socialist dreams of a peaceful England in 2090.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It first ran in the paper Commonweal in 1890. Britannica says a book followed later that same year. The Iowa Morris Archive says the serial ran from January to October 1890. It dates the trade book to 1891 and the Kelmscott Press book to 1892. The University of Maryland guide dates the book to 1891. The database year 1890 is the serial.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Guest (The dreamer, a thin disguise for Morris himself)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
William Guest leaves a socialist meeting and falls asleep.
He wakes beside the Thames in a future England.
Money, ugly factories, and harsh government have gone.
People work for pleasure, and art is part of daily life.
He learns that a hard revolution made this rest possible.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Emily Dickinson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first book of her poems, edited by friends and published four years after her death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1890 and the posthumous flag are correct. She died in 1886. Roberts Brothers of Boston published this first book in 1890.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems and kept most private.
She sent some poems inside letters to friends.
She copied poems into 40 fascicles (small hand-sewn booklets).
Only 10 poems were printed while she was alive.
After her death, her sister Lavinia found the manuscripts.
Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Higginson edited the 1890 book.
Those editors changed capitals, punctuation, and some wording.

items.title: "The Picture of Dorian Gray" (1890) — Oscar Wilde

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Picture of Dorian Gray

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young man stays beautiful while his portrait grows old and wicked in his place.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The shorter text appeared in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in July 1890. The expanded book came out in 1891.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dorian Gray (A beautiful young man whose portrait bears his sins); Lord Henry Wotton (The witty lord who corrupts Dorian with ideas); Basil Hallward (The painter of the portrait); Sibyl Vane (An actress whom Dorian loves and then rejects)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Basil Hallward paints Dorian Gray.
Lord Henry tempts Dorian with a life of sensation.
Dorian wishes the portrait would age instead of his face.
He lives for pleasure.
The picture records every cruelty.
He murders Basil, who painted the truth he cannot bear.
He stabs the portrait and dies.
The servants find an aged body and a young picture.

items.title: "The Sign of the Four" (1890) — Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Sign of the Four

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1890 (Sort Year: 1890)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Holmes and Watson trace an Indian treasure and the pact of four men who stole it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1890 is correct. Lippincott's Monthly Magazine published it in February 1890 as The Sign of the Four. A book followed in 1890. Some title pages drop one word and print The Sign of Four.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sherlock Holmes (The detective, shown here using a cocaine solution); Dr John Watson (The narrator, who falls in love with Mary Morstan); Mary Morstan (The client whose father vanished with a secret); Jonathan Small (A convict who claims a share of the Agra treasure)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mary Morstan asks Holmes why she receives mysterious pearls.
Her missing father is tied to a stolen Agra treasure.
Four men had sworn a pact, marked as the sign of the four.
Jonathan Small and his companion Tonga are hunted through London.
Watson falls in love with Mary, and they marry at the end.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: New Grub Street

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1891 (Sort Year: 1891)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gissing

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two London writers face a book market that pays the clever salesman, not the artist.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1891 is correct. Smith, Elder published it in three volumes in 1891.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edwin Reardon (A talented novelist destroyed by poverty and pride); Jasper Milvain (A shrewd journalist who writes for money and status); Amy Reardon (Edwin's wife, who wants comfort and success); Marian Yule (A researcher worn out by literary hack work); Alfred Yule (Marian's father, a failed and jealous man of letters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edwin Reardon is a serious novelist who cannot write to order.
Poverty and failure break his marriage to Amy.
Jasper Milvain treats writing as a trade and chases useful friends.
Marian Yule drudges in the British Museum for her bitter father, Alfred.
Harold Biffen writes a harshly real novel and is crushed by want.
Milvain prospers.
Reardon and the uncompromising artists do not.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Barrack-Room Ballads

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1892 (Sort Year: 1892)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems in soldiers' speech about barracks, battle, and empire.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Barrack-Room Ballads and Other Verses was published in 1892. Some poems had appeared in magazines earlier. Britannica and the Nobel bibliography date the book 1892. The database year 1892 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tommy Atkins (The common British soldier who speaks many of the poems); Danny Deever (The soldier hanged in front of his regiment); Gunga Din (The Indian water carrier praised after his death)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speakers are ordinary British soldiers, not officers.
Danny Deever tells of a soldier hanged before his regiment.
Tommy complains that civilians cheer a soldier only in wartime.
Gunga Din praises an Indian water carrier who dies in battle.
Mandalay and The Ballad of East and West are in the book.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Iola Leroy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1892 (Sort Year: 1892)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Frances E. W. Harper

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about a mixed race woman who will not hide her Black family.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1892 is correct. A University of North Carolina copy was entered in 1892. The full title adds the words or Shadows Uplifted.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Iola Leroy (A mixed race woman who claims her African family); Robert Johnson (An enslaved man who shares secret news of the war); Harry Leroy (A member of Iola's family named in the chapter list); Doctor Frank Latimer (A young doctor whose mother had been enslaved)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Enslaved men pass war news by talking about fresh butter and eggs.
Iola is taken out of slavery and brought to a Union general.
She had been treated as property, with no power to protect herself.
She says her best blood is African blood, and she will not deny it.
Doctor Frank Latimer, whose mother had been enslaved, plans work in the South.
The closing chapters turn to affection and a wedding.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lady Windermere’s Fan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1892 (Sort Year: 1892)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wife nearly leaves home, then learns that a woman she despises is her mother.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Produced in 1892. Database year 1892 matches the premiere, which is the date exams ask. The exact book year is not fixed in the sources used here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lady Windermere (A young wife sure of her own moral rules); Lord Windermere (Her husband, who secretly helps Mrs Erlynne); Mrs Erlynne (A woman with a past, who is Lady Windermere's mother); Lord Darlington (A witty admirer who wants Lady Windermere to leave)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lady Windermere believes her husband is unfaithful with Mrs Erlynne.
She plans to run away with Lord Darlington.
Mrs Erlynne stops her and is found in a compromising place instead.
Lord Windermere and the guests misread the fan and the scandal.
Lady Windermere never learns in public that Mrs Erlynne is her mother.

items.title: "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" (1892) — Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1892 (Sort Year: 1892)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first book of Holmes short stories, gathered from The Strand Magazine.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1892 is the book. The stories first appeared in The Strand from July 1891 to June 1892. George Newnes published the book on 14 October 1892.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sherlock Holmes (The detective in twelve separate cases); Dr John Watson (The friend who writes the cases down); Irene Adler (The woman in A Scandal in Bohemia, who outwits Holmes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sherlock Holmes is a fictional character created by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle and it is full of detective stories.
The character first appeared in print in 1887, and was featured in 4 novels and 56 short stories. Among the 4 novels the famous two are: A Study in Scarlet The Sign of The Four.
The first series of short stories appeared in The Strand Magazine beginning with "A Scandal in Bohemia".
Out of 56, 52 stories are narrated by Holmes' friend Dr. John H. Watson, while 2 are narrated by Holmes himself and two other are written in third person.
Holmes' primary intellectual detection method is "Abductive Reasoning".
Lines from Silver Blaze: "Is there any point to which you would wish to draw my attention? To the curious incident of the dog in the night time."
Sherlock Holmes respond to it as "That was the curious incident."
Twelve stories ran in The Strand from July 1891 to June 1892.
A Scandal in Bohemia introduces Irene Adler, the woman.
The Red Headed League and The Speckled Band are famous cases in the set.
Sidney Paget's pictures fixed the public image of Holmes.
George Newnes published the collection as a book in 1892.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Widowers’ Houses

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Bernard Shaw

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Shaw's first staged play shows a young doctor caught in slum rents.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Shaw began it with William Archer and finished it alone. The Independent Theatre staged it at the Royalty Theatre on 9 December 1892. Henry and Company published it in 1893. It was revised in Plays Unpleasant in 1898. The database year 1892 is the first night. The first book came in 1893.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harry Trench (A young doctor whose small income depends on slum property); Blanche Sartorius (Sartorius's proud daughter, and Trench's fiancee); Mr Sartorius (A self-made slum landlord); Lickcheese (The rent collector whom Sartorius dismisses); William de Burgh Cokane (Trench's fussy friend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Doctor Harry Trench meets Blanche Sartorius while they are on holiday.
Her father, Sartorius, grows rich by renting bad houses to the poor.
He fires the rent collector Lickcheese for being too easy on tenants.
Trench refuses the tainted money, then learns his own income comes from the same rents.
He drops the moral pose and joins a shady housing plan.
He and Blanche come back together.

items.title: "A Woman of No Importance" (1893) — Oscar Wilde

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Woman of No Importance

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A witty rake discovers that the woman he once abandoned is the mother of his son.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Produced in 1893. Database year 1893 matches the premiere. The book date is not fixed in the sources used here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lord Illingworth (A witty aristocrat and Gerald's father); Mrs Arbuthnot (The woman of the title, who raised Gerald alone); Gerald Arbuthnot (Their son, who does not know his father at first); Hester Worsley (A young American woman who judges English society)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lord Illingworth, a charming man of the world, visits an English country house.
He offers a post to Gerald Arbuthnot, a serious young man.
Mrs Arbuthnot refuses to let Gerald go, for a secret reason.
She reveals that Lord Illingworth is Gerald's father and once refused to marry her.
Gerald wants a duel or a marriage.
His mother chooses dignity over the lord's name.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Keynotes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short stories that enter women's private thoughts, desire, and uneasy marriages.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1893 matches the London first book. Victorian Web names Elkin Mathews and John Lane, 1893. The Project Gutenberg file is a Boston printing of 1894.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The wife in A Cross Line (A married woman who wants to be understood); The fisherman (A grey eyed stranger who talks with her by the river); The woman with the grey glove (A newly divorced woman who will not rush into love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Cross Line follows a married woman who talks with a strange fisherman.
She is not happy at home, and she dreams of a wilder life.
Now Spring Has Come shows a woman drawn to a modern foreign book.
A Little Grey Glove gives a divorced woman time before she chooses.
Under Northern Sky, in three parts, shows hard men and tired women.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Salomé

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A one act tragedy in French: Salome dances, demands the head of Jokanaan, and is killed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The French book was published on 22 February 1893 in Paris and in London. The English translation by Lord Alfred Douglas came in 1894. The first performance was in Paris in 1896. Database year 1893 is the French publication. Database genre Poetry is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Salome (Herodias's daughter, who demands Jokanaan's head); Jokanaan (John the Baptist, a prophet in prison); Herod (The tetrarch who bargains for Salome's dance); Herodias (Salome's mother and Herod's wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Herod lusts after his stepdaughter Salome during a banquet.
Salome desires Jokanaan, John the Baptist, who is held in a cistern.
Jokanaan rejects her.
She will not be refused.
She dances the dance of the seven veils.
Herod must grant her wish.
She receives the head and kisses it.
Herod orders the soldiers to kill her.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Heavenly Twins

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sarah Grand

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A New Woman novel about bad marriages and the danger of syphilis.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1893 is correct. The novel made her reputation under the name Sarah Grand.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Evadne Frayling (A learned young woman who refuses a corrupt husband); Edith Beale (A conventional girl who marries a diseased man and dies); Angelica (A bold twin who wants a man's freedom); Major Colquhoun (Evadne's husband, whose past she rejects); Dr Galbraith (The doctor Evadne marries after Colquhoun dies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Evadne Frayling teaches herself and learns the risk of a bad husband's past.
She marries Major Colquhoun, then refuses to live as his wife.
Edith Beale ignores a warning, marries Sir Mosley Menteith, and becomes very ill.
Edith and her child suffer from his disease, and Edith dies.
Angelica, one heavenly twin, hates the limits placed on a girl.
She marries the older Mr Kilroy for freedom, and she dresses as a boy.
That disguise ends in harm, and she must face what she has done.
After Colquhoun dies, Evadne marries Dr Galbraith, but the old fear remains.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Odd Women

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1893 (Sort Year: 1893)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Gissing

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about surplus women, marriage, and the fight for independent work.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1893 is correct. Lawrence and Bullen published it in three volumes in 1893.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rhoda Nunn (A single woman who trains other women for independent work); Mary Barfoot (Rhoda's partner in a school for women clerks); Monica Madden (The youngest Madden sister, who enters a possessive marriage); Edmund Widdowson (Monica's older, controlling husband); Everard Barfoot (Mary's cousin, who tests Rhoda's ideas about marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
There are more women than men, so many women cannot marry.
Rhoda Nunn and Mary Barfoot train women for office work.
The Madden sisters, Alice, Virginia, and Monica, slip toward poverty.
Monica marries the jealous older man Edmund Widdowson.
Rhoda is drawn to Everard Barfoot but refuses a dependent marriage.
The book shows how money and gender trap both wives and single women.

items.title: "The Second Mrs Tanqueray" (1895) — Arthur Wing Pinero

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Second Mrs Tanqueray

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Wing Pinero

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A widower marries Paula, and her past returns to break the household.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First acted at the St. James's Theatre on 27 May 1893. Mrs. Patrick Campbell played Paula. William Heinemann's first printing is 1895. The database year 1893 matches the first performance, which is the date to remember.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aubrey Tanqueray (A wealthy widower who marries outside his social circle); Paula (His second wife, whose earlier life good society will not forgive); Ellean (Aubrey's daughter, raised in a convent); Captain Hugh Ardale (Ellean's suitor and Paula's former lover); Cayley Drummle (Aubrey's friend, who doubts the marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aubrey Tanqueray tells his friends he will marry Paula, a woman with a past.
His daughter Ellean comes home and stays cold toward Paula.
Ellean loves Captain Hugh Ardale, who was once Paula's lover.
Aubrey stops that marriage, and father, daughter, and wife all split.
Ellean goes to make peace and finds that Paula is dead by her own hand.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Bayou Folk

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1894 (Sort Year: 1894)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Kate Chopin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1894 book of short stories about Louisiana families, speech, and hidden pain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1894 is correct. The University of North Carolina copy shows the Houghton Mifflin title page dated 1894. Virginia Commonwealth University dates the publication to March 1894. Project Gutenberg reprints that book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Desiree (A young wife whose baby brings a crisis at L'Abri); Armand Aubigny (Her husband, proud of his name and harsh when afraid); Madame Valmonde (The woman who raised Desiree and visits the baby)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bayou Folk collects short stories of Creole and Cajun life.
Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York in 1894.
The stories use local speech, customs, and family conflict.
Desiree's Baby is the best known story in the book.
That story turns on race, marriage, and a hidden family letter.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Candida

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1898 (Sort Year: 1898)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Bernard Shaw

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A clergyman's wife must choose between her husband and a young poet.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Shaw wrote the play in 1894. A copyright performance was given at the Theatre Royal, South Shields, on 30 March 1895. The Independent Theatre revived it at Aberdeen on 30 July 1897. It was published in Plays Pleasant in 1898. The database pair 1894 and staged 1895 matches the writing year and the South Shields night. Many short lists give only 1897.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Candida Morell (Morell's capable wife, who sees which man is truly weak); Reverend James Mavor Morell (A confident Christian Socialist clergyman); Eugene Marchbanks (A young poet who idealises Candida); Miss Proserpine Garnett (Morell's secretary); Mr Burgess (Candida's father)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a comedy by G.B. Shaw.
The play is set in the northeast suburbs of London in the month of October.
It tells the story of Candida, wife of a famous clergyman James Morrel, a Christian socialist but Candida is responsible for his success.
Candida returns to London with Eugene Marchbanks who loves Candida and considers her divine.
But ultimately Candida selects her husband.
Famous "Auction Scene" of Candida appears at the end.
Reverend James Mavor Morell is a popular Christian Socialist preacher.
A Christian Socialist ties the Gospel to plans that help the poor.
His wife Candida keeps much of his public success steady.
The poet Eugene Marchbanks offers her what he thinks is a higher love.
Candida must choose between the poet and her husband.
She chooses the weaker man, and that man is Morell.
Marchbanks goes out into the night, free of the comfortable house.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Discords

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1894 (Sort Year: 1894)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A second story book about hard marriages, work, and women who feel trapped.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1894 is correct. Victorian Web dates Discords 1894. A Harvard library copy also prints 1894.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The woman of the three periods (The figure followed as a child, a girl, and a woman); The wife in Wedlock (A lonely wife in a new house at the edge of town)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Psychological Moment at Three Periods moves from child, to girl, to woman.
The nursery lamp is still unlit when that story opens.
Wedlock begins with bricklayers building a wall behind a new house.
A tired wife speaks of her husband's cousin and of loneliness.
Other stories are Her Share, Gone Under, Virgin Soil, and The Regeneration of Two.
One woman says she can get a living, and she means to.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Daughters of Danaus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1894 (Sort Year: 1894)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mona Caird

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hadria Fullerton wants to compose music, but marriage and family duty pull her back.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1894 is correct. Bliss, Sands, and Foster of London published the novel in 1894. The exact year of composition is unknown.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hadria Fullerton (A composer whose marriage and mother's claims block her art); Algitha Fullerton (Hadria's sister, who leaves home for independent work); Hubert Temperley (The husband whose household rules limit Hadria); Professor Fortescue (A learned friend who tells Hadria to train her musical gift); Valeria du Prel (A visitor who brings Hadria a new, lonely friendship)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title uses a Greek legend of women doomed to endless, useless work.
Hadria Fullerton longs to be a composer.
Her sister Algitha leaves home to work.
Hadria marries Hubert Temperley, and household life chokes her music.
Professor Fortescue urges her to develop her gift.
She escapes to Paris and feels free, then returns because her mother demands her.
The ending stays open.
She is not saved by a happy marriage or by death.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Jungle Book

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1894 (Sort Year: 1894)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Animal stories, including Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves in India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Jungle Book was published in 1894. Britannica, the Poetry Foundation, and the Nobel bibliography agree. The database year 1894 is correct. The Second Jungle Book is a separate volume from 1895.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mowgli (A boy raised by wolves, called the man cub); Baloo (The bear who teaches Mowgli the Law); Bagheera (The black panther who protects Mowgli); Shere Khan (The lame tiger who claims Mowgli as prey); Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (The mongoose who fights cobras in a garden)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a collection of stories by Rudyard Kipling.
It was first published in magazines in 1893-94.
It is evident that it was written for his daughter Josephine, who died at the age of six in 1899.
"The Jungle Book" and "The Second Jungle Book" are stories about Mowgli.
Among all stories, three stories are best known. These stories revolves around the adventures of an abandoned "man cub" Mowgli, who is raised by wolves in Indian jungle.
The most famous stories are:.
Rikki Tikki Tavi.
The Story of a Heroic Mongoose.
Toomai of the Elephants.
Rikki Tikki Tavi deals with the adventure of young Mongoose.
Mowgli, a boy is raised by wolves in the Indian jungle with the help of Baloo, the bear and Bagheera, the black panther, and then he has to fight the tiger Shere Khan.
Songs of The Jungle Book:.
Hunting-song of the Seeonee Pack.
Road song of the Bandar-Log.
Mowgli's song.
Lukannon.
Darjee Chaunt.
Rikki Tikki Tavi.
Shiv and the grasshopper.
Parade song of the camp animals.
Characters:.
Akela: an Indian wolf.
Bagheera: black panther.
Baloo: a sloth bear.
Bandar Log: a tribe of monkeys.
Chil: a kite Recessional: a Victorian Ode: (1897)
The poem expresses the sincerity of his religious devotion.
It was occasioned by Queen Victoria's 1897.
Mowgli is adopted by a wolf pack in the Seeonee hills.
Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther teach him the Law.
Shere Khan the tiger wants to kill the man cub.
Rikki-Tikki-Tavi the mongoose and a white seal have their own tales.
Poems sit between the stories, stating the law of the pack.

items.title: "The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes" (1894) — Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1894 (Sort Year: 1894)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A second collection of Holmes stories, ending with his apparent death at Reichenbach.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1894 matches the London book from George Newnes. The stories ran in The Strand from December 1892 to December 1893. The Final Problem is the December 1893 story. Some American reprints move The Cardboard Box to a later book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sherlock Holmes (The detective who seems to die in the last story); Dr John Watson (The narrator who mourns Holmes after the falls); Professor Moriarty (The crime lord Holmes calls the Napoleon of crime); Mycroft Holmes (Sherlock's older brother, first seen in The Greek Interpreter)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Twelve more stories ran in The Strand from December 1892 to December 1893.
Silver Blaze and The Musgrave Ritual are well known cases here.
The Greek Interpreter introduces Holmes's brother Mycroft.
In The Final Problem, Holmes faces Professor Moriarty.
Holmes and Moriarty seem to die together at the Reichenbach Falls.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Almayer’s Folly

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Joseph Conrad

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A trader in Borneo loses his daughter and his dream of gold.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Conrad worked on the novel from about 1889 to 1894. T. Fisher Unwin published it in April 1895. This book first used the pen name Joseph Conrad. The database year 1895 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kaspar Almayer (A failed trader who dreams of wealth and Europe); Nina Almayer (His daughter, who chooses Dain and the Malay world); Dain Maroola (The Malay prince Nina loves); Mrs Almayer (Nina's Malay mother, who opposes Almayer's plans)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
2- An Outcast of the Island (1896); set in Malay.
Kaspar Almayer trades on a river in Borneo and hopes for gold.
He wants his daughter Nina to live as a European lady.
Nina loves Dain, a Malay chief, and rejects her father's plan.
The lovers escape, and Almayer's great house falls into ruin.
People call that unfinished house Almayer's Folly.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Ideal Husband

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A perfect public man is blackmailed for an old crime, and his wife must face the truth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Produced in early 1895. Database year 1895 matches the premiere. The later book date is not fixed in the sources used here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Robert Chiltern (A rising politician with a guilty secret); Lady Chiltern (His wife, who demands moral perfection); Mrs Cheveley (The blackmailer from Sir Robert's past); Lord Goring (A dandy whose wit solves the plot)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sir Robert Chiltern has a spotless name built on a secret stock tip from his youth.
Mrs Cheveley returns with a letter that can ruin him.
She wants his support for a dishonest scheme.
Lady Chiltern, who worships an ideal husband, learns the flaw.
Lord Goring untangles the blackmail, and the marriage survives a more honest love.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lilith

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: George MacDonald

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A man follows Mister Raven through a mirror world of death, children, and Lilith.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1895 is correct. Britannica dates Lilith 1895. The London book was published by Chatto and Windus in 1895.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The man of the story (The man who crosses from his house into the other world); Mister Raven (A guide whom the man first takes for a bird); Lilith (The powerful woman named by the book's title)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The man is lost between his library, a mirror, and another world.
He meets Mister Raven and at first thinks the man is a bird.
He walks through graveyards, woods, and a house of death.
He even wonders if he himself is dead and does not know it.
The journey pictures a soul trying to come back to God.

items.title: "The Importance of Being Earnest" (1895) — Oscar Wilde

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Importance of Being Earnest

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Oscar Wilde

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two men who pretend to be named Ernest find that the name, and the lie, both matter.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Produced in early 1895. Database year 1895 matches the premiere, which exams ask. The book publication came later and is not dated in the sources used here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jack Worthing (A country guardian who calls himself Ernest in town); Algernon Moncrieff (A London dandy who uses the name Bunbury); Gwendolen Fairfax (Lady Bracknell's daughter, who loves the name Ernest); Cecily Cardew (Jack's ward, who also dreams of marrying an Ernest); Lady Bracknell (A grand lady who treats marriage as a bargain)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
8. De Profundis (epistle)
It is a romantic comedy play by Wells.
Characters:.
Hon. Gwendolen Fairfax.
Algernon Moncrieff ('Algy')
Jack Worthing,.
J.P. - protagonist.
Miss Prism.
Lady Bracknell.
Jack Worthing invents a wicked brother, Ernest, so he can escape to London.
Algernon Moncrieff invents a sick friend, Bunbury, for the same kind of escape.
Gwendolen and Cecily each insist they can love only a man named Ernest.
Lady Bracknell blocks the matches over family, money, and a handbag.
Miss Prism's old secret shows that Jack's name really is Ernest.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Second Jungle Book

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: More Mowgli stories and other animal tales, published a year later.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Second Jungle Book was published in 1895. Britannica and the Nobel bibliography agree. The database year 1895 is correct. Do not merge this book with The Jungle Book of 1894.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mowgli (The wolf boy, now older, who leads and then leaves the pack); Kaa (The python who helps Mowgli against the red dogs); Purun Bhagat (A former prime minister who becomes a holy man)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mowgli returns in new stories of fear, revenge, and the pack.
How Fear Came tells of a drought and a truce in the jungle.
Red Dog shows the pack fighting the dhole, wild red dogs.
The Miracle of Purun Bhagat follows a holy man and the beasts.
These tales are a separate book from the 1894 Jungle Book.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Sorrows of Satan

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Marie Corelli

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor author inherits a fortune and meets Satan in disguise.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1895 is correct. The Project Gutenberg text says the first publication was November 1895. Many further editions appeared in 1895 and 1896. Britannica calls it a melodramatic religious novel with a very wide sale.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Geoffrey Tempest (A starving author who becomes a millionaire and tells the story); Prince Lucio (A charming prince who reveals himself as Satan); Lady Sibyl (A famous beauty whom Tempest meets in high society)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Geoffrey Tempest is a hungry young author alone in London.
He suddenly inherits an enormous fortune.
Prince Lucio befriends him and leads him into rich society.
Tempest meets Lady Sibyl, a celebrated beauty of the season.
Lucio later shows that he is Satan, once called Lucifer.
The story warns that wealth without God brings misery.
Methuen published the book in November 1895, and many editions followed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Time Machine

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1895 (Sort Year: 1895)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. G. Wells

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Victorian inventor rides to the year 802,701 and finds humanity split in two.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A college sketch called The Chronic Argonauts appeared in 1888. The New Review serialized The Time Machine from January to May 1895. Henry Holt published the American book on 7 May 1895. Heinemann published the London book on 29 May 1895. The database year 1895 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
