fields.value: The Time Traveller (A Victorian scientist who builds the machine and tells the story); Weena (An Eloi whom the Traveller saves and then loses); The Eloi (Small, gentle people of the far future, descended from a leisured class); The Morlocks (Underground workers of the future who tend machines and eat the Eloi)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is also a science fiction novella by Wells, published in 1895, set in Victorian age. The daily newspaper "Pall Mall Gazette" appears in it.
Wells popularized the concept of 'Time Travel' that allows an operator to travel purposefully and selectively.
The term "Time Machine" coined by Wells is said to refer such a vehicle.
Book's protagonist is an English scientist and gentleman inventor living in Richmond, Surrey in Victorian England.
The narrator identifies the gentleman inventor as time traveler.
The time traveler reveals that he has built a machine that is capable of carrying a person through time.
The time traveler tests his device with a journey that takes him to AD 802, 701, where he meets Eloi (a society of small, elegant childlike adults).
Time traveler lost his time machine.
At the end, time traveler returns to his Victorian age.
The Time Traveller tells his dinner guests that time is a fourth dimension.
He rides his machine far forward and stops in the year 802,701.
The childlike Eloi live in ease on the surface and fear the dark.
The Morlocks live underground, run the machines, and hunt the Eloi for food.
He befriends the Eloi girl Weena and loses her in a fight with the Morlocks.
He escapes, looks at a dying Earth, and returns with only two strange flowers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Shropshire Lad

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1896 (Sort Year: 1896)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: A. E. Housman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sixty-three short poems on youth, soldiers, love, and early death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Poetry Foundation, Britannica, and Project Gutenberg all date the book to 1896. Gutenberg calls it a collection of 63 poems. The database year 1896 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Shropshire lad (A young country speaker. He is not Housman himself.); The dead athlete (A runner praised because he dies while still in glory)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker is a young country man, not Housman himself.
The poems are short lyrics about love, soldiers, and graves.
A publisher refused the book when Housman first offered it.
Kegan Paul published it in 1896, at Housman's own cost.
Sales were slow at first, then the book became famous.
Young readers of the First World War knew many poems by heart.

items.title: "An Outcast of the Islands" (1896) — Joseph Conrad

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Outcast of the Islands

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1896 (Sort Year: 1896)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Joseph Conrad

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A failed clerk betrays his friends and is destroyed by passion.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Conrad wrote the novel in 1894 and 1895. T. Fisher Unwin published it in March 1896. The database year 1896 is correct. Willems, not Jim, is the outcast of this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Peter Willems (The outcast clerk who betrays his protector); Aissa (The Malay woman whose love turns to a killing); Tom Lingard (The sea captain who tries to save Willems); Kaspar Almayer (The trader whose business Willems helps to ruin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Peter Willems is cast out after he steals from his employer.
Tom Lingard, a sea captain, gives him a second chance.
Willems falls in love with Aissa and betrays Lingard's secret.
His treachery ruins Almayer's trade and Lingard's trust.
Aissa kills Willems when she sees that his love has failed.

items.title: "The Island of Doctor Moreau" (1896) — H. G. Wells

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Island of Doctor Moreau

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1896 (Sort Year: 1896)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. G. Wells

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A castaway finds a scientist turning animals into suffering beast-people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann published the London book, and Stone and Kimball the American book, in 1896. A common cited day is 1 January 1896. The story's inner dates run from February 1887 to January 1888. The database year 1896 is the publication year. The database calls the work drama. It is a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Prendick (The shipwrecked narrator who records the island); Doctor Moreau (A physiologist who tries to manufacture humans from animals); Montgomery (Moreau's alcoholic assistant, who rescues Prendick); The Sayer of the Law (The Beast Folk leader who recites Moreau's rules)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edward Prendick is shipwrecked and taken to a lonely Pacific island.
Doctor Moreau, a banished vivisectionist, cuts living animals into human shape.
Vivisection means cutting living animals for experiment.
The Beast Folk chant the Law and ask, Are we not men?
The creatures slip back toward animal habits, and Moreau is killed.
Prendick escapes, but ordinary people in England now look half animal to him.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Seven Seas

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1896 (Sort Year: 1896)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems of ships, empire, and hard work across the oceans.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Seven Seas was published in 1896. Britannica and the Nobel bibliography agree. The database year 1896 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: McAndrew (The Scottish engineer who speaks McAndrew's Hymn); Sir Anthony Gloster (The dying shipowner who speaks The Mary Gloster)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems praise sailors, engineers, and the sea routes of empire.
McAndrew's Hymn gives a voice to a Scottish ship's engineer.
The Mary Gloster is a dying shipowner's bitter speech.
Sestina of the Tramp-Royal follows a wanderer who loves the road.
The book continues the sailor verse begun in the ballads.

items.title: "The Well at the World’s End" (1896) — William Morris

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Well at the World’s End

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1896 (Sort Year: 1896)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: William Morris

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long prose romance about a young man's quest for a healing well at the edge of the world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Iowa Morris Archive lists a Kelmscott Press edition of 1896 and a Longmans two-volume edition of 1896. A University of Delaware exhibition also dates the Kelmscott book to 1896. The exact year he finished writing is not fixed here. The database year 1896 is the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph (The young hero who seeks the well)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ralph leaves home to seek the Well at the World's End.
He travels through strange lands, dangers, and love.
Friends and rivals share news of the well.
He and his companion drink from the well.
The drink brings renewed life, and they return glad.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Captains Courageous

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1897 (Sort Year: 1897)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rudyard Kipling

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rich boy falls from a liner and is hardened by Grand Banks fishermen.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the Nobel bibliography date the book 1897. Some lists also show 1896, which may mark an earlier serial. The book year used here is 1897. The database year 1897 matches that book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harvey Cheyne (The rich boy who learns work at sea); Disko Troop (The captain of the fishing schooner We're Here); Dan Troop (Disko's son, who works beside Harvey); Harvey Cheyne Sr. (The railway millionaire who comes for his son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Harvey Cheyne, a spoiled rich boy, is washed overboard.
Disko Troop's schooner, the We're Here, picks him up.
He must work as a fisherman on the Grand Banks.
The season teaches him skill, humility, and respect for labor.
His father finds a son who can now stand on his own.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Dracula

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1897 (Sort Year: 1897)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Bram Stoker

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Count Dracula, a Transylvanian vampire, comes to England and is hunted back to his castle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1897 is correct. Archibald Constable published it in London in 1897. Working notes survive, but they are not a complete earlier book. Dracula's Guest was published later, in 1914, after Stoker's death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Count Dracula (A Transylvanian vampire who wants a home in England); Jonathan Harker (A young lawyer who first enters the castle); Mina Harker (Jonathan's wife, whose mind Dracula tries to invade); Lucy Westenra (Mina's friend, who becomes a vampire and is destroyed); Professor Abraham Van Helsing (The scholar who knows how to fight the vampire); Dr John Seward (A doctor who keeps an asylum and a phonograph diary)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jonathan Harker visits Count Dracula in Transylvania to arrange a London house.
The Count sails to England and preys on Lucy Westenra.
Lucy dies and rises as a vampire, and her friends must destroy her.
Mina Murray, later Mina Harker, is threatened next.
Professor Van Helsing leads the hunt, and they destroy Dracula near his castle.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Beth Book

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1897 (Sort Year: 1897)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sarah Grand

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A life story of Elizabeth Caldwell Maclure, a woman of genius.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1897 is correct. The New York Appleton title page is dated 1897. Some London lists print 1898 for a Heinemann volume.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elizabeth Caldwell Maclure (Beth, the gifted heroine, close to Grand's own life); Dan Maclure (Her coarse doctor husband); Mrs Caldwell (Beth's worn mother, who accepts suffering without question); Angelica Kilroy (A friend who already knows the harm of bad marriages)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Beth is born into a tired, poor house with too many children.
Her mother accepts pain as her lot and never asks about causes.
Beth grows up gifted and marries Dan Maclure, a coarse doctor.
The marriage is cruel, and Beth begins to see his selfish habits.
Friends from her other books, including Angelica and Ideala, enter her life.
She keeps writing, judges her own faults, and vows that she will succeed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Invisible Man

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1897 (Sort Year: 1897)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. G. Wells

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The scientist Griffin makes himself invisible and becomes a violent outcast.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wells drafted a shorter tale in 1896 and then expanded it. Pearson's Weekly serialized The Invisible Man in June and July 1897. Pearson published the London book in 1897. The database year 1897 covers both the serial and the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Griffin (The invisible scientist, brilliant, selfish, and increasingly violent); Doctor Kemp (A former acquaintance who hears Griffin's story and resists him); Mrs Hall (The innkeeper who first shelters the bandaged stranger); Thomas Marvel (A tramp whom Griffin forces to help him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(It's also a novel by American author Ralph Ellison)
A bandaged stranger arrives at an inn and hides his face.
He is Griffin, an optics scientist who has made his body invisible.
He cannot reverse the change, so hunger and cold drive him to theft.
He explains the method to Doctor Kemp and then tries to start a reign of terror.
A crowd corners him.
When he dies, his body can be seen again.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Liars

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1901 (Sort Year: 1901)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry Arthur Jones

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1897 society comedy in which friends pile up lies to hide a flirtation.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1897 is the first performance. It opened at the Criterion Theatre, London, in October 1897. The printed text followed in 1901.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lady Jessica Nepean (A wife who flirts and then faces the result); Edward Falkner (A South African hero who loves Lady Jessica); Gilbert Nepean (Jessica's jealous husband); Sir Christopher Deering (The friend who wants the truth told)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lady Jessica Nepean enjoys the notice of Edward Falkner.
Falkner is a hero lately returned from South Africa.
She dines with him while her husband, Gilbert, is away.
Friends invent lie after lie to hide that meeting.
Sir Christopher stops Falkner from running away with Jessica.
He sends her home and tells Gilbert to court his own wife.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Morality of Marriage

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1897 (Sort Year: 1897)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mona Caird

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of essays that calls Victorian marriage unfair to women.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1897 is the book year. George Redway of London published the essay collection in 1897. The full title adds Other Essays on the Status and Destiny of Woman. The essays were written earlier. The famous Westminster Review essay Marriage is from 1888.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mona Caird (The essayist speaking for a freer and equal marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Her essay Marriage appeared in the Westminster Review in 1888.
She said the present form of marriage failed women.
The Daily Telegraph then asked readers if marriage was a failure.
The 1897 book gathers her essays on marriage, motherhood, and women's status.
She wants equal partners, shared home duties, and money of a woman's own.
This is a book of arguments.
It is not a novel.

items.title: "The War of the Worlds" (1898) — H. G. Wells

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The War of the Worlds

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1898 (Sort Year: 1898)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: H. G. Wells

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Martians invade England, and ordinary germs destroy them after armies fail.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Pearson's Magazine printed the story from April to December 1897. Cosmopolitan printed it in the United States in the same months. Heinemann published the London book in 1898. The database serial span says 1897-98. The serial year is 1897. The book year is 1898.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A philosophical writer in Surrey who survives the invasion); The narrator's brother (A medical student whose chapters show the flight from London); The curate (A terrified clergyman who hides with the narrator); The artilleryman (A soldier with grand, empty plans for a human underground); The Martians (Invaders from Mars who feed on blood and die of Earth germs)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A narrator in Surrey watches a cylinder fall from Mars near Woking.
Martians emerge and burn people with a heat ray.
Tripod machines stride over towns, and a red weed spreads.
The narrator hides with a frightened curate, then meets a boastful artilleryman.
London collapses, but Earth bacteria, harmless to humans, kill the Martians.
The narrator finds his wife alive and sees how small human power was.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Love Songs and Elegies

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1898 (Sort Year: 1898)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Manmohan Ghose

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A small 1898 book of love lyrics and poems of grief.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1898 is correct. The title page was printed by Elkin Mathews in Vigo Street, London, as Shilling Garland number 9. The printed first word uses a hyphen. The database marks this book posthumous. That flag is wrong. Ghose died on 4 January 1924. The posthumous book is Songs of Love and Death, edited by Laurence Binyon, in 1926. This 1898 book is poetry, not fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Love (The boy god who begs a kiss in The Kiss of Cupid); Beauty (The sleeping woman whom Love finds in that poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Elkin Mathews of London published it in April 1898.
It is number 9 in his Shilling Garland series of thin poetry books.
Ghose dedicated the verses to Laurence Binyon.
Early poems include Myvanwy and The Kiss of Cupid.
Later pieces turn to grief, including Lament, Elegy, and The Exile.
An elegy is a poem of mourning.
He was already teaching in Bengal, and he lived until 1924.

items.title: "The Turn of the Screw" (1898) — Henry James

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Turn of the Screw

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1898 (Sort Year: 1898)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Henry James

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A governess believes two dead servants haunt the children in her care.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates The Turn of the Screw 1898. The database year 1898 is correct. It is a late Victorian tale. It is not The Ambassadors, which is 1903.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The governess (The narrator, who believes the children are haunted); Miles (The boy, sent home from school, who dies at the end); Flora (Miles's sister, who is taken away from Bly); Mrs Grose (The housekeeper, who knew the former servants); Peter Quint (The dead valet whom the governess claims to see)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Christmas group hears of a governess and two children.
The governess is hired to care for Miles and Flora at Bly.
She is told not to bother their uncle in London.
She sees a man and a woman whom the housekeeper knew as dead servants.
She becomes sure the children see the ghosts and are hiding it.
The story ends with Miles dead in her arms, and the truth still disputed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Trelawny of the ‘Wells’

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1899 (Sort Year: 1899)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Arthur Wing Pinero

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Rose leaves the stage for a grand marriage, then returns to a newer kind of play.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: All checked sources place the first performance in 1898 at the Court Theatre in London. The 1911 Britannica says 30 January. A later account says 20 January, and another note says 29 January. The exact day is disputed, so remember the year 1898. Project Gutenberg marks the book 1899. The database year 1898 matches the premiere.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rose Trelawny (An actress who leaves the Wells company for a society marriage); Arthur Gower (The man she means to marry, who later becomes an actor); Sir William Gower (Arthur's strict grandfather, who at last backs the new play); Tom Wrench (An actor-playwright based on Tom Robertson, writer of quieter plays)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rose Trelawny, a star of melodrama, is engaged to Arthur Gower.
She tries life with his stiff family and cannot fit their manners.
She returns to the theatre, but the old loud style no longer suits her.
Tom Wrench writes a quieter play, and Sir William Gower helps to stage it.
Arthur has become an actor, and the lovers meet again in rehearsal.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Heart of Darkness

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1899 (Sort Year: 1899)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Joseph Conrad

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Marlow tells of his river journey to the ivory trader Kurtz.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Blackwood's Magazine printed it in February, March, and April 1899, under the title The Heart of Darkness. The book Youth: A Narrative and Two Other Stories collected it in November 1902.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Marlow (The sailor who tells the story of his Congo journey); Kurtz (The ivory agent whose last words are the horror); The Intended (Kurtz's fiancee in Europe, to whom Marlow lies); The Manager (The company man who wants Kurtz removed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It first appeared in a three part series in Blackwood Magazine in 1899.
It was published as a complete novella in 1902.
It is based on a trip that Conrad took through modern-day Congo during his years as a sailor from London.
The novella narrates the story of Marlow's job as an ivory transporter down to Congo. The novel is narrated by an un-named narrator.
Through his journey, Marlow develops an intense interest in investigating Kurtz, an ivory procurement agent and Marlow is shocked upon seeing what the European traders have done to the natives.
Kurtz is one of the main figures of the novel. He is a pretty tyrant, an embodiment of Europe and an assault on European values.
He is the unique victim of colonization; the wilderness captures him and he turns his back on the people and customs that were once a part of him.
Marlow story is told by the anonymous narrator who listens to Marlow on the deck of "The Nellie".
In the novel Marlow takes a job as a riverboat captain with the company, a Belgian concern organized to trade in the Congo.
When Marlow reaches Congo he encountered wide-spread inefficiency and brutality in the company stations.
The native inhabitants of the region have been forced into the company's service and they suffer terribly from overwork and ill treatment at the hands of the company's agent.
Marlow arrives at central station run by the General Manager, his steamship was sunk and he spent several months to repair it.
There he found Kurtz to whom everybody fears.
After Marlow repairs his ship he moves for a voyage through the native villages along with general manager and other pilgrims.
When their steamer reaches near firewood, it is surrounded by a dense fog and when the fog clears, the ship is attacked by an unseen band of natives who fire arrows towards them.
Marlow frightens the natives with the ship's steam whistle but the African helmsman was killed in the attack.
Marlow and his companions arrive at Kurtz inner station to find him dead, but there they find a Russian trader who informs them that everything was fine there.
There Kurtz has established himself as god and goes on brutal raids in the surrounding territory in search of ivory.
Now Kurtz falls ill and the Russian trader reveals that it was Kurtz who had ordered the attack on them to make them believe that he was dead.
Kurtz is disappeared but Marlow finds him crawling on all fours and convinces him to return to the ship.
Marlow listens to Kurtz talk while sailing and Kurtz entrusts Marlow with a pocket of personal documents with a pamphlet that says: "Exterminates all the brutes".
The steamer breaks down and they stop for the repair.
Kurtz dies uttering his last words: "The Horror! The Horror!"
When Kurtz was dead Marlow cried to his companions "Mistah Kurtz - he dead".
Marlow eventually returns to Europe and goes to see Kurtz's fiancée (intended).
She was still mourning, even though it has been over a year since Kurtz death and she praises him as a paragon of virtue and achievement.
She asked Marlow, what was the last word of Kurtz, but Marlow cannot bring himself to shatter her illusions with the truth.
And instead Marlow lies and tells her that Kurtz's last word was her name.
On the Thames, Marlow tells friends about his youth in Africa.
A company sends him up a great river to fetch Kurtz.
He sees cruelty, waste, and dying workers at the stations.
Kurtz, once a gifted agent, has become cruel and is dying.
Kurtz dies saying the horror, and Marlow later faces the Intended.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Awakening

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1899 (Sort Year: 1899)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Kate Chopin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An 1899 novel about Edna Pontellier, who leaves the limits of her marriage and swims out to sea.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1899 is the publication year. She wrote it in 1897 and 1898. Herbert Stone and Company published it on 22 April 1899. Britannica also dates the book to 1899. It was attacked then for its frank picture of a wife's desire.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edna Pontellier (A wife and mother who wakes to her own desires); Leonce Pontellier (Her husband, a New Orleans businessman); Robert Lebrun (The young man she loves at Grand Isle); Adele Ratignolle (A friend who embodies the devoted wife and mother)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edna Pontellier spends a summer at Grand Isle with her husband and children.
She grows close to Robert Lebrun and wants a life of her own.
Back in New Orleans she paints and drifts from her marriage.
Her friend Adele Ratignolle cannot calm her restless mind.
At the end she swims far out to sea and does not return.

items.title: "Love and Life Behind the Purdah" (1901) — Cornelia Sorabji

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Love and Life Behind the Purdah

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1901 (Sort Year: 1901)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cornelia Sorabji

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short stories of Indian women who live behind the curtain of purdah.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1901 is correct. The title page says London, Freemantle and Co., 1901. Lord Hobhouse dated his letter October 1901. Some catalogues print the title as Beyond the Purdah. The printed title is Behind.

fields.value: The Marchioness of Dufferin and Ava (A British public figure who introduces the stories); Lord Hobhouse (A British official whose letter discusses women in purdah and the law)

fields.value:
The book gathers stories of Indian home life, duty, and fear.
Many women in the tales live in purdah and rarely meet outsiders.
The Pestilence at Noonday opens with a lover who may forget the woman he leaves.
Later pieces, such as Behind the Purdah, show custom pressing on women.
Lord Hobhouse's letter says secluded women need women who know the law.
The Marchioness of Dufferin wrote a short note of praise at the front.

items.title: "The Lake of Palms" (1902) — Romesh Chunder Dutt

fields.label: Work Title

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Romesh Chunder Dutt

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His English version of a Bengali story of Indian home life.

Dutt first wrote social romances in Bengali.
Bankim Chandra Chatterji had urged that work.
The Lake of Palms is one of those stories put into English.
The subtitle calls it a story of Indian domestic life.
Domestic life here means home and family life.
London published the English book in 1902.
A second edition followed in 1903.

Peter is one of four rabbits, with Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cottontail.
Their mother warns them not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden.
Peter goes in, eats the vegetables, and is chased.
He loses his blue jacket and shoes and hides where he can.
He escapes and comes home ill, while his sisters enjoy supper.

items.title: "The Jewel of Seven Stars" (1903) — Bram Stoker

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

Margaret Trelawny summons Malcolm Ross with a night message: come at once.
Her father, Abel Trelawny, is found unconscious and strangely wounded.
Margaret bears the likeness of the ancient queen Tera.
Trelawny plans a great experiment to restore Tera to life.
The 1903 ending is grim.
The 1912 book cuts a chapter and ends more gently.

items.title: "The Way of All Flesh" (1903) — Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Way of All Flesh

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1903 (Sort Year: 1903)

fields.value: Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A family novel about a clergyman's son who escapes a cruel religious home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He died in 1902. Gutenberg dates the writing from 1873 to 1884. Britannica says the book came out in 1903, long after it was written. Posthumous means printed after the writer died. The database publication year 1903 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ernest Pontifex (The hero, based on Butler as a young man); Theobald Pontifex (Ernest's father, a strict clergyman); Christina Pontifex (Ernest's mother, loyal to that harsh home); Edward Overton (The narrator, close to Butler's mature view); Alethea Pontifex (A kind aunt who helps Ernest toward freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story follows four generations of the Pontifex family.
Ernest grows up under Theobald, a harsh clergyman father.
His mother Christina supports that strict religious house.
Ernest becomes a minister, then goes to prison after a naive error.
A bad marriage follows, and he slowly breaks the family pattern.
Overton, the narrator, speaks with the older Butler's voice.

items.title: "The Playboy of the Western World" (1907) — J. M. Synge

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Playboy of the Western World

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1907 (Sort Year: 1907)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: J. M. Synge

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Mayo village cheers a young man who claims he killed his father.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written in 1905-1906. First acted at the Abbey Theatre on 26 January 1907. The database year 1907 is right for that opening. The crowd rioted at the first nights.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Christy Mahon (A shy young stranger who boasts that he killed his father); Pegeen Mike (The publican's daughter, who loves the story and then rejects the deed); Old Mahon (Christy's father, who walks in alive with a wounded head); Widow Quin (A sharp local widow who competes for Christy's attention)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Christy Mahon enters a pub in County Mayo and says he killed his father.
The villagers, led by Pegeen Mike, treat the shy stranger as a hero.
Christy grows bold, wins the village games, and plans to marry Pegeen.
Old Mahon arrives alive, with a bandaged head from Christy's blow.
When Christy strikes his father again in public, the crowd turns on him.
Pegeen rejects him.
Christy leaves proud of his own story, and Pegeen laments.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Intermediate Sex

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1908 (Sort Year: 1908)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Edward Carpenter

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose study of men and women whose feelings fall between the two usual sexes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1908 is the first edition of this book, from Sonnenschein in London and Clarke in Manchester. The title essay had already appeared in the 1906 edition of Love's Coming of Age. A second edition came in 1909. A third edition came in 1912. Do not take 1912 as the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Carpenter (The essayist who argues for understanding of the intermediate sex)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The 1908 book collects papers written over many earlier years.
Carpenter says many people stand between male and female in temperament.
He uses the words Uranian and intermediate sex for this group.
He argues that they are not simply ill, and that society should understand them.
He gives them a social role as interpreters between men and women.
An appendix adds quotations from other writers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hind Swaraj

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1909 (Sort Year: 1909)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mahatma Gandhi

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dialogue in which Gandhi defines swaraj as self rule, not mere expulsion of the English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written in Gujarati in November 1909. Chapters ran in Indian Opinion on 11 and 18 December 1909. Gandhi's English translation, Indian Home Rule, was published in 1910.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Editor (Gandhi's voice, a newspaper editor who argues for self rule); The Reader (A young Indian who questions the Editor and wants a Western path)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gandhi wrote the Gujarati text on a ship from England to South Africa in November 1909.
A Reader and an Editor debate modern civilization, railways, doctors, and lawyers.
The Editor says India is harmed by copying British machine life.
He defines swaraj as learning to rule oneself, and he calls passive resistance soul force.
The Gujarati serial appeared in December 1909. Gandhi's own English version came out in 1910.

items.title: "English Gitanjali" (November 1912 (English, India Society of London)) — Rabindranath Tagore

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: English Gitanjali

fields.value: November 1912 (English, India Society of London) (Sort Year: 1912)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Rabindranath Tagore

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: This is Tagore's own English book of prayer poems, made from his Bengali songs.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Bengali Gitanjali is 1910. The Nobel Prize was given in 1913 for this English book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A humble singer who offers songs to God)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tagore first wrote Gitanjali in Bengali in 1910.
He then made English prose versions of many of these poems.
He added poems from other Bengali books too.
W. B. Yeats wrote the introduction.

fields.label: Work Title

fields.label: Author

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1918 book, edited by Robert Bridges, that first collected Hopkins's mature poems.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Robert Bridges edited the first collected Poems in 1918, long after Hopkins died in 1889. A second edition followed in 1930.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hopkins died in 1889 with his best poems still in manuscript.
His friend Robert Bridges kept the copies.
In 1918 Bridges published Poems with notes.
The book includes The Wreck of the Deutschland and God's Grandeur.
It also prints The Windhover, Pied Beauty, and the later sonnets.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Last Poems

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1922 (Sort Year: 1922)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: A. E. Housman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A second book of lyrics, published in 1922 while Housman was still alive.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Project Gutenberg both date Last Poems to 1922. He was alive then. More Poems is a different book, edited by his brother Laurence after the 1936 death. The database year 1922 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A voice facing death, nature, and a godless world)

Housman gathered strong poems left out of the earlier book.
Many of them had been written years before 1922.
He published the book in 1922.
The poems still face death, soldiers, and a cold world.
One poem honors hired soldiers who held a breaking line.
The book sold quickly, unlike the slow start of A Shropshire Lad.

items.title: "An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth" (1927) — Mahatma Gandhi

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1927 (Sort Year: 1927)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Mahatma Gandhi

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Gandhi tells the story of his moral experiments, from childhood to his public work.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Serialised in the Gujarati Navajivan from 1925 to 1929. The English version also ran in Young India. English book volume one is 1927 and volume two is 1929. The database span matches these years. The catalog calls it fiction, but it is a life story in prose.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mohandas Gandhi (The narrator, telling his own experiments with truth); Kasturba Gandhi (His wife, whom he married when both were still children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He recalls childhood in Gujarat, his marriage as a boy, and his fear and small lies.
He studies law in London and keeps his vow to avoid wine, women, and meat.
In South Africa he faces racism and builds satyagraha.
He returns to India and links his inner search for truth with political action.
He says he worships God as Truth, and that ahimsa is the way to Truth.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Elaine Showalter

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 0 (Sort Year: 0)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Elaine Showalter

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1941 - )
Elaine Showalter is an American literary critic, feminist and writer on cultural and social issues.
She is one of the founders of feminist literary criticism in United States academia developing concept and practices of Gynocritics.
Showalter is a specialist in Victorian Literature.
Her most innovative work in this field is in Madness and Hysteria in Literature specifically in women's writing and in the portrayal of female characters.
Showalter's best known works are.
Toward a feminist Poetics (1979)
The Female Malady: Women, Madness and English Culture (1830 - 1986)
Sexual Anarchy: Gender and Culture at the fin de Siecle (1990)
Hystories: Hysterical Epidemics and Modern Media (1997)
Inventing Herself: Claiming a Feminist Intellectual Heritage (2001)
Showalter's book Inventing Herself (2001), a survey of feminist icons was the culmination of a lengthy interest in communicating the importance of understanding Feminist Tradition.
In "Towards a Feminist Poetics" Showalter traces the history of women's literature suggesting that it can be divided into three phases 1. Feminine Phase (1840 - 1880)

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Harold Bloom

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 0 (Sort Year: 0)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Harold Bloom

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1930 - )
Harold Bloom is an American literary critic.
He has written several books of literary criticism and edited hundreds of anthologies for Chelsea Housing Publishing Firm.
Hart Crane's Collected Poems inspired his lifelong fascination with poetry.
Bloom began his writing career by defending the reputations of the High Romantics through a sequence of highly regarded monographs beginning with his Doctoral Dissertation on P. B. Shelley, W. B. Yeats, and Wallace Stevens, against neo-Christian critic influenced by such writers as T. S. Eliot who becomes a recurring intellectual foil.
His first book 'Shelley's Myth Making' charged many contemporary critics with sheer carelessness in their reading of Shelley.
He once in an interview said to Paris Review that "I am using Gnostic in a very broad way. I am nothing if not Jewish. … I really am a product of Yiddish culture."
W. B. Yeats challenged the conventional critical view of his poetic career.
Bloom set out the basic principles of his new approach to criticism: "Poetic Influence as I conceive it is a variety of melancholy or the anxiety - principle".
"School of Resentment" is a term coined by Bloom.
"Flight to Lucifer" is the only novel by Harold Bloom.
Bloom's book - "The Anxiety of Influence" drew upon the examples of 17th and 18th century poets about their ability to match the achievements of their predecessors. He dedicated it to six different revisionary ratios (Viz.- Clinamen, Tessera, Kenosis, Askesis…)
Bloom drew a sharp distinction between Strong Poets, who perform "strong misreading" of their precursors and "Weak Poets" who simply repeat the ideas of their precursors as though following a kind of Doctrine.
Bloom described this process in terms of a sequence of "Revisionary Ratios" through which each strong poets passes in the course of his career. In this book he developed the idea of Misreading.
Bloom's fascination with fantasy novel A Voyage to Arcturus by David Lindsay led him to take a brief break from criticism in order to compose the sequel of Lindsay's novel as the only fiction book of Bloom entitled "The Flight to Lucifer" (only novel by Bloom).
In American Religion (1992), Bloom surveyed the major varieties of Protestant and Post-protestant religious faiths that originated in the United States.
In 1994, Bloom published, The Western Canon, a survey of the major literary works of Europe and the Americans since 14th century focusing on 26 works he considered sublime and representatives of their nation and of Western canon.
In his 1998 survey, Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human, Bloom provides an analysis of each of Shakespeare's 38 plays, 24 of which are masterpieces.
The two paragons of Bloom's theory are Sir John Falstaff of Henery IV and Hamlet, whom Bloom sees as representing self-satisfaction and self-loathing respectively.
He consolidated his work on the western canon with the publication of How to Read and Why (2000) and Genius: A Mosaic of One hundred Exemplary Creative Minds (2003).
In 2003, Hamlet: Poem Unlimited was published.
He began a book under the working title Living Labyrinth centering on Shakespeare and Whitman was published in 2011, as Anatomy of Influence: Literature as a Way of Life.
Harold Bloom dedicated his "Anxiety of Influence" to W. K. Wimsatt.
In Omens of Millennium, Bloom posits that America is Obsessed with angels prophesies and other millennial omens and that Americans are ironically, Gnostic without knowing it.
Blooms Doctoral dissertation is "Shelly's Myth Making".

fields.value:
(1819-1891)
James Russel Lowell was an American Romantic poet, critic, editor and diplomat.
He is associated with Fireside Poets.
He published his first collection of poetry in 1841.
He gained notoriety in 1848, with the publication of A Fable for Critics, a book length poem satirizing contemporary critics and poets. The same year he published "The Biglow Papers" (1848) which increased his fame.
He became the editor of "The Atlantic Monthly" (1857).
Henry James referred him as - "Conspicuously American" and "One of the strongest and manliest of our writers".
He became the god father of Virginia Woolf.
Greenleaf Whither praised Lowell as "Our New Theocritus".
His poem "The Present Crisis", an early work that addressed the national crisis over slavery leading up to the civil war.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jules Verne was a French novelist of science fiction (stories that mix science with adventure).
He was born in Nantes in 1828 and died in Amiens in 1905. He studied law, wrote for the theatre, and later left the stock market to write full time.
His Extraordinary Voyages (imagined trips full of science) were translated into English.
He joins a careful scientific idea to a fast adventure plot.
The series name Voyages extraordinaires means Extraordinary Voyages.
The series began in 1863 with Five Weeks in a Balloon.
Early books trust exploration. Later books worry about dangerous machines.
English readers met him in translation, not in a British novel tradition.

fields.value: Pearl S. Buck

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1802 - 1973)
Pearl Sydenstricker Buck also known by her Chinese name Sai Zhenzhu was an American writer and novelist.
As the daughter of missionaries Buck spent most of her life before 1934 in China.
Her novel The Good Earth (1931) won the Pulitzer Prize.
In 1938, she was awarded the Nobel Prize in literature for her rich and truly epic description of Peasant Life in China and for her biographical masterpieces.
She was the first American woman to win the Nobel Prize in literature.
Her novel East Wind: West Wind appeared in 1934, and in the same year she left China forever.
During the "Cultural Revolution" Buck as a prominent American writer of Chinese village life was denounced as an "American Cultural Imperialist".
Her 1962 novel "Satan Never Sleeps" described the communist tyranny in China.
She died of lung cancer and she designed her own tombstone.
In 1938, when she got Nobel Prize in her speech to the academy she took as her topic "The Chinese Novel". She explained - "I am an American by birth and by ancestry but my earliest knowledge of story of how to tell and write stories came to me in China".
Her important Chinese novels are.
Romance of the three Kingdoms.
All Men are Brothers.
Dream of the Red Chamber.
She concluded that in China "The novelists did not have the task of creating art but of speaking to the people". And like the Chinese novelist she concluded "I have been taught to want to write for these people. If they are reading their magazines by the million, then I want my stories there rather than in magazines read only by a few".
The biography of her parents is entitled Fighting Angel and The Exile.
In 1964, to support kids who were not eligible for adoption, she established The Pearl S. Buck Foundation.
She once said that "Sexual allegations were 'a bunch of downright lies'." Important Works of Pearl S. Buck 1. My Several Worlds: A Personal Record (1954)

fields.value: Sinclair Lewis

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1885 - 1951)
Harry Sinclair Lewis was an American novelist, short-story writer and playwright.
In 1930, he became the first writer from the United States to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, which was awarded "for his vigorous and graphic art of description and his ability to create with wit, humour and new types of character".
He was known for his insightful and critical views of American capitalism and materialism between the wars.
He has been honoured by the U.S. Postal Service with a postage stamp in the Great American series.
Lewis's first published book was "Hike and Aeroplane", a Tom Swift style potboiler that appeared in 1912 under the pseudonym Tom Graham.
His first serious novel Our Mr. Wrenn: The Romantic Adventures of a Gentleman (1914) followed by The Trial of the Hawk: A Comedy of Seriousness of Life (1915) and The Job (1917).
Innocents: A Story for Lover an expanded version of a serial story that had originally appeared in Woman's Home Companion in 1917.
'Free Air' another refurnished serial story was published in 1919.
Lewis followed up this first great success with Babbitt (1922), a novel that satirized the American Commercial Culture and boostering (act of boosting). The story was set in the fictional Midwestern town Zenith, Winnemac, a setting to which Lewis would return in future novel including Gideon Planish and Dodsworth (1929).
He continued his success in 1920's with Arrowsmith (1925), a novel about the challenges faced by an idealistic doctor. It was awarded Pulitzer Prize in 1926, but Lewis declined it.
The next book of Lewis is Elmer Gantry (1927) which depicted an evangical minister as deeply hypocritical.
After winning the Nobel Prize in Literature, Lewis wrote 11 more novels. The best one among these is It can't Happen Here (1935), a novel about the election of a fascist to the American presidency.
Lewis's final novel World So Wide (1951) was published posthumously.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(1938 -)
Stanley Eugene Fish is an American literary theorist, legal scholar, author and public intellectual.
Fish is a major figure associated with Postmodernism, instead he views himself as an advocate of Anti Foundationalism,.
He is also viewed as being a major influence in the rise and development of Reader Response Theory.
He started his career as Medievalist.
His first book was on the late medieval/ early Renaissance poet John Skelton.
Fish revealed in his partly biographical essay Milton, Thou Shouldst be Living at this Hour that he came to Milton by accident.
Fish is best known for his analysis of Interpretive Communities an off shot of Reader-Response Criticism.
Terry Eagleton, a prominent British Marxist, excoriates Fish's "discreditable epistemology" as 'Sinister'.
Camille Paglia, author of "Sexual Personae" and "Public Intellectual", denounced Fish as Totalitarian Tinkerbell.
The concept of "Interpretive Community" was developed by him.
